reposition.c: REPOSIT ION, in Grammar, is an Inde - clinable Word, by which a Noun and Verb are joined together, in order to signifie the Cause of any thing, the Time, Place, Conjunction, Pri - vation, &c. ’ Tis called Proposition, because ’ tis most frequently in the Latin Tongue placed be - fore other Words j and this either separately, as Ad patrem ', or conjunctively, as Admirer.

run.c: RUN I F E ROU S - Trees or Shrubs, are such whose Fruit is pretty large and soft, with a Stone in the middle; in this kind the Flower adheres to the bottom of the Base of the Fruit.

RUN of a Ship, is so much of her Hull as is al - ways under Water, growing thinner and canker by degrees from the Floor Timbers to the Stern Poll:. This is alio calied her Way aft ward on and they fay a Ship hath a good Run when ’ tis long, and that the Water passes cleverly to her Rudder, her TucR not lying too low, which is of great Importance to her Sailing; for if the Water don ’ t come strongly to her Rudder, by reason of her being Built too broad below, fire can never Steer well; and a Ship that can ’ t Steer well, Can ’ t keep a good Wind, and will have no frefli way through the Sea, but will be Hill falling to Lee - ward, and therefore can ne - ver be a good Sailor. Never thelels, a Ship with at large and good Run, will lose much Stowage, be - cause site is narrow. below.

rabbetting.c: RABBETTING in a Ship, is the letting in of her Planks to the Keel which in the Rake and Ru n of the Ship, is hollowed away, that the Planks may join the Better and Closer, and this hallow - ing away, is called the Rabbet of the Keel.

radialisinterims.c: RADIALIS Interims & Externus, are Muscles of the Wrist, the one serves to bend it, and the other to extend it. Blanchard.

radiation.c: RADIATION, signifies the calling forth of Beams, or Rays of Light; and in Opticks, it is considered as threefold, vi. Direl't, Reflected, and Refracted. See Bay.

radicalmoisture.c: RADICAL Moisture, is a Term used by some, for the Fundamental Juice of the Body, which they will have to Nourilh andPrelerve the Natural heat, as the Oil in a Lamp Prelerves and Feeds the Flame. Blanchard.

radicleaword.c: RADICLE, a Word used by Botanists, to de - note that Part of the Seed of a Plant, which Upon it ’ s vegetation becomes it ’ s Root: This in Corn is that which Malfters upon its shooting forth, call the Come. ’ Tis not easily to be discerned in many Seeds, by the naked Eye: but in that of Fenugreek, ’ tis as big as one of the Lobes: And in the Garden - bean it appears visible on the Separation of the Coats, it is of a White Colour, more glossy than the Main Body, and Hands at the greater End without the Lobes: Therefore this End in setting Seeds, should, always be placed lowermost.

radiusingeometry.c: RADIUS, in Geometry, is the Semi - diameter or half the Diameter of a Circle: See under the Word Circle.

radius.c: RADIUS, is the less Bone of the Cubit, called Focile minus, it is more oblique than the great Bone, called Vena, and is distant a little from it in the middle, where there occurs, a ' small Ligament a - above the Vena, which receives the Radius, and be - low the Radius receives it. The upper part of the Radius is jointed with the outward Process of the Arm by Dlarthrofts ( which fee ); the lower by way of Appendix with the Wrist Bone, at the Middle, Finger. It ’ s upper end isfmall, and the lower thick. The greater Bone of the Leg also is called Radius. Blanchard.

ragguledtheheraldsterm.c: RAGGULED, the Heralds Term for any Ordinary, Ex. gr a Cross whose out Lines are of this Form. He beareth Sable, a Cress Rag - guled Or, by the Name of St ova ay. This differs from Indented, be - came that il regular, and this is not so, but rather ragged. R A I

rainboworiris.c: RAINBOW or Iris, the very Learned and In - genious Mathematician, Mr. Edvoard Halley, in a Discourse de hide in Phil. Tranfacl, Ns, gives the best account, that we have ever had, of the Cause of the various Colours of the Rainbow, and the Solution of their several Phenomena, He tells us there that the Ingenious Des Chartes was the first, that by applying Marhefnaticks towards the Inve - fatigation of this surprising Appearance, ever gave a Theory of the Iris And he found the Laws of Refraction, which the Lucid Rays suffer in passing thro any Diaphanous Bodies: And clearly demons ftrated the Primary Iris to be only the Suns Image, reflected from the Concave surfaces, of an Innumera - ble Quantity offmall spherical drops of falling Rain With this necejjary Circumstance, that those Rays which fell on the Objects, Parallel to each other, should not after one RefleBicn, and two Refractions ? ( viz. At going into the drop, and coming out again ) be dispersed, or made to Diverge, but come lack, again also to the Eye, parallel to each other. He ( lie wed also, that the Colours, in the Rays of Light were produced by those Refradions as they are by palling through a Triangular Glass Prism. The Secondary Iris, he supposes produced by those Rays of the Sun, which fall more Obliquely, but after the fame manner as before, only in thele there are two Refledions before the Sun ’ s Rays re - shaded a second time, and tending towards the Eye, in a parallel Position, can get out from the A - queous Globules, The Magnitude of the Iris, he makes to depend on the degree of Refraction which is different, in different Liquors, or Trans - parent solids: But supposing the Ratio of the Sines of Incidence,. to those of the Refracted Angles, to be in Water as::. to he determined thence the Semi - diameter of the Iris, near enough to Observation, vi. The Primary one to be Degrees Minutes, and the secondary one to be Degrees Minutes, see the Chap, of his Meteors. Mr. Halley observes, that Des Cartes using only a Tentative and Indired Method, in determining his Angles, seems not to underhand the easiness of sol - ving his own Problem. Wherefore because hardly any one hath written well on this Subject since Des Cartes, he shews you there how to determine the Angle by which the Iris is did ant from the opposite Point of the Sun, and the Ratio of the Refraction being given Geo - metrically, or vice versa the Iris being given, td determine the Refradive Power of the Liquor. And first he faith, It is plain from Des Cartes's Demonstrations, That the Primary Iris is made by the Sun ’ s Rays, where the Excels of the two Re shaded Angles above the one of Incidence, is the greatest poilible. And the Secondary Iris is formed by those Rays where the Excess of three Refracted Angles above one of Incidence, is ado the greatest polnble. And thus you may go on to,,, or Iris's, which will all be formed where the; Rays Emerge out of the Watery Cloud after, ",, or Reflecti - ons; but none but the Second will be ordinarily visible in the Heavens, because the Rays of the Suit ft A I - - - R. A I Sun grow at last very much attenuated and weak - ened. Now if you double this greatest possible Excess of the RefraCted Angles above that of Incidence, ( if the Number of Reflections be odd ) it will give the Distance of the Iris from the Point opposite to the Sun. But if the Number " of Reflections be even, then the double of the greatest Refracted Angle, will be the Distance of the Iris from the Sun himself. Now to gain these Greatest Excejfes, having the Refraction of any Liquor, or the Ratio of the Sine of the Angle of Incidence to the Sine of Refracted Angle, you must observe, that the Excess of two Refracted Angles, above one of Incidence, will be Greatest where the Momentaneous Augment or Fluxion of the Angle of Incidence, is precisely dou - ble to the Momentaneous Augment of the Refra - cted Angle. And if there be three Refracted An - gles, the Greatest Excess, will be where the Mo - mentaneous Augment of the Angle of Incidence is Triple of the Moment of the Refracted Angle, and so on, which is sufficiently evident. But in order to find the Angles themselves, Mr. Halley premises the following Lemma. Let there be a Triangle ABC, whose Vertex is I at A its Legs B A and C A, and the Base BC; on which produced, let fall the Perpendicular A D. Then let the Vertical Angle BAC be supposed to be encreased by a Quantity infinitely small, as sup - pose by the Moment C A c: Then drawing the Lines B C d, and c D, they will he only imagine - rily different from BCD and C D. This done, I lay, That if the Legs of the Plane i riangle BAC, for any other ) continuing the fame, the Vertical Angle be imagined to be en - creased by any Infinitely small Moment or Fluxion, then will the Moments of the Angles at the Base, be reciprocally as the Segments of the Base: That is, C B c, is to the Moment of the Angle A C B, or AND:: as C D is to B D. For since the external Angle AND toABC Angle BAC, its Moment must also be equal to the Sum of their Moments, or to C B c C A c: but now because the Triangle AND is right angled at D, A. C may be the Diameter of a Circle, whose Periphery will pass thro ’ A, D, C, and c, and consequently the Angles C A c, CDc being in the fame Segment are equal. So that the Sum of the two Fluxionary Angles C B c, and c D C ( /. e. the external Angle D c d ) will be the Mo - ment of the Angle A C D, or AC B. But those C B c, and D c d, being infinitely small, will be to each other;, as the Sides opposite to them, or as c D or C D is to B D: That is, reciprocally as the Segments of the Base. E. D. If B and C had been both Acute the way of Proof is the fame, all things considered.

rake.c: RAKE of a Ship, is so much of her Hull as over - hangs at both ends of her Keel. That part of it which is before, is called her Hake forward on; and that part which is at the setting on of the Stern - Post, is called her Bp k. e aft - ward on: When a Ship hath but a small Bake forward on, but is built with her Stern too strait up, slie is called Bluff e - headed. The common Proportion for a Ship's Haky for - ward on, is more than a Third, but less than the length of her Keel: and the Bake aft is about a th or th of her Bake before. Tho ’ in this Proportion, there is no certainty, some Nations, and some Carpenters building with longer Bakes than others. A Long Bak ? forward on, if a Ship have also a good fat Bow, gives her a good Way, and helps her to keep a good Find; but then this makes her ape to pitch under Water in a Head - Sea, and besides is a great Stress and Charge to a Ship, because she over - hangs so a Head. therefore the middle Pro - portion is best, considering all things.

raked.c: RAKED liable, a term in Architecture. See table.

ramhead.c: RAM Head, is the Name of a great Block ( a - board a Ship ) belonging to the Fore and Main - Halliards; it hath in it Shivers, into which the Halliards are put, and at its Head the lyes are reeved into an Hole made there for that Purpose.

ramification.c: RAMIFICATION, is a Colledion of final ! Branches issuing out from one large one. Thus in Anatomy, the several Branches of the Aorta or Great Artery, by which the Arterial Blood is convey ’ d to all the extream Parts of the Body, are called the Bamifi cations of the Artery; and when they are ex - ceeding small, they are called Capillary Arteries f which fee.

rammer.c: RAMMER, is a Staff with a round piece of Wood at one end, in order to drive home the Pou - der to the Breech of the Great Gun, as also the Shot and the Wad, which keeps the Shot from rowling out. At the other end of these R / wiram, areulually rolled in a certain Piece of Ships - skin fitted to the Bore of the Piece, in order to clear her after Are has been discharged: And this is called Spunging the Piece.

rampant.c: RAMPANT: The Term in Heraldry for a Lion, or any Beast of Prey, in a Posture of Climb - ing, or Standing upright on his hinder Legs, and rearing up his Fore - feet. T ’ is different from Sali - ent, which is a Posture not so ered. See Salient.

rampartinfortification.c: RAMPART, in Fortification, is the mass of Earth which is railed about the Body of any Place, to covert it from Great Shot, and consists of several Bastions and Curtains having its Parapet, Plat - form, interior and. exterior Talus, and Berme, as alio sometimes a Stone Wall, and then they fay it is Lined. he Soldiers continually keep Guard here, and Pieces of Artillery are Planted for the Defence of the Place. The FI eight of the Bpmpart must not exceed three Fathom, as being sufficient to cover the Houses from the Batteries of the Cannon: Neither ought its Thickness to be above teu or twelve, unless more Earth be taken out of the Ditch, than can be otherway bellowed. The Bfmparts of Half - Moons are the better for being low, that the small Fire of the Defendants may the better read ) the Bottom of the Ditch; but yet R U P et it mud be so high, as not to be commanded, by the Covert - way.

ramusanterior.c: RAMUS Anterior, Sc. Verne Subcut ance, is a Branch of the Subcutaneous Vein, ( which takes its Name from its ( hallow running just under the Skin ) and is it self a Branch of the Basilica it goes un - der the Muscles of the Vena to the little Finger, where it joins a Branch of the Cephalica.

ramuspojlerior.c: RAMUS Pojlerior, another Branch of the Sub - cutaneous Vein of the Arm, running near the Elbow; it fends out a Branch which goes to the Wrist, then it unites with the Cephalica Interior, and forms the Mediana.

random.c: RANDOM - S & ?, is a Shot made when the Muzzle of a Gun is raised above the Horizontal Line, and is not designed to Shoot directly or Point - blank. The utmost Random of any Piece, is about ten times as far as the Bullet will go Point - blank; and the Bullet will go far theft when the Piece is mounted to about Degrees above the Level - Range. The Distance of the Random is reckoned from the Plat - form to the Place where the Ball fxrft Grazes.

rangeatermingunnery.c: RANGE, a Term in Gunnery, ( signifying the Line a Shot goes in from the Mouth of the Piece, If the Bullet go in a Line parallel to the Horizon, that is called the Right or Level - Range if the Gun be mounted to Degr. then will the Ball have the highest or utmost Range, and so proportionably all others between Degr. and, are called the Intermediate Ranges.

ranges.c: RAN GES, in a Ship, are two pieces of Timber going a - cross from Side to Side; one aloft on the Fore - Cafile a little abaft the Fore - mast; and the other in the Beak - Head before the Wouldings of the Bovo - Sprit. That in the Fore - Castle, is fattened into the Timbers of the ShipVSides, and hath two Knees about the Middle, on either side the Fore - Matt, fattened to the Deck and the Timber, in which the Top - Sail - Sheets run in a Shiver: In it also are fe - veral Wooden Pins to belay the Fore - bowling, the Fore - Tack, and the Fore - loof Hook. That in the Beak - Head lies in the form of the other, and hath the Sprit - Sail, and Sprit - Sail - Top - Sail - Sheets and Ropes belayed about its Pins.

ranger.c: RANGER, is a Sworn Officer of the Forest, whereof there are Twelve: His Business chiefly consists in three Points; To Walk daily through his Charge, to fee, hear, and inquire, as well of Trespasses, as Trefpalfers in his Balywick; To drive the Beads of the Forests, both of Venery and Chafe, out of the Disforefted into the So - rested Lands; And, To present all Trespasses of the Forest. This Rangtr is made by the King ’ s Letters - Patent, and hath yearly Pension our of the Exchequer.

ranulares.c: RANULARES, are those Branches of the enter - nal Jugular Veins which run to the Tongue, and are very apparent under it.

rapineinlaw.c: RAPINE, in Law; to take a thing in private against the Owner s will, is properly Theft; but to take it openly, or by violence, is Rapine.

rapsody.c: RAPSODY, originally signifies a Connexion to - gether, or a Repetition of a vast Number of He - roick Verses, such as those of Homer, &c. But now we usually understand by it, a long, tedious, impertinent spinning out of a Discourse to little or no purpose or benefit to the Reader.

raptuhxredis.c: RAPTU Hxredis - is a Writ lying for the taking away of ah Heir holding iri Socage j of wfiic there are tWo forts; one when the Heir is Mar - ried, the other when he is not. Of both these, see the Reg. Orig. Sol..

rarebodies.c: RARE Bodies, are such as have more space, or take up more room in proportion to their Matter, than other Bodies do.

rarefacientia.c: RAREFACIENTIA, ratifying Remedies, are such as by difijpating a little the Vapours and Hu - hours make the Pores of Bodies larger. Blanchard.

rarefaction.c: RAREFACTION, of any natural Body, is when it takes up more Dimenfioris or a larger Space than it had before. There are three ways of Explicating of Rare - fall ion. . That of the Arifiotelians, which is called the Rigorous way; who suppose the fame Body doth not only obtain a greater space in Rarefaction, but also adequately fill it; and acquires larger Semen - signs, without either having any Pores or Vacuities between its Corpuscles, or admitting any other Body or subtil Matter to be joined with them. . That of the Cartesians, which was also the Opinion of many of the Old Philosophers, who assert, That in Rarefaction the Pores of the rare - fied Body are dilated, and replenished with some fine subtil and ethereal Substance, which infinu - ates it self freely into the Interstices between its disjoined Particles. . That of the Atomijls of Vacuifls, who suppose the Parts of the rarefied Body to be disjoined and removed farther from each other, and yet no other Body ( necessarily ) comes in between them. See this explained under Air.

rasantlineofdefence.c: RASANT Line of Defence, in Fortification, is a Line drawn from the Point of the Bastion along the Face, and prolonged till it come to the Curtain, and therefore ( hews how much of the Curtain will clear or scour the Face. This is called also the Second Fiank, the Hanking, or Stringent Line.

raspatoriumorscalprumraforium.c: RASPATORIUM, or Scalprum Raforium, is & Chirurgeon ’ s Instrument to scrape or ( have filthy or fcaby Bones with.

ratch.c: RATCH, is a fort, of a Wheel of large Fangs, that runneth Concentrical to the Dial - Wheel, and ferveth to lift up the Dentes every Flour, and make the Clock strike: and are by some called Rash.

ratchet.c: RATCHET, in a Watch, are thefmall Teeth at the Bottom of the Fusy or Barrel, that flop it in winding up.

rate.c: RATE - Ty, is when Sheep of other Cattle are kept in a Pari ( h for a less time than a Year, the Owner must pay Tythe for them pro rata, accord - ing to the Custom of the Place.

RATE of a Ship of War is its distil & ion as to Bigness and Capacity and this is usually accoun - ted by the Length and Breadth of the Gun - deck, the Number of Tuns they contain, and the Num - ber of Men and Guns they carry. For such Men of War as have their Gun - decks from to Feet in length, and from to Foot broad: That contain from to r z Tuns, that have from to Men, and carry from to to Guns: We reckon of the Fir ft Rate. Second Rate Ships, have their Gun - decks from to Feet long j and from to broad: Contain from to I z Tuns and carry from to Men, and from to Guns. Third Rates have their Gun - decks from to Feet in length from to Foot broad: They contain from to Tuns carry from to Men, and from to Guns. Fourth Rates are in length on the Gun - deck from to Foot, and from to broad: They contain from to - Tuns carry from ( to Men and from to Guns. Fifth Rates have their Gun - decks from to Foot long, and from to Feet broad: Contain from to Tuns carry from to Men and from to Guns. Sixth Rates have their Gun - decks from to Feet long, and from to Feet broad: They contain from to: Tuns; carry from to Ho Men, and from to Guns. Our New - built Ships are much larger, as well as better, than the Old ones of the fame Rate; and that is the Reason of the double Numbers all a - long the larger of which express the Proportions of t - he New - built Ships.

ratificationalaw.c: RATIFICATION, a Law - Term, used for the Confirmation of a Clerk in a Prebend, &c, sort merly given him by the Bisliop, &c. where the Right of Patronage is doubted to be in the King.

ratio.c: RATIO. When two Quantities are compared one with another in respect of their Greatness or Smallness. That Comparison is called Ratio, and signifies the Rate, Reason or Proportion in Quantity, that one hath to the other. Tho ’ ( ome, indeed, confine Ratio or Reason only to Numbers, and call it Proportion, when it is between,, or more Numbers or Quantities. But the Word Proper - tion is often used instead of Ratio or Reason, tq express the Comparison of one single Quantity to another, by very good Authors. - B RATIO - R E C

ratiocinationarational.c: RATIOCINATION, a Rational way of Ar - going.

rationabili.c: RATIONABILI parte bonorum, is a Writ that lies for the Wife against the Executors of her Hus - band, denying her the Third part of her Husband ’ s Goods.

rationabilibus.c: RATION ABILIBUS divifis, is a Writ that lies where two Lords, in divers Towns, liave Seignio - ries joining together, for him that fendeth his Waste by little and little to have been encroached upon, against the other that hath Encroached, thereby to rectifie their Bounds. And this is a King of Ju - Jlicies, and may be removed by a Pone, out of the County to the Common Bench. By the Civilians It is called Judicium finium Pegundorum.

rationalquantities.c: RATIONAL Quantities. Any Quantity being proposed, ( Tor which we may always put i. ) and which Euclid ( Book i o. ) calls Rational, there may be Infinite others which are Commensurable, or In - commensurable to it, and that either Simple, or in Power. Now, all such as are Commensurable any how to the given Quantity, he calls Rational Quan - tities, and all the others Irrational.

ratlines.c: RATLINES, ( or as the Seamen call them, Pyit - things ) are those Lines which make the Ladder Steps, to get up the Shrouds and Puttocks; there - fore they are called the Rattlings of the Shrouds.

ravelininfortification.c: RAVELIN, in Fortification, is a small Trian - gular Work composed only of two Faces, which make a Saliant Angle, without any Flanks, It is generally raised before the Curtains or Counterscarp, and commonly called a Half - Moon by the Sol - diers. A Pavelin is like the Point of a Bastion with Flanks cut oft; The reason of its being placed be - fore a Curtain, is to cover the opposite Flanks of the two next Bastions. ’ Tis used also to cover a Bridge or a Gate j and ’ tis always placed without the Moat. What the Engineers call a ravelin, the Soldiers generally call a I - Ialf - Moon, which lee.

raycommon.c: RAY Common, is a right Line drawn from the Point of the Concourse of the two Optical Axes, through the Middle of the right Line which pass. set by the Centre of the Pupil of the Eye. '

raydirect.c: RAY Direct, is that which is carried from a Point of the visible Object directly to the Eye, through one and the fame Medium.

rayofincidence.c: RAY of Incidence, or Incident pay, in Catoptricky, is a right Line which falls from some Point of an Object: upon the Surface of the Looking - Glass or polished Metal.
RAY of Incidence, or Incident Pay, in Diop - trick, is the Pay of Light which goes in a right Line from a certain Point of the visible Objects in one Medium, until it meet with a Second Me - dium.

rayinopticky.c: RAY, in Opticky, is a Line imagined to pass from the Eye toward the Object, or from the Ob - jed: toward the Eye, and is called a Visual Pay. But there is also a Pyramid of Pays, which strike the Tunica Petina of the Eye, and are broken or re - fracted in the Chrystalline.

rayprincipal.c: RAY Principal, in Perspective, is the perpen - dicular Distance between the Eye and the Vertical Plane, or Table, as the French call it.

rayofreflection.c: RAY of Reflection, is the right Line whereby the pefiebiion is made.

ray.c: RAY of fleer action, or Broken Pay, is a right Line whereby the pay of Incidence changeth its re - titude, or is broken in traversing the Second Me - dium, whether it be thicker or thinner.

raysorbeams.c: RAYS, or Beams of the Sun, or Pays of Light, are either according to the Atomical Hypothesis, those very minute Particles or Corpuscles of Mat - ter, which continually issuing out of the Sun, do thrust on one another all around in Physically short Lines j ( und that this is the right Opinion ) many Experiments do evince, particularly the Incompa - table Sir. i / Newton about Light and Colours ' ( or else as the Cartesians assert, they are made by the Addon of the Luminary on the Contiguous either and Air, and so are propagated every way in strait Lines, through the Pores of the Medium.

raysconvergent.c: RAYS Convergent, are those which going from divers Points of the Object, incline towards one and the fame Point tending to the Eye,

raysdivergent.c: RAYS Divergent, are those which going from a Point of the visible Object:, are dispersed, and continually depart one from another, according as they are removed from the Object:.

raysparallel.c: RAYS Parallel, are those that keep an equal Distance from the visible Object to the Eye, which is supposed to be infinitely remote from the Object.

razantlineofdefence.c: RAZANT Line of Defence. See Pyfant Line of Defence.

reach.c: REACH, is the Distance between any Points of Land, that lie in a right Line one from ano - ther.

rear.c: REAR - GwW, is that part of an Army which follows the main Body, to hinder and flop De - ( enters.
REAR - Half - Files, are the Hindermost Ranks of a Battallion when it is drawn up deep.

REAR - JLAze of an Army encamped; is the second Line: this lies about or Yards di - stant from the first Line, which is called the Front Line. Sometimes there is a Third, which is called I the Reserve Line.

REAR - Rank, is the last Rank of a Battallion when drawn up. REA - RE, A SON or Eefon, and, as fame Teem to.. write it mere truly, fifing Pieces, are those Pieces of Timber which lie tinder the Beams on the Brick or Timber in the Side of a House.

reasoninmathematicks.c: REASON, in Mathematicks, the fame with Proportion, ’ tis better called by the Latin Name Patio ( which fee ) to avoid confounding it with the common signification of the Word Peafon. RE ATTACHMENT, is a Second Attachment of him that was formerly attached and dismissed the Court without Day, as by the not coming of the Justices, or some such Casualty. And is said to be either General or Special. General Pe - attach - ment, is where a Man is reattached for his Appear - rance upon all Writs of Assize lying against him: Special Pe - attachment, must be for one or more certain.

rebusses.c: REBUSSES, are in Heraldry such Coats of Arms as bear an Allusion to the Sirname of the Person, as Coneys for Ccnisby, Cups for Butler, Castles for Caftleton: And such Bearings are very ancient.

rebutterincommon.c: REBUTTER, in Common - Law, when a Man grants Land to the use of himself, and the Issue of his Body, to another in Feu with Warranty: And the Donee leafeth out his Lands to a Third for Years; the Heir of the Donor impleadeth, the Tenant alledging, That the Land was in Tail to him: The Donee comes in, and by virtue of the Warranty made by the Donor, repelleth the Heir, because tho ’ the Land was Intailed to him, yet he is Heir to the Warrantor like wife; and this is cal -, led a Ppbutter. And if I grant to my Tenant, to hold Sine impetitione vasti, and afterwards Implead him for Waste made; he may debar me of this Aiftion, by ( hewing my Grant, and this is also a Pebutter.

recaption.c: RECAPTION, is a Second Distress of one for - merly distrained for the fame Cause, and also. du - ring the Plea grounded on the former Distress: It like wife R EC R E C likewise signifies a Writ lying for the Party thus Distrained.

receiver.c: RECEIVER is commonly used in the Civil Law in an ill Sense, for one that receives stolen Goods, and conceals them j but when annexed to other words, ’ tis used in a very goo cl one j as the
RECEIVER of the Fines, which is an Officer that receives the Money of - all such as compound with the Crown upon an Original Writ in the Court of Chancery. There is also the

receptaculumchyli.c: RECEPTACULUM Chyli, was first found our by Pecquet, A. D., ’ tis a Cavity into which all the Lacteal Veins empty themselves: it is of a Vesicular Substance, which is thicker in Men than In Beasts, but the Cavity is larger in Beasts than Men: Out of it goes the Ductus Thoracicus; which fee.

recession.c: RECESSION of the Equinoxes, Is the going back of the Equinoctial Points every Year about Seconds. The Reason of which is, That the Axis of the Earth, after many Annual Revolutions round the Sun, really deviates from that Parade - list, which it seems to keep with it self all the time of one Annual Revolution: By this Aberra - tion it describes a Conical Superficies and the Earths Equator moving round the Sun, together with the Earths Axis, the InterfeClions of the Cele - still Equator with the Ecliptick, will run back, or move in Antecedentia, as will all other Points of the Ecliptick, ( as well as those Equinoctial ones. ) And therefore the Signs or Fix ’ d Stars that make the. Zodiacal Constellations, will appear to move forward, or in Confequentia as they now seem to have done by the Quantity of a whole Sign; for which Reason, you find the Picture of the Ram painted on our Globes at the beginning of the Sign Taurus, &c. Dr. Gregory in his Excellent Aftronomia Physica & Geometrica, Prop. LXIV. Lib.. makes the Pro - late Spheroidical Figure of the Earth, to be the Primary Occafioniof this Recefilon of the Equi - I noCtial Points and withal slews that the Earths Axis in every Annual Revolution round the Sun, twice changes its Inclination to the Ecliptick, and as often returns again to its former Position.

recidivusmorbus.c: RECIDIVUS Morbus, a Relapse, is when the Morbifick Matter, that was left in the first Di -. temper, begins to work and ferment again.

recipientsorreceivers.c: RECIPIENTS, or Receivers, are those Vdfels, which in Distillation, are Luted to the Beak, or Nose of Alimbeck, Retort, &c. to receive the Matter which is raised or forced over the Helm by the Fire. That Glass also which is exhausted of Air by Mr. Boyle ’ s Air - Sum, and within which any Animal or other Bodies, are included to make Ex - periments upon, is by him usually called the Receiver.

reciprocalfiguresingeometry.c: RECIPROCAL Figures in Geometry, are such as have the Antecedents and Consequents of the Ratio in both Figures, Here A: B:: C: i. e. i::::. A ', That is, as much longer as the Side A in the first ReCtangle, is than B:: so njuch deeper is the Side C in the second ReCtangle, than the Sde D in the first; and consequently the Length of one is compensated by the Depth of the other; and also as the Side A is i longer than the Side C, so the Side B is one th longer than D. Wherefore the ReCtangles must needs be equal. And this is the Foundation of theCathoiick. The - rem That the ReBangle of the Extr earns must al - ways be equal to that of the Means: And consequents ly the Reason of the Rule of Three, or Golden Rule, for suppose there was given any three Numbers or Quantities Geometrically proportional, as A, B, and C, and that it Were required to find a fourth D proportional to them. Since it is that A: B:: C: D, therefore A D B C C, and consequently D, that is, the Fourth Term is equal to the Quotient of Second, multiplied by the Third Term, divided by the First: Or thus in Numbers. Suppose given,, and j required a fourth Proportional. Now as i:::: Q, But ia Q. x b Therefore Q. (:. by dividing both x Sides by i.

reciprocalproportion.c: RECIPROCAL Proportion, is when in four Numbers, the Fourth is Idler than the Second, by so much as the Third is greater than the First, and vic & R E C R E C vice versa; on which is founded the Inverse of In - direct Rule of Three, thus. ::. See the Corollary after Reciprocal Figures. j There is great use made of this Reciprocal Pro - portion, by Sir Isaac Newton, and others, in their Demonstrations of the Laws of " Motion, &c. and indeed without a clear knowledge of it, they can - not be understood.

reclination.c: RECLINATION of a Plain, is the Quantity of Degrees which any Plain, on which a Dyal is supposed to be drawn, lies or falls backwards from truly upright or vertical Plain.

RECLINATION of a Plane, is the Number of Degrees which any Dial Plane lies or falls back - ward from the Zenith. This is found easily by the means of long Rules, and a Quadrant; for having drawn an Horizontal Line on the Plane, by a Level or Quadrant, and to it another Line at Right - angles, to which apply a Ruler so, that one End of it may hang over or reach beyond the Plane: Then will a Quadrant applied to the under Edge of that Ruler, shew you the Degrees and Minutes of the Plane ’ s Reclination: accounting VqUl. R E C from that Side of the Quadrant that is contiguous to the Edge of the Ruler.

recliningindyalling.c: RECLINING, in Dyalling, the Plane that leans from you when you hand before it, is said to be a Reclining Plane.

recliningdecliningdyals.c: RECLINING Declining Dyals. See Declining Reclining Dyals.

recognizanceinlaw.c: RECOGNIZANCE, in Law, is as a Bond or Obligation of Record, testifying the Recognifor to owe to the Recognisee a certain Sum of Money, and is acknowledged in some Court of Record, or be - fore feme Judge, Matter of the Chancery, or Ju - ftice of Peace j and those that be meer Recognifan - ces, are not Sealed but Enrolled, and Execution by force thereof, is of all the Recognifor s Goods or Chattels, ( except Draught Beasts and Simple - ments of Husbandry ) and the Moyety of his Lands.

recognisee.c: RECOGNISEE, is he to whom one is bound in a Recognisance.

recognitions.c: RECOGNITIONS adnullanda per vim & dura - tiem faEla, is a Writ to the Justices of the Com - mon Bench, for the fending of a Record touching a Recognisance which th tRecognifor suggests to have been ackno wedged by force and duress, that if it be so, it may be annulled.

recognitors.c: RECOGNITORS, is a Word often used for the Jury Impannelled upon an Assize: The reason why they are so called, is, because they acknowledge a Disseisin by their VerdicSt.

recollection.c: RECOLLECTION, is a Mode of Thinking, whereby those Idea ’ s fought after by the Mind, are with Pain and endeavour found, and brought again to view.

recordinlaw.c: RECORD, in Law, signifies an Authentick and Uncontroulable Testimony in Writing, con - tained in Rolls of Parchment, and preserved in Courts of Record; and they are said to be vet - fiatis veritatis vestigia. An Ad: committed to Writing in any of the King ’ s Courts, during the Term wherein it is Written, is alterable, being no Record; but that Term once ended, and the Ad Enrolled it is a Record, and of that Credit that admits no alteration or proof to the contrary. Lawyers reckon three forts of Records, vi. Re - cord Judicial, as Attainder, &c. Record Minifte - rial upon Oath, as an Office or Inquilition found. And a Record made by Conveyance and Consent, as a Fine or Deed Enrolled, or the like. R COR. DARE facias, or Recordari facias, is a Writ directed to the Sheriff, to remove a Cause depending in an Inferior Court, as Court of anci - ent Demesne, Hundred or County, to the King ’ s - Bench, or Common - Pleas it seems to be called Recordare, because it commands the Sheriff to make a Record of the Proceedings by himself and others, and then to fend up the Cause.

recorder.c: RECORDER, is he whom the Mayor, or other Magistrate of any City, or Town Corporate ha - ving Jurifdi & ion, or a Court of Record within their Precin & s, by the King ’ s Grants, doth affoci - ate unto him for his better Dire & ion in Matters of Justice and Proceedings according to Law j and is therefore for the molt part a Man versed and ex, perienced in the Law.

recqrdo.c: RECQRDO prccejfu Mittendis, is & Writ to call a Record together, with the whole Proceeding in the Cause out of an Inferior Court into the King ’ s - Bench Court.

record.c: RECORD utlagaria Mittendo, is a Judicial Writ; which see in Reg. Judic. sol..

recovery.c: RECOVERY, in a Legal Sense, signifies an ob - gaining any thing by Judgment or Tryal at Law, as Eviftio doth among the Civilians. And there is a True and a Feigned Recovery: A True Recovery is an dual or real Recovery of any thing, or the Value thereof by Judgment; as if a Man sue for any Land, or other thing moveable or immoveable, and have a Verdid and Judgment for him. A Feigned Recovery, is, ( as the Civilians call it ) Quadam fiftio Juris, a Certain Form or Course fee down by Law, to be observed, for the better af - furing of Lands and Tenements unto us; and the end and effed thereof is to discontinue and destroy Estates Taile, Remainders and Reversions, and to bar the IntaiJs thereof. And in this Formality are required three Per - sons, vis (. The Demandant, Tenant, and Vouchee. The Demandant, is he that brings the Writ of Entry, and may be termed the Recoverer. The Tenant, is he against whom the Writ is brought, and may be termed the Recoveree. The Vouchee, is he whom the Tenant voucheth, and calls to Warranty for the Land in demand. A Recovery with double Voucher, is, where the Tenant voucheth one, who voucheth another, or the common Vouchee. And a Recovery with treble Vouchers, is where three are vouched As when a Man that is defi - rous to cut off an Estate Taile in Lands or Tene - ments, to the end, to fell, give, or bequeath it, causes a Feigned Writ of Entry, Sur dijfeifm en le pojl, to be brought for the Lands of which he in - tends to cut off the Entaile, and in a Feigned Count, or Declaration thereupon made, pretends he was disseised by him, who by a Feigned Fine or Deed of Bargain and Sale, is named and supposed to be the Tenant of the Land. This Feigned Te - nant, if it be a Single Recovery, is made to appear and Vouch the Bag - bearer of Writs for the Cujlcs brevium, in the Common Pleas, ( for there only can such Recoveries be suffered ) who makes Default. Whereupon the Land is recovered by him that brought the Writ, and a Judgment is by such ficti - on of Law entred, that the Demandant shall rec - ver the Value of the Lands against the Lands of the Vouchee. Bag - bearer is a Poor Unlanded and Illiterate Per - fon, which is feigned to be a Satisfaction to the Heir in Taile, tho ’ he is never to have or ex - prest it. This Feigned Recovery, is also called a Common Recovery, because it is a beaten and common Path that end for which it is appointed, v to cut off the Estates above specified. ' But a True Recovery is as well of the Value as of the Thing: As if a Alan buy Land of another with Warranty, which Land a third a third Person afterwards by Suit, of Law recover - ed against me, I have my Remedy against him that fold it me, to recover in Value that is, to recover so much in Money, as the Land is worth or so much other Land by way of Exchange.

recoupeinlaw.c: RECOUPE, in Law, is a quick and fliarp Re - ply to a peremptory Demand; and used by Law - yers to defalk or difeount; as if a Man hath Ten Pounds issuing out of certain Lands, and he diflei - fes the Tenant of the Land in an Assise brought by the Diifeifee, the Dilfeifor ( hall Pjecoupe the Rent in the Damages. RECPvEMENT, any Superfluous Matter in the Blood or Body, or any of its parts.

recrementsaword.c: RECREMENTS, a Word used by the Phyfici - ans and Anatomists, for such Juices as are fepara - red in the several Glands of the Body for Proper and Peculiar Uses; as the Spirits, the Lympha, the Call, the Pancreatic ! Juice, the Proper Ferments of the Stomach, Guts, &c. and these are distinguish ’ d from Excrements, which are expelled out of the Body, as being of no further use to it.

rectangleinarithmetick.c: RECTANGLE, in Arithmetick, is the fame with ProduEl; which fee.

rectanglesingeometry.c: RECTANGLES in Geometry, are Parallel - grams, whose Sides are unequal, but Angles right. Their Area is found by Multiplying the two one - qual Sides one into another, for then the ProduCt is the Superficial Content or Area.

rectangledtriangle.c: RECTANGLED Triangle, the fame with Pjght - angled Triangle. All PeH angles, ( as A and B ) which have the fame height, are to one another as their Bales. That is, A: B:: a h: b c. For A is made by the Multiplication of b d its Bale by the Line b e; and B is also made by Mul - tiplying c b its Bale by the fame Line be ( or its equal c f. ) But the ProduCl of any two Numbers Multiply - ed by the fame Third Number, are as those Num - bers were to each other before Multiplication. Therefore, A: B:: ab: b c. Q. E. D, Hence all PeB angles, or Parallelograms, between the fame Parallel Lines, or which have the fame Height, must be to one another as their Bales are. For they are all equal to Pp angles, on the lain or equal Bales with themselves, and consequently must have the lame Proportion to each other, as such Rectangles; that is, be to each other as their Bales.. E. D. And the fame thing must be true of all Trian - gles that are between the lame Parallels, or which - have the fame Height because they are the halves of those Parallelograms. See the Figure.

rectangularorright.c: RECTANGULAR, or Right - angled is spoken of a Plain Figure in Geometry, when one or more of its Angles are right. Of Solids, ’ tis spoken in respect of their Situation: For it their Axis be perpendicular to the Plane of the Horizon, they are therefore Rectangular, or Right Cones, Cy - hinders, &c.

rectangularsection.c: RECTANGULAR Section of a Cone, by this the Ancient Geometers always meant a Parabola, which Conick. Section, before Apollonius, was only considered in a Cone, whole SeCtion by the Axe would be a Triangle, Right - angled at the Vertex. And hence it was that Archimedes entitled his Book of the Quadrature of the Parabola, ( as ’ tis now called ) by the Name of peBanguli Coni Section.

rectifie.c: RECTIFIE, or peBification, in Chymistry, is the Distilling over again of any Spirit, in order to a more fine, and pure hate and to separate from it any PIctergoeneous Parts, that might rile with it before.

RECTIFIE, is a word used in the Description and use of Globe, or Sphere. For the first thing, to. be done before any Problems can be wrought on the Globe is to PeBifie it. That is, to bring the Sun ’ s Place in the Ecliptick on the Globe, to the graduated Side of the Brass Meridian, to elevate the Pole above the Horizon, as much as is the La - titude of the Place, and to fit the Flour Index ex - actly to twelve at Noon, screwing also the Qua - drant of Altitude, ( if there be occasion ) to the Zenith. All this is comprehended under the Word Peel i fie the Globe: And when this is done, the ( Celestial ) Globe represents the true Posture of the Heavens, for the Noon of that Day it is peBified for.

rectifier.c: RECTIFIER ( in Navigation ) is an Instru - ment confiding of two Parts, which are two Cir - cles either laid one upon, or let into the other, and so fastned together in their Centres, that they represent two Compasses, one fixed, the other moveable; each of them divided in the gl roifits of the Compass, and Degrees, and numbred both ways both from the North and the South, ending at the East and Weft, in Degrees. The Fixed Compass, represents the Horizon, in which the North, and all the other Points of the Compass are fixed and immoveable. The Moveable Compass represents the Mariners Compass, in which the North, and all the other Points are liable to Variation. In the Centre of the Moveable Compass is fastned a Silk. Thread, long enough to reach the ou tilde of the Fixed Compass. But if the Instrument be made of Wood, there is ad Index instead of the Thread. Its Use is to find the Variation of the Compass, to ReCtifie the Course at Sea having the Amplitude or Azimuth given.

rectifyingofcurves.c: RECTIFYING of Curves, ( in Mathematicks ) is to find a strait Line, equal to a Curved one or a Plane equal to a Curved Surface, R E C r iccctj Of this Dr. Wallis gave the first Hint to the World, hi his Arithmetick of Infinites, Prop.. ? Scholium. Soon after which Mr. William Neil applyed chose Considerations to the Semi - cubical Paraboloid, where the Cubes of the Ordinates, are as the Squares of the Diameters: And ( hewed that there the small Segments of the Curve, cut by the Ordi - nates at equal Distances, are as the Ordinates in a Parabola, and therefore their Squares encreased by Equals, in Arithmetical Progression: Where - fore that Curve must be to a Right Line:: as the Trunk of a Parabola, to the Parabola: Which the Quadrature of the Parabola being known, is a known Proportion, and this was the first Attempt of this Nature. But it was afterwards soon de - monftrated also by Sir Christopher Wren, my Lord Brouncker, and by Dr. Wallis. And the Year sol - io wing, vi. ', Sir Chhrijlopher Wren ( hewed the Curve of the Cycloid, to be Quadruple of its Axis: Which was the second Demonstration of a Straight Line equal to a Crooked one. Of which, fee Dr. Wallis ’ s. Englijh Algebra, p., &c. See more also in his Excellent Book de Cycloide.

rectilinealorright.c: RECTILINEAL, or Right - lined, in Geometry, . is spoken of such Figures as have their Extremities all Right Lines.

rectiminor.c: RECTI Minor es, are two ( mall Muscles of the Head, appearing both in fight at once: They arise deftly from the Posterior Part of the first Vertebrce of the Neck j and are so inserted to the middle part of the Os Occipitis in two ( hallow Depreffures of thd said Bone. These from their Use, ' may be called Renuentes or Nodders backwards, and are Antagonists to thole we call Annuentes.

recto.c: RECTO, is a Writ of Right, and is of so high a nature, that whereas other Writs in real Actions are only to recover the Possession of Lands or Tene - ments in Question, which have been loft by our Ancestors or our ( elves; this aimeth to recover both the Seisin, which some of our Ancestors or ' we had, and also the property of the thing whereof j the Ancestor died not Seised, as of Fee, and where - by are Pleaded and Tried both their Rights toge - ther, vi. As well of Possession as Property: So that if a Man once lose his Cause upon this Writ, either by Judgment, Assize, or Battle, he is with - out all remedy, and ( hall be excluded per ex - eeptionem rei Judicata. It is divided into two kinds, ReBum Patens, a. Writ of right Patent j and Recium Clausum, a Writ of right Close. This the Civilians call Ju - dicium Petitorum. The Writ of right Patent is so called, because it is lent upon, and is in nature the highest Writ of all others, lying always for him that hath Fee - simple in the Lands or tenements sued for, and not for any other. And when it lieth for him that Challengeth, Fee - simple, and in what Cafes, fee F. N. B. Sol... This Writ is also called Breve Magnum de recto. A Writ of right Close, is a Writ directed to a Lord of Ancient De - mesne, and lieth for those which hold their Lands and Tenements by Charter in Fee - simple, or in Fee - tail, or tor term of Life, or in Dower, if they be ejected out of such Lands, &c. or diflfeifled. In this case, a Man or his Heirs may sue out this Writ of right Close, dire died to the Lord of the An - cent Dcmefne, commanding him to do him right, &c. in his Court. And this is called Breve par - vum de reffo.

RECTO de dote under nihil habet, is a Writ of Right, which lies in case where the Husband hav - i ing divers Lands or Tenements, hath assured no Do wertphis Wife; and ( lie thereby is driven to sue for her Thirds, against the Heir, or his Guardian.

RECTO de rationabili parte, is a Writ that lies always between Privies of Blood, as Brothers in Gavelfind, or Sifters, or other Coparceners, as Nephews or Nieces, and for Land in Fee - simple; as if a Man lease his Land for Term of Life, and afterwards dies, leaving Issue two Daughters, and after that the Tenant for term of Life, dieth also, the one Sifter entreth upon all the Land, and lo deforcing the other, the Sifter so deforced ( hall have this Writ to recover part.

RECTO quando Dominus revisit, is a Writ of Right, which lies in case where Lands or Tene - ments that being in the Seigniory of any Lord, are in Demand by a Writ of Right for if the Lord hold no Court, or otherwise, at the Prayer of the Demant, or Tenant, ( hall fend to the Court of the King his Writ, to put the Cause thither for that time, ( favingto him at other times the right of his Seigniory ) then the Writ issues out Tor the other Party, and hath the Name from the Words contained, being the true occasion thereof. This W rit is Close, and must be returned before the Ju - ftices of the Common - Bench.

RECTO / r Difclaymer, is a Writ that lies when a Lord in the King ’ s Court of Common - Pleas avows upon his Tenant, and the Tenant difclaimeth to hold of him j upon which disclaimer he ( hall have this Writ; and if the Lord averr and prove, That the Land is held of him, he ( hall recover the Land for ever.

rectodeadvccationeecclefuc.c: RECTO de Advccatione Ecclefuc, is a Writ of Right lying where a Man hath right of Advowson and the Parson of the Church dying, a Stranger presents his Clerk to the Church, and he not hav - ing brought his Adlion of Quare Impedit nor Dar - rein Presentment within fix Months, but Inhered the Stranger to Usurp upon him. And this Wfip he only may have, that claimeth the Advowson to himself, and to his Heirs in Fee; and as it lies for the whole Advovofn, so it lies also for the half, third or fourth Part.

rectodecustodia.c: RECTO de Custodia terra & harcdis, was a Writ that lay for him whose Tenant holding of him in Chivalry, died in Nonage against a Stranger that entred upon the Land, and took the Body of the Heir; and is now become useless as to Lands h. ol - den in Capite, of by Knights Service, but not when there is Guardian in Socage, or appointed by the last Will and Testament of the Ancestor.

rectodedote.c: RECTO de Dote, is a Writ of right of Dower, which lieth for a Woman that hath received part of her Dower, and purposes to Demand the re - mainder in the fame Town, against the Heir, or his Guardian, if he be a Ward.

rectumintefinum.c: RECTUM Intefinum, is the strait Gut which begins at the first Vertebra of the Os Sacrum, and passeth strait downward to the extremity of the Rump or utmost end of the Back bone. It is about a Foot in length, and not so wide as the Colon, but its Membranes are thicker.

rectusfemoris.c: RECTUS Femoris, is a Muscle of the Leg, ( o named from its ( freight Progress and Situation; it ariseth fleftiy from the Tubercle of the Os Ilium, that is in the Mid - way between the fore - part of its Spine and the Acetabulum, from thence descending directly between the Vastus Externus and Intemus, and over the Crureus. Its Fibres externally descend from a middle Line obliquely Laterally: Inter - nally. they run according to the Length, and be - come entirely Tendinous four Fingers breadth a - above the Patella, where it is united with the Ten - dons of the Vajlus Externus and Interims, an d Cru - reus, and inferred together with em at the Upper part of the Tibia. It serves to help to extend the Tibia.

rectusincuria.c: RECTUS in Curia, signifies one that stands at the Bar, and no Man objects any thing against him. Also, when a Man hath reversed the Outlawry, and can participate of the benefit of the Law, he is Reclus in Curia.

rectusinternusmajor.c: RECTUS Internus Major, is a Muscle of the Head which arises Tendinous but chiefly Fleshy, from the fore - part of all the Transverse Processes of the Vertebra of the Neck, except the first and second, and in its Ascent becoming Fleshy, passes over those two superior Vertebra, and is inferred to the Anterior Appendix of the Os Occipitis, near the great Foramen, that transmit the Medulla Oblongata. This manifestly bends the Head for - wards, and therefore may be called Flexor Capitis, from its Use. -

rectusinternusminor.c: RECTUS Internus Minor, is a Muscle of the Head, Which with its Partner appear on the -. Fore - part of the i ft Vertebra, like the Recli Minor. es on the Back - part, and arise near its Transverse Pro - celTes, and ascending directly, are inferred to the Anterior Appendix of the Os Occipitis immediately under the former. These nod the Head forward, and are Antagonists to the Rest Minor es. Where - fore they may be called Annuentes.

rectuslateralis.c: RECTUS Lateralis, is a short, thick, fleshy Muscle of the Head, arising from the superior part of the Extremity of the Tranverfe Process of the first Vertebra of the Neck, between the former and ebliquus Superior, thence ascends directly to its In section to the Os Occipitis in the Interstice made by the Prcceffus Mammillaris and Styloides. This nods the Head to one side.

rectusmajor.c: RECTUS Major, is a Muscle of the Head, which ariseth partly Tendinous, but chiefly Fleshy:, from the superior Part of the double Spines of the second Vertebra of the Neck, and in its ascent, be - comes broader and Fleshy, and is so inferred to the posterior Part of the Os. Occipitis: This Muscle with its Partner acting, pulls the Head directly back on the first Vertebrae.

rectusmuf.c: RECTUS Muf cuius, one of the Muscles of the Abdomen, so called from the Uprightness of its position. Its Use in common with the other Muscles of this Part, is to help to exclude the Faces and Urine, by the com predion of the Ab - women.

rectuspalpebr.c: RECTUS Palpebr ce Superioris, is a Muscle which lifts up the upper Eye - lid.

recurrentnerves.c: RECURRENT Nerves, by some called Vocal, because they are spent upon the Instruments of Speech, and which Galen faith he tried to cut, a'nd by that means rendred the Animal Mute. This Dr. Willis takes to be a distinct Pair by it self, but tis usually reckoned a Branch of the Par - va - gum or, th Pair, springing out of their Trunks, and so called, because first they descend and then ‘ ascend again to supply the Muscles of the Larynx.

reddendumaword.c: REDDENDUM, a Word used substantively for the Clause in a Lease, &c. whereby the Rent is reserved to the Lessor.

reddition.c: REDDITION, is a Judicial. Confession and Ac - knowledgment, that the Land or thing in Demand, belongs to the Demandant, or at least not CO ' the person so surrendering.

redent.c: REDENT, iii Fortification, is a Work made in Form of the Teeth of a Saw, with Saliant and Reentring - Angles, to the end that one part may de - fend another. These fort of Works are usually erected on that side of a Place which looks to - wards a Marsh or River.

redintegration.c: REDINTEGRATION,, a restoring any Mixd Body or Matter whose Form is destroyed, to the fame Nature and Constitution, and that it ’ shail have the fame Properties it had before. The Honourable Mr. Boyle, hath a particular Trad about the Redintegration of Salt - petre; in which he proves, that after Nitre had been fluxed in a Crucible over a strong Heat, and after all its vo - latine Parts had been forced away by the injedioh of lighted Coals so often into the Crucible, that no farther Detonation would happen - by which means the Salt - petre was ruined into That Body which is Called Fixt Nitre, and which is very nearly akin, in all its Properties, to fixt Salt of Tartar, yet he could very speedily, by pouring to this fixt Salt - petre, either diluted with a due proportion of Water, or let run per fe into a Deliquium, a fuf - scient quantity of Spirit of Nitre, ( which by the by amounted nearly to the quantity of that vol - tile Part which was burnt off; he could, I fay, fud - denly reproduce true Chrystals of Salt - petre of the common Form and Virtue.

redisseisin.c: REDISSEISIN, is a Dijfeifin made by him that once before was made and adjudged to sive Dis - fered the fame Man of his Lands or Tenements; for which there lies a special Writ, called a Writ of Redejfeifin. JL & D - Lead, how made. Set Minium.

redoubtinfortification.c: REDOUBT, in Fortification, is a small Fort of a square Figure, having no Defence but in the Front, its use being to maintain the Lines of CircumvalU - tion, Contravallation, arid Approach. In Marfliy Grounds, these Redoubts are often made of Mason ’ s Work for the Security of the Neighbourhood. Their Face consists of from ten to fifteen Fathom; the Ditch round about being from eight to nine Foot broad and deep, and their Parapets having the fame thickness. f

redubbors.c: REDUBBORS, are those which buy ftolleri Cloath, knowing it sti'ch, and change it into some other Form or Colour that it may not be known.

reducingscale.c: REDUCING Scale, is a thin broad piece of Box with several different Scales of equal Parts, and Lines to turn Chains and Links into Acres and Rods, by Infpebfcion; and is used by Surveyors to reduce any Map or ‘ Draught. It is sometimes cal - led, the Surveying - Scale. , REDUCT, a Military term, signifying an ad - vantageous piece of Ground, intrenched and sea - rated from the reft of the Place, to retire ' to in case of surprize.

reductioninastronomy.c: REDUCTION, in Astronomy, is the difference between the Argument of Inclination and rhe Ec - centrical Longitude; that is to fay, the Difference of the two Arches of the Orbit, and the Ecliptick, intercepted between the Node and the Circle of In - clination.

reductionofequations.c: REDUCTION of Equations, in Algebra, is the clearing of them from all superfluous Quantities, and the separating of the known Quantities from the unknown, to the end that at length every respective Equation may remain in the feweft and simples Terms, and so disposed, that the un - known Quantity or Quantities may poffeis one C pars part thereof, and the unknown the other. See E - equation.

reductionofmoney.c: REDUCTION of Money, Weights, Measure, &c. is of two kinds, i. When a Quantity is to be brought from any higher Denomination into a lower and this is done, by considering how many of the next lesser Denomination is contained in the next greater before, and by that number multiply - ing the greater; as Pounds are brought into Shil - lings by Multiplying by, Shillings into Pence by, and Pence into Farthings by. Also, Frog - Weight may be reduced into Grains, by Multiply - ing by,, and. And Averdupois Great Weight into Ounces, by,, and. . If it be to bring the lower to a higher, then divide the least by so many of its Denominations as are contained in the next greater. Thus Pence is Pounds: But if there remains any thing after Division, they are the odd Pence and Shillings; as Pence Reduced, gives /. s. d. Note, That to reduce Shillings into Pounds, is to cut off the last Figure, and take half of the reft, as in the last Instance. ) ( ( L V ) s. d. x After the fame manner may Troy Weight, Aver - dupois Weight or any other Weight or Measure be reduced. Likewise Foreign Coin may be reduced into Eng - lifh, by turning the Value into Englijh Coin of any Part: As, what is the value of Scotch Marks, each equal to d. ? Englijh ? which is Farthings, and by a Farthings, which reduced backwards to Pounds, Shillings and Pence, makes /. /. d.

reduplicativeproportions.c: REDUPLICATIVE Proportions, are such where - in the Subject is repeated: Thus, Men, as Men, are Rational j Kings, as Kings, are subject: to none but God. RE - ENTRING Angle, a Term in Fortification. See Angle. RE - ENTRY, in Law, signifies the resuming and retaking that Possession which we had lately foregone: As if I make a Lease of Land or Tene - ment, I do therefore forego the Possession; and if I do condition with the Lessee, That for Non - pay - ment of the Rent at the Day, it shall be lawful for me to Re - enter; this is as much as if I condition ’ d to take again the Lands, &c. into my own Hands, and to recover the Possession by my own Sad, without the assistance of Judge, or other Process.

reefaterminnavigation.c: REEF, a Term in Navigation: When there is a great Gale of Wind, they commonly roll up part of the Sail below, that by that means it may be - come the narrower, and so notdraw so much Wind. And this contracting or taking up the Sail, they call a Reef or Reefing the Sail j and when it is done, they fay the Sail is Reefed. Also, when a Top - Mast is Sprung, as they call it, i. e. crackt or almost broken in the Cap, they cut off the lower piece that was near broken off: and setting the other part, now much shorter, in the Step again, they call it a Rest Top - Mast.

reeve.c: REEVE, is to put a Rope through a Block - and to pull a Rope out qf a Block is called Un - reeking.

reflection.c: REFLECTION, in general, is the regress or return that happens to a moving Body, because of the meeting of another Body, which it cannot pe - nitrate. Thus the material Rays of Light are re - fleded variously from such Bodies as they cannot pass through.

REFLECTION of the Rays of Light. Sir Isaac Newton, finding by Experiment that Light was an Heterogeneous Body, consisting of a Mixture of differently refrangible Rays; and conlequeritly concluding no farther Improvement could well be made in Optical Instruments in the Dioptrick way, he took Reflections into Consideration, and tells us, that by their help, Optick Instruments might be brought to any degree of Perfection, if we Could but find a refleding Substance which would Polifii as finely as Glass, rested as much Light as Glass transmit, and be formed into a Parabolical Fi - gure. An Experiment of which he made in the kind of a Catoptrick Telescope, ( which I have seen at Grejham College ) and by which, tho ’ not above two Foot long, he could ( he faith ) discern the Jo - vial Satellites, and the Phases of Venus. Phil. Trans. N. -. See Vol..

reflectioninmetaphyfickj.c: REFLECTION, in Metaphyfickj, Mr. Loch de - fines to be, That Notice which the Mind takes of its own Operations, and the Manner of them; by reason whereof there come to be Ideas of thole O - operations in the Understanding.

reflectedray.c: REFLECTED Ray, or Ray of Reflection, is that whereby the Reflection is made upon the Surface of a refleding Body.

reflectingorreflectivedials.c: REFLECTING, or Reflective Dials, are made by a little piece of Looking - Glass - Plate, duly pla - ced, which refleds the Sun ’ s Rays to the top of a Ceiling, &c. where the Dial is drawn. This Glass should be as thin as can well be ground. For the making of these Dials, there are many Methods: Of the two following, the ist is Mr. Collins, the d Dr. Clarks. First, Determine the m oft / Convenient Point in the Window, where to place the Reflecting Glass, as near the Ceiling as you can conveniently, pro - vided it be not so near as that the Cornilh of the Window will shadow the Glass when the Sun is high in Summer; suppose within about or Inches of the Ceiling, at least of that Ceiling which belongs to the Window it self; then from that Point draw a true Meridian upon a plane Hori - zontally placed against the determined Point in the Window, and to that Meridian, fit an Horizontal Dial; but invert it so, that the Axis or Stile may point downward, and be under the Horizontal Plane, according to the Elevation of the Pole, which Stile must be placed truly also in the Plane of the Meridian; then by the help of a Thread running from the Centre along the Stile, find where: that Stile would cut the Floor, or any other Place, if it were produced, and drive a Nail into - that Point, and fallen also a Third there Jong enough to be extended to any part of the Ceil - ing. Fallen. A Fatten also another long Thread to the Centre of the Horizontal Dial, which let it be extended Horizontally, as the Plane will direct, and exactly over every Hour - line in order, whilst in the mean time you extend the Thread which was fattened to the Nail in the Stile, to the Ceiling, but so as it may touch the other Horizontal Thread: Then mark that Point in the Ceiling which the extended Thread toucheth, and make more such Marks, whereby to draw the Hour - Lines upon the Ceil - ing j and do this in like manner for the reft of the Hours, Half Hours, and Quarters. Then take ail away, and place your Glass Horizontally; and because your Glass hath some Thickness, place it a little under the determined Point, that the Centre of the Glass may be just in the imaginary Axis, which goes to the Nail; for wheresoever you place it, in that it will go true. But because it may be troublesome to place an Horizontal Dial fast enough and exactly, as also to find the Point where the Nail is to be driven, I will ( hew you another Method, which may be more easily praised. Fir ft, Draw an Horizontal Dial upon the back of some Table or Floor, and draw a Meridian upon the Bay - board of the Window, by a Thread or perpendicular black Line, passing through the Point where you intend your Reflecting Glass shall be, and by a Plumb - Line translate it from the Bay - board to the Ceiling. Take the nearest distance between the Glass and the Ceiling; with this di - stance come to the Horizontal Dial, and fet one end of it on that part of the Axis where the other will just touch the Meridian; that Point in the Axis may be called the Glass Point; from which ered a Perpendicular; and where it cuts the Meridian, make a Point, which will be the Equinoctial Point, from which also ered a Perpendicular, which will be a Tangent then at some distance on which side of the Equinoctial Point you find most convenient ered another Tangent there, two Tangents will cut the Hour - Lines in Points, which may be called the Hour - Points. Then take the distance betwixt the Glass - Points and the Equinoctial - Point, and extend it from the Glass toward the Meridian, and where it toucheth, that is the Equinoctial-Point upon the Ceiling. Lastly, Set offcorrefpondenc Tangent - Lines up - on the Ceiling, and make like Hour - Points, draw the Hour - Lines, you need not blot out the Equi - noctial Tangent, it being pleasant to fee how the Sun will go in that Line all Day, when it is in the Equinoctial. Besides, the Equinoctial - Point will tell you on that Day whether your Glass lie Hori - zontally, which is somewhat difficult otherwise to determine. Or upon any Day you may Calculate the Sun ’ s Meridian Altitude, and fee whether it falls just upon that Point in the Meridian at a Clock. This Dial is nothing but an Horizontal Invert - ed, the Centre whereof is in the Air without, ex - cept you make a North Dial, and then it will be upon the Ceiling, which you must find by its di - stance from the Equinoctial - Point, and let that Centre govern your Tangents. The ground of this Dial is, that the Angles of Reflection are equal to the Angles of Incidence. Sometimes, instead of two Tangents, you may use two Circles, especially when tlie Centre of the Dial is upon the Ceiling, or when your Glass is near the Window - Ceiling, then the Equinoctial - Point will be upon that Ceiling, and you may pro - ” jed the Hour - Lines upon the Chamber - Ceiling or the Walls, by one Thread extended over the Hour - Lines, and another Thread touching that, and extended from the Equinoctial - Point, or any Point in the imaginary Axis to the Ceiling or Wail.

reflexion.c: REFLEXION of the Moon, is ( according to Bullialdus ) her d inequality of Motion: This Tycho calls by the name of her Variation, which fee.

reflux.c: REFLUX of the Sea, is the Ebbing of the Wa - ter off from the Shore, as its coming on upon it, or Tide of Flood, is called the Flux of the Sea. See Tide.

refractedangle.c: REFRACTED Angle, in Opticks, is the Angle contained between the refracted Ray and the Perpendicular.

refracteddials.c: REFRACTED Dials, may be made thus; Stick up a Pin, or assign any Point in any Concave Bowl, and make that the Centre of the Horizontal Dial, assigning the Meridian - Line on the edges of the Bowl, and taking away the Horizontal Dial, elevate a String or Thread from the end of the said Pin fattened thereto over the Meridian - Line, equal to the Elevation of the Pole or Latitude of the Place; then with a Candle, or if you bring the Thread to the Shade upon any Hour - Point formerly marked out on the edges of the Bowl, at the fame time the Shade in the Bowl is the Hour - Line. And if the Bowl be full of Water, or any other Liquor, you may draw the Hour - Lines, which will never Ihew the true Hour, unless filled with the said Liquor again. , REFRACTION, in general, is the Incurvation f or change of Determination in the Body moved, which happens to it, whilst it enters or penetrates I any Medium. In Dioptricks, it is the variation of a Ray of Light from that right Line which it would have passed on in, had not the density of the Medium turned it aside. Dr. Hoc discovered by Experiment, That the ] Sines of the Angles of Incidence of the Rays of I Light are proportionable to the Sines of Refraction, See the Preface to Micrographia, where his Instru - ' ment is described, by which he made the Difco - very. Sir Isaac Newton found that the Rays of Light are Incurvated or Refracted in their Motion when - ever they come near the edges of any Body, tho ’ it be not Diaphanous. See Light. And he thinks that the Errors of Refraction in Optick Glasses might be corroded if two Sphere - cal Glasses were combined together with Water included between them. And such Glasses he judges preservable to Elliptical or Hyperbolical ones, because ( besides that they can be more ea - fily ground ) they do more accurately refra the Pencils of Rays posited without the Axis of the Glass. Dr. Wallis in Philo f Trans, N., faith. That tho ’ Refraction by Vapours near the Horizon, may make a thing appear higher, yet it cannot make it appear broader; whereas in Refraction by Glasses, the thing is apparently enlarged every way. From whence it is, that the diverse Power of Refraction in Fluids arises, is not easie to deter - mine, tho ’ it would be of great Advantage if it could be discovered: Pure clear Water, of all Flu -, Ci ids RES REG ids, refrads the Rays of Light the least; and if it be impregnated with Salts, it encreases the Re - fraction in proportion to the Quantity and Weight of the Saits dissolved in it. , The Aqua Stygire, or Corrosive Menstruums, such as Aqua fonts, &c. which are Salt dissolved and rendred Corrosive by the Violence of the Fire, do yet much more Refrad the Suns Rays; which need not be woridred at, because these are much denser and heavier Fluids than the former. But then why in such light fine Fluids as Spirit of Wine and other Ardent Spirit; in Oil of Tur - pontine, which is so light and fine a Fluid, as to be generally called, an Ethereal Oil; why these fay, Ihould produce lo great a degree of Refradi - on, as ’ tis known they do, is a thing of great difficulty to account for, and well deserves a far - ther Enquiry into. Dr. Gregory in hisAftronomy, very well accounts for the Oval Figures which the Sun near the Hori - zon ( especially in high Latitudes ) is sometimes seen to put on from Refraction. For having be - fore demonstrated, That because of the Earths At - mosphere all Bodies near the Horizon, will appear something higher in the Vertical Circle than they really are, and this the more, the nearer they are to the Horizon: He strews that the upper Margin of the Sun ’ s Disk being raised a little more than it ought to be, and the lower one a great deal more, the Sun ’ s Vertical Diameter will seem to be con - traded, but the Horizontal one will not, and there - fore he will appear Oval. And for the fame rea - fon, the observed Distance of two Fix ’ d Stars, is sensibly less ( when meafuredby an Instrument ) if they are in the fame Vertical Circle, and one of them near the Horizon, than when they both have a confide table Altitude. After this he ffiews how to determine the Quan - tity of the Refraction in any given degree of Alti - tude, and to make a Table of it; thus. Let some Fix ’ d Star having no sensible Parallax, and much elevated above the Horizon be chosen, whose Place he ( hews how to determine at P., Prop, z, by Observations made when the Star is so high as to have no sensible Refraction. Then let the Time be noted when this Star hath any known Altitude, ( as taken by an Instrument, ) and Calculation made for the true Altitude, ( according to the Star ’ s known Place ) the Excess of the ob - served Altitude above this is the Refraction.

refractionajhonomical.c: REFRACTION Ajhonomical, is that which the Atmosphere produceth, whereby a Star appears more elevated above the Horizon than really it is.

refractionhorizontal.c: REFRACTION Horizontal, is that which cau - set the Sun or Moon to appear on the edge of the Horizon, when they are as yet somewhat be - low it.

refraction.c: REFRACTION from the Perpendicular, is when a Ray falling, inclined from a thicker Medium into a thinner, as from Glass into Air, in breaking, de - parts farther from that Perpendicular.

REFRACTION to the Perpendicular, is when a Pay falling incline ’ d from a thinner or more diapha - nous Medium, upon a thicker or less transparent, as from Air upon Water, in breaking, comes nearer the Perpendicular, drawn from the Point of Inch - dence at Right Angles, on the Surface of the Water wherein the Refraction is made.

refrangible.c: REFRANGIBLE, is whatever is capable of be - ing Bpf railed.

refrigeratory.c: REFRIGERATORY, is that part of an Alem - back or Distilling Vessel which is placed about the Head of the Still, and filled with Water to cool the Head of the Alembick, that the Spirituous Va - pours may the sooner and the more easily Condenie into Drops. Cold Water must continually be put into the Refrigeratory, as the Vessel grows hot. Most Apothecaries, Diftillers, &c. that have Occa - sion for drawing off large quantities of Spirits, do now - a - days use the Vesica or Copper Body with its Moors Head of the fame Metal; and without any Refrigerations about the Head of the Still: But then there is below, a long VVcrnt or Serpentine in a Tub of Water, where the Spirituous Vapours are very easily condensed into a Liquor. And this may as well be called a Refrigeratory as the former.

rest.c: REST I ATIO Feodi, a term in Civil - Law fig - nifying the Loss of a Feudal Tenure by Forfeiture; which is of two kinds, either by not performing the Service required, or by committing some vii - lanous Ad against the Lord or Soveraign.

regaliatheroyalrights.c: REGALIA, the Royal Rights of a King, reckon - ned by the Civilians t o be Six.. Power of Ju - dictature.. Power of Life and Death.. Power of War and Peace.. Materlefs Goods.. Af - feffments.. Minting of Money. AHo, the Crown Scepter with the Cross, Scepter with the Dove, St. Edward ’ s Staff, four several Swords, the Globe, the Orb with the Cross, and such other like things used at the Coronation of our Kings, are called Regalia.

regardanttheheralds.c: REGARDANT, the Heralds term for a Lion or such kind of Beast of Prey born in a Posture of looking back behind him.

regelorpygel.c: REGEL, or Pygel, a fix ’ d Star of the first Mag - nitude in Orion ’ s left Foot; it ’ s Longitude is deg. min. Latitude o '.

regiment.c: REGIMENT, is a Body of Troops of Horse or Companies of Foot Commanded by a Colonel; but the Number is as undetermin ’ d as that of the Men in a Troop or a Company. There are Regi - ments of Horse that are not above Men; and there are some in Germany of; and the Re - piment of Picardy in France consists of Men.

regionajsensu.c: REGION Ajsensu, is a Writ whereby the King gives his Royal Assent to the Eledion of a Bi - ( hop.

region.c: REGION: Fernelius with some Anatomists, di ftinguifh the Cavities of an Animal Body into see - ral Regions or Parts, which they Specifick into Pub - lick. and Private. The Publick are Three. The First includes the Vena Porta, and all Parts to which its Branches reach.. The Second begins at the Roots of the Vena Cava, and ends in the small Veins before they become Capillary. The Third they make to contain the Muscles, Bones and Bulk of the Body: But this is not much received. The Abdomen is usually diftinguiffied also into Regi - ons, the Vppermoft, Middle, and Lower.

REGION, is also taken for our Hemisphere, or the, space within the four Cardinal Points of the Heavens, or of the Air, &c. In Geography, it signifies a large ex - tent of Land inhabited by many People of the fame Nation, and Enclosed within certain Limits or Bounds.
REGION. Elementary, according to the Arijlo - telians, is a Sphere terminated by the Concavity of the Moon ’ s Orb, comprehending the Earth ’ s At - mosphere. REGION
REGION / Ethereal, in Cosmography, is the vast Extent of the Universe; wherein are compri - zed ail the Heavens and Celestial Bodies.

regions.c: REGIONS of the Air, are diftinguiflied into Zipper, Middle, and Lower.

registers.c: REGISTERS, in a Chymical Furnace, are Holes purposely left in the Sides of the Furnace with floppies to them, to let in or keep out the Air, according as the Fire is required to be greater or less. REGIUS Morbus. See IClerus.

regrator.c: REGRATOR, signifies him that Buys and Sells any Wares or Victuals in the fame Market or Fair, or ' within five Miles thereof. In the Civil Law, such an one is called Dardanarius.

regularbody.c: REGULAR Body, is a Solid whose Surface is composed of Regular and Equal Figures and whose Solid Angles are all equal. Such as the, r. Tetrahedcn, which is a Pyramid, comprehend - ded under Four Equal and Equilateral Trian - gles. . Hexahedron, or Cube, whose Surface is com - posed of fix equal Squares. . OCtahedron, which is bounded by eight Equal and Equilateral Triangles. . Dodecahedron, which is contained under Equal and Equilateral Pentagons. . Icosihedron, consisting of Equal and Equi - lateral Triangles. That there can be no more Regular Bodies be - sides these, may be thus proved. . Of Equilateral Triangles, there mud be three at least to make a Solid Angle; and three of them joined together will make the Tetrahedron; for those three Triangles meeting in a Point, do form a Triangular Bale similar and Equal to the Sides; as appears by the bare Composition of the Figure. Four such Triangles joined together in a Point, make the Angle of the O & ahedron. By joining five such Triangles together, the An - gle of the Icosihedron is formed. But fix such Triangles joined in a Point, cannot make a Solid Angle; because they make four right ones; ( for every Angle of an Equilateral Triangle is f of two; or f of one right Angle; either of which Fractions multiplied by Six, gives four right Angles ) whereas every Solid Angle is made up of four such plane Angles as all together must be less than four right ones: So that with Triangles ’ tis impossible to form any more Regular Bodies than these three. If you take Squares and join three of them toge - ther, they will make the Angle of a Cube and there can no other Regular Body but a Cube be made with Squares; for four Squares joined toge - ther, will not make a Solid Angle, but a Plane. If you join the Angles of three Pentagons toge - ther, you will constitute the Angle of the Dodeca - heron. But four such Angles cannot make a So - lid one. And three Hexagons joined together, do make EE G just four fight Angles, and therefore they cannot make a Solid Angle. And as for three Heptagons, or other Figures yet of more Sides, they can muds less do it; because their Angles being very obtuse, three of them will exceed four right ones. So that upon the whole, ’ tis plain, that of these Five Re - gular Bodies, three are made of Triangles, one of Squares, and one of Pentagons, and there can be no other.
