regularfigure.c: REGULAR Figure, in Geometry, are such whose Sides, and consequently their Angles, are all equal to one another. Whence all Aguiar Multilateral Planes are call ’ d Regular Polygons. The Area of such Figures is speedily found by multiplying a Perpendicular let fall from the Cen - tre of the Inscribed Circle to any Side by half that Side, and then that Product by the Number of the Sides of the Polygon.

regularcurves.c: REGULAR Curves, are such Curves as the Peri - meters of the Conick Sections, which are always Curved after the lame Regular Geometrical man - ner. But Irregular Curves, are such as have a Point of Inflexion; and which being continued, do turn themselves a contrary way, as the Conchoid, and the Solid Parabola which hath a Square for its Para - meter.

regulator.c: REGULATOR, a small Spring belonging to the Ballance in the new Pocket - Watches.

regulus.c: REGULUS, or flegul. When any Metal or Mineral is separated in a Crucible, by Purification, from its more gross and terrene Parts, the finer and metalline Parts will sink to the Bottom of the Cru - cable. And this the Chymifts call flex or flegulus, the Royal or Noble Part of the Mixt.

regulusofantimony.c: REGULUS of Antimony, is thus made. Mix together Ounces of Antimony, of Crude Tartar, and of Salt - peter, all well powdred; then heat a large Crucible red hot, and throw into it a Spoonful of the Mixture, presently Covering the Crucible with a Tile; repeat this Spoonful by Spoonful till all the Matter is thrown in. Then make a great Fire about the Crucible, and when the Matter had been a while melted, pour it into nn Iron Mortar greased a little with Suet, and warm ’ d; knock the Mortar on the Side with the Pestle, to make the Regulus precipitate to the Bot - tom. When ’ tis cold separate it from the Dross, then Powder it, and melt it again in another Cru - cable, with a little Salt - peter thrown on it when ’ tis in Fusion, Call it out as before into a greased Morter, or mould it into Pills, Cups, &c. For of this Regulus is made the Antimohial Cup, and the Regulus. If you powder four Ounces of it, and Calcine it in an Earthen Pan, unglazed, o - ver a final ! Fire, stirring the Powder all the while with a Spatula, a Fume will arise, for about an Hour and half or two Hours, the Powder will turn grey, and at the End of that small Time, will Weigh near two Drams and an half, more than the Powder did at first, tho ’ it fumed all the time; which may satisfie us, that some Bodies have their Peres so adapted, that they can retain the very Par - titles of Fire themselves, and Incorporate with them. An augmentation of Weight, happens in making the Calx of Lead, and some others, but not in such a degree, nor so soon as this. If an Ounce of the Dross of the Regule of An - simony, be boiled in a Pint of Water, and then fet to stand and cool without stirring it, it will coagulate into a Substance very like to Blood, but not so red. The Chymifts make much ado about a Regulus of Antimony made with Steel, because of a kind of Star that appears in the Bottom of it: But it hath no other Virtues than this described above. You may see the way of making it in Lemery, p.,. last: Edit, and in many other Chymical Authors. If Antimony be calcined in an Earthen Pot un - glazed, and continually stirring till no more Fumes arise, and afterwards the Matter be put into a Crucible, and in a very violent Fire melted and kept an Hour in Fusion, it will be turned into a reddish Opake Glass, which they call Glass of An - simony, and is a most violent Emetick.

rejoinderinlaw.c: REJOINDER, in Law, signifies an Answer or Exception to a Replication; for first the Defend - dant puts in an Answer to the Plaintiffs Bill, which is sometimes called, An Exception, the Plaintiff ’ s Answer to that is called, a flejoynder, especially in Chancery. ’ Tis by the Civilians called Duplicatio.

relaisafrenchterminfortification.h: RELAIS a French Term in Fortification
relaisafrenchterminfortification.c: RELAIS, a French Term in Fortification, the fame with Berme.

relationinharmonical.c: RELATION Inharmonical, a Term in Musical Composition, signifying a harsh Refledion of Flat against Sharp, in a cross form, vi. When some harsh and displeasing Discord is produced, in com - paring the Present Note of another Part.

relativegravity.c: RELATIVE Gravity, the fame with Specifick - which fee.

relativepropositions.c: RELATIVE Propositions, are those that include some Comparison, add some Relation, thus: Where the Treafureis, there is the Heart: As much as thou haft, so much art thou worth. RELAXANTIA. See Chalaftica.

relaxation.c: RELAXATION, is a Dilatation of Parts or Vessels.

releaseinlaw.c: RELEASE, in Law, is an Instrument whereby Estates, Rights, Titles, Entries, - Adions, and o - ther things, be sometimes extinguished, sometimes transferred, sometimes abridged, and sometimes enlarged; and is either in Fa l or in Law. A fleleafe in Fall, is that which the very Words expressly declare. A fleleafe in Law, is that which doth Acquit by way of Consequence or Intendment, of Law.

relegationinlaw.c: RELEGATION, in Law, signifies a Banishment for a certain time.

releife.c: RELEIFE, or fleleivo, is the Protuberant jet - ting or standing out of any Figures or Images a - above the Plain on which they are formed. And whatever Figures or Representation are thus cur, stamped, or otherwise wrought, so that not the entire Body, but only part of it is raised above the Plain, is said to be done in fleleife - and when the Work, is low, flat, and but a little raised, ’ tis cal - led Baffle fleleife, or Low fleleife. When a Coin or a Medal hath its Figure low and thin, and hardly distinguishable from the Plain, we fay its fleleife is low and weak; but when ’ tis much raised, we fay ’ tis Bold, and its Releife is Strong. RELEViSH, in Law, signifies to let one to Mainprise upon Surety. RELICT

relictverifications.c: RELICT Verifications, is when a Defendant hath Pleaded, arid the Iffiie is entred of Record, and after that the Defendant Relitta Verification, ( que eft f on Plea ) acknowledges the Adion and thereupon Judgment is entred for the Plaintiff.

remainderinlaw.c: REMAINDER, in Law, is an Estate limited in Lands, Tenements, or Rents, to be enjoyed af - ter the Expiration of another particular Estate. As a Man may let to one for Term of his Life, and the Remainder to another for the Term of his Life and this Remainder may be either for a certain Term, or in Fee - simple, or Fee - taile j the Diffe - rence between a Remainder and Reverjion, is this, That by a Reverjion, after the appointed Term the Estate returns to the Donor, or his Heirs, as the proper Fountain; whereas by Remainder, it goes to some third Person, or a Stranger.

remembrance.c: REMEMBRANCE, is when the Idea of some thing formerly known, recurs again into the Mind, without the Operation of the like Object on the External Sensory.

remembrancers.c: REMEMBRANCERS of the Exchequer, are three Officers or Clerks there, viz. The Kings Re - membrancer, ihe Lord Treasurer s Remembrancer, and the, Remembrancer of the Fist Fruits. T he Kings Remembrancer enters into his Office all Recognifances taken before the Barons for any of the King ’ s Debts, for Appearance, or for obfer - ving Orders; and maketh our Process against the Colledors of Customs, Subfidies, and Fifteenths for their Accounts: All Informations upon Penal Statutes, are entred in this Office, and there all Matters upon English Bills in the Exchequer - Chamber remain: He makes the Bills of Compo - sition upon Penal Laws, takes the Stalment of Debts, has Delivered into his Office all manner of Indentures, Fines and other Evidences whatsoever, that concern the alluring of any Lands to the Crown: He every Year in crastino animarum reads in open Court, the Statute for Election of Sheriffs, and gives them their Oath: and he reads in open Court the Oath of all the Officers of the fame, when they are admitted, besides many other things. T he Lord Treasurer ’ s Remembrancer, upon whose Charge it lies, to put the Lord Treasurer, and the reft of the Judges of that Court, in Remembrance of such things as are to be called on, and deal in for the King ’ s Behoof. He makes Process against all Sheriffs, Efcheators, Receivers, and Bailiffs, for their Account: He makes Process of Fieri fa - cias & Extent, for any Debts due to the King either in the Pipe or with the Auditors, makes Process for all such Revenues as are due to the King, by reason of his Tenures: He makes Record, where - by it appears whether Sheriffs, and other Accoun - tants, pay their Prefers due at Easter and Michael - mas. He makes another Record, whether She - riffs, and other Accountants, keep their Days of Prefixion. Ail Estreats of Fines, Issues, and Amer - ciaments, fet in any Courts at Wcftminftcr, or at the Assizes, or Sessions, are certified into this Of - sice and are by him delivered to the Clerk of the Estreats, to Write Process upon them, CSc.. The Remembrancer of the Firji Fruits, takes all Compositions and Bonds, for First Fruits, and Tenths, and makes Process against such as. do not pay the fame.

reminiscence.c: REMINISCENCE, is the Power which the Humane Mind hath of recolleding it self, or cal - ling again to its Remembrance such Ideas or No - tions which it had really forgot: In which it dis - R E N I fers from Memory, which is a treafuring up of things in the Mind, and keeping them there with - out forgetting them.

remission.c: REMISSION, is a Word used by Physical Writ - ters, to signifie the Abatement of the Power or Ef - ficacy of any Quality, oas when it is encreased, they fay ’ tis Intended; and all Qualities are thus capable of Intension or Remijfton. See in the Word Quality a Demonstration that the Intension of all Qualities decreases, as the Squares of the Distance from the Centre of Adion reciprocally.

remitter.c: REMITTER in a Legal Sense, is to restore one that hath two Titles to Lands or Tenements, and is seized of them by a latter Title which is dis - covered to be defective, to the former and more ancient Title, that so he may continue in Quiet PoffeiEon.

renalartery.c: RENAL Artery, is said by some, to come out of the Aorta, and to enter into the Sidneys, bring - ing to it the Serosity of the Arterial Blood,

renderinlaw.c: RENDER, in Law, is a Wore ! used in levying of a Fine, which is either single, whereby nothing is granted or rendred back again by the Cognisee to the Cognisor; or double, which containeth a Grant or render back again of some Rent, Com - mon or other thing out of the Land it self to the Cognisor, &c. Also, there be some things in a Mannor that lie in Prender; that is, which may be taken by the Lord or his Officer, when they change, without any Offer made by the Tenant, as Escheats, and the like; and some that lie in Render that is, must be delivered or answered by the Tenants, as Rents Reliefs, Heriots, and other Services. Also some Service consists in Seifance, some in Render.

rends.c: RENDS in a Ship, are the fame as the Seams between her Planks.

renesthereinsorkidneys.c: RENES, the Reins or Kidneys there are always two of them, and placed in the Abdomen between the two Membranes of the Peritoneum, and ad - joyning to the Sides of the Aorta and Vena Cava j the Right Kidney lies lower in Men, and is some - thing less than the left: They are covered with a double Membrane j of which the outwardmoft is common proceeding from the Peritoneum; and is called the Membrana Adiposa, from its being co - vered with Fat, in Fat and Corpulent People; into this the Arteria Adiposa enters from the Aorta s and the Vena Adiposa goes out from it; which the right Kidney usually fends into the Emulgent Vein, rarely into the Cava, but the left Kidney general - ly into the Cava. By means of this Membrane, both the Kidneys are joined to the Loins and Din - phragma. - The right one to the Cecum Intestinum, andlometitnes to the Liver, and the left is coned - ed by it to the Spleen and Colon - Its Interior Membrane or Tunick, and which is proper to it, is taken from the External Roat of thole Vessels which enter the Kidneys, ( and which do enter it but with a single Coat: ) and this hath some small Nerves from a Branch of the sixth pair,, and from the Stomachicfi Branch, which give the Kidneys but a dull small sense, but afterwards branching out into the Ureters, render them ex - treamly sensible; and those Nerves ( by consent of Parts ) cause that Vomiting which usually accoy - sanies Nephritick Pains. The Kidneys have two Eminent Blood Vessels, the Emulgent Vein and Ar - tery of which the other distributes the Blood from the R E P v the Aorta vs zo the Body of the Kidneys, and the former brings it back again.

renessuccenturiati.c: RENES Succenturiati, are a pair of Glandulous Bodies placed above the Reins or Kidneys: Their Use ( by home ) is supposed to be, to receive the Lympha into their Cavities, thereby to attenuate and render more fluid and capable of Circulation, the Blood returning from the Kidneys, where it hath parted with its Serum. But we are yet, faith Dr. Gibson, in the Dark as to their true use: They are called also Glandules Renales, and by Bartholin Capfulce Atrabilana: By Dr. Wharton, Glandule ad Plexum Nerveum fit a. They are larger in Chil - dren than in Men; being in the former near as big as the Kidneys but they do not encrease pro - portionably as other Parts do.

renitency.c: RENITENCY, is that Resistence which there is in Solid Bodies when they press upon, or are impelled one against another, or that Resistence that any heavy Body makes on the account of its Weight, to our Arm or Hand when we lift it up.

rent.c: RENT, signifies a Sum of Money, or other con - sideration issuing Yearly out of Lands or Tene - ments; of which Lawyers reckon three forts, vi. Rent fer vice, Rent - charge, and Rent - feck. ' j Rent - fer - vice, is where a Man holds his Lands of his Lord by Fealty, and certain Rent, or by Fealty Service, and certain Reht, or that which a Man making a Lease to another for Term of Years, referveth Yearly to be paid for them. Rent - change, is where a Man makes over his Estate to another, by Deed indented, either in Fee, or Fee - taile, or for Term of Life, yetreferves to himfeif, by the fame In - venture, a Sum of Money Yearly to be paid to him, with Cause of Distress, for Non - payment. Rent - feck, or Dry Rent, is that which a Man ma - king over his Estate by Deed indented, referveth Yearly to be paid to him without Cause of Di - stress, mentioned in the Indenture.

reparation.c: REPARATION facienda, is a Writ which lies, in divers Cafes, whereof one is, where three are Tenants in Common, or Joynt - tenants, pro in - divisor, of a Mil ! or House which is fallen to decay, and the one being willing to repair it, the other two will not; in this Case, the Party willing lhal have this Writ against the other two.

repellent.c: REPELLENT ' Medicines, are such things as by flopping the Heat and Afflux of Humours, and by fllutting up the Pores with their cold and bind - ing Qualities, decrease thefwelling of a part, and drive the Humours another way.

repetition.c: REPETITION, fa Figure in Rhetorick ) is when a Person thinking his first Expression not well understood, and is impatient to make his hear - ers know what he means, repeats or explains them, another way.

repleaderinlaw.c: REPLEADER, in Law, is to plead against that which was once pleaded before.

replegiare.c: REPLEGIARE, signifies properly to redeem a thing detained or taken by another, by putting in legal sureties. See Replevin.
REPLEGIARE de averiis, is a Writ bought by one whose Cattle are distrained, or put in the Pound, upon any Cause by another, upon surety given to the Sheriff to Prosecute or Answer the Adfion in Law.

replevin.c: REPLEVIN, is a Writ that lies where a Man is Distrained for Rent or other thing, then he shall have this Writ to the Sheriff, to deliver to him the Distress, and shall find Surety to pursue his Action against the Distrained; and if he pursue it nor, or if it be found or judged against him, then the DR strainer shall again have the Distress, and he shall have in such Case a Writ called, Returno habendo. Goods may be replevied two ways, vi. by Writ; and that is by the Common Law; or by Plaint and that is by Statute Law for the more speedy having again of their Cattle and Goods.,

replication.c: REPLICATION, is an Exception of the second degree, made by the Plaintiff, upon the first An - fwer of the Defendant: It is also, that which the Plaintiff replys to the Defendants Answer in Chan - very, which is either General or Special. The Special is grounded upon Matter arising out of the Defendant ’ s Answer, &c. The General is lo called from the general Words therein used.

reportinlaw.c: REPORT, in Law, is a publick relation of Cafes Judicially argued, debated, resolved, or adjudged, in any of the King ’ s Courts of Justice, with the Cause and Realons of the fame delivered by the Judges. Also when the Chancery, or other Court, refer the starting of some Case, or comparing an Account, &c. toaMafterof Chancery, or other Referree, his Certificate therein is called, a Re - port.

reprises.c: REPRISES, is commonly ( in Law ) taken for Deductions and Duties which are Yearly paid out of a Mannor and Lands, as Rent - charge, Rent - feck, Pensions, Corrodies, Annuities, Fees of Stewards or Bailiffs, See. Wherefore when we speak of the clear Yearly value of a Mannor, we fay it is so much per Annum ultra reprifas, besides all Reprifes.

reprieveinlaw.c: REPRIEVE, in Law, is properly to take back, or suspend a Prisoner from the Execution and Pro - ceeding of the Law for that time.

reptjls.c: REPTJLS, are all those Creeping Animals which reft upon one part of their Body, while they ad - vance the other forward; as Adders, Afps, Snakes, Earthworms, Sxc.

rescelt.c: RES CELT, is an admission, or receiving a third Person to Plead his Right in a Cause formerly com - menced between other two; as if a Tenant for Life or Years bring an Action, he in the Rever - sion comes in, and prays to be received to defend the Land, and to Plead with the Demandant. The Civilians call this Admiffionem tertii pro suo in - ter esse. Refceit is also applied to an admittance of Plea, ' tho ’ the Controversie be only between two.

rescousorrescue.c: RESCOUS, or Rescue, in Law, is a resistance against lawful Authority; as if a Bailiff, or other Officer, upon a Writ do Arrest a Man, and others by Violence take him away, or procure his Escape, this is a Res ecus in Fail: So, if one distrain Beasts for Damage - feafantin his Ground, and as he drives them in the High - way towards the Pound, they enter into the owner ’ s House, and he witholds them there, and will not deliver them upon De - and, this Detainer is a Rescous in Law. It is also used for. a Writ which lies for this Salt, called Breve de Refcuffu. Rescous, in Matters relating to Treason, is Trealon; and in Matters concerning Felony, is Felony.

rescussor.c: RESCUSSOR, is he that commits such a Res - cous.

reservationinlaw.c: RESERVATION, in Law, signifies a Keeping or Providing; as when a Man Lets his Land, he reserves a Rent to be paid to himfeif for his Main - tenancy. Sometimes it signifies as much as an Ex - caption; as when a Man Lets a House, and re - serves. “ Te s serves to hiffifelf one Room, that Room is excepted out of the Demise. f

resianceorresidence.c: RESIANCE, or Residence, signifies a Man's A - bode or Continuance in one Place: And it is all One indeed with residence; but that Custom ties this only to Persons Ecclesiastical.

residence.c: RESIDENCE, is a Word peculiarly used both in the Common and Canon - Law, for the Com tinuance or Abode of a Parson or Vicar upon his Benefice.

residualfigure.c: RESIDUAL Figure, in Geometry, signifies the remaining Figure after Subtraction of a Lesser from a greater.

residualroot.c: RESIDUAL Root, in Mathematicks, is one composed of two Parts or Members only connected together with the Sign: Thus a b, or, is a Residual Root and is so called, because its true Value is no more than its residue or difference between the Parts a and b.

resignation.c: RESIGNATION, is a Word used for the giv - ing up of a Benefice into the Hands of the Ordi - nary, otherwise by the Canonijis termed Renuncia tion: And tho ’ it signifies all one in nature with the Word Surrender, yet it is by Custom restrained to the yielding up a Spiritual Living, and Surrender to the giving up of Temporal Lands into the Hands of the Lord.

retinainpharmacyandbotany.c: RETINA, in Pharmacy and Botany, is a fat and oleaginous Liquor flowing either Spontaneously, or else let out by Incision from any Tree or Plant. It will not dissolve in Water, but in Oil only, and is easily Inflammable.

resineorrefine.c: RESINE, or Refine, of Jalap, Benjamin, Scam - many, Turbith, &c. or of any Vegetable which abounds with Rofinous Particles, is thus made in Chymistry. The Vegetable grosly Powdered, is put into a Matrass, and then well rectified Spirit of Wine is poured on it to the height of four Fingers above the Matter; then another Matrass hath its Neck fitted and luted into the former to make a double Vessel; and thus the Matter is digested for or Days in a Sand Heat, or till it hath given a good TinChire to the Spirit of Wine: Then the DifTolution is fil - trated; and two Thirds of the clear Liquor is eva - ported off, the remainder is poured into a large Vessel of Water, and it will turn into a Milk, and the Refine will in time precipitate to the Bottom in a white Powder. It must be wash ’ d and dry ’ d in the Sun, and it will grow hard like common Ro - fine. RESfSTENCE of the Medium, is the opposition against, or hinderance of the Motion of any Body moving in a Fluid; as in the Air, the Water, the / Ether, &c. And this, together with the gravity of Bodies, is the Cause of the Cessation of the Mo - tion of Projectiles, ( c. This Resistence, in Me - diums which are very Dense and Rigorous, so that Bodies can there move but Very slowly, is nearly as the Velocity of the moving Body: But in a Me - dium free from all such Rigor, as the Squares of the Velocities, Newt. Princip. P.. For by the Action of a swifter Body, there is communicated to the fame Quantity of the Medium, a greater Mo - tion, in proportion to that greater Swiftness or Ve - locity; and therefore in an equal time, ( by reason of the greater Quantity of the Medium being mo - ved ) the Motion will be communicated in a dupli - case Ratio: But the Resistence must always be as the Motion communicated, because ACtion and Re - action are equally contrary. He found also the thing to be true by FxpefL ment, in a Pendulum of Feet in Length; that the Resistence against a Globe or Bail moving swift - ly in our Air, is nearly in a duplicate Ratio of its Velocity: But if it move Slower, a little greater than in that proportion, P.. He found also by making a Leaden Bullet swing as a Pendulum in a Vessel of Water, that the Re - fiftence of Water in proportion to Air is as LU art - Dr. Wallis hath an entire Discourse on this Sub - ject in Phil. Trans. N, where he premises as a Lemma, That supposing all other things equal, the Resistence of Bodies is always proportion a b; e to the Velocity; since in a double degree of Velo - city there is twice as much Air to be moved in the fame time, &c. As to the different Refiftences which Bodies of different Figures will find in palling through any Medium, Sir If. Newton proves, Prop s, Their.. That if a Globe and Cylinder with equal Dia - meters be moved according to the Direction of the ’ Axis of the Cylinder, that the Globes Resistence will be but half of the Cylinders. And in the following Scholium, he shew's what kind of Figure revolving round an Axis, will gent - rate a Solid that ( hall move in any Medium, with the least Resistence; and gives a hint of the Use that this may be of for Building of Ships. After this, several Inveftigations of the Figure of a roundish Solid, which should move through a Medium with the least Resistence, were Publish ’ d by the Marquis Hospital, Bernoulli, and very briefly and clearly by Mr. John Craig in the Phil. Tran fact, N. Where he solves the Problem, to deter - mine the Curve, by whose Rotation round an Axis, a round Solid shall be generated, which being moved according to the Direction of that Axis, shall have the least Resistence in any Medium.

resnaturales.c: RES Naturales: Natural things are Three Health, the Causes of Health, and its Effedfs. O - thers reckon Seven; as the Elements, Tempera - ments, Humours, Spirits, Parts, Faculties, Actions j but Elements and Temperaments belong to Natu - ral Philosophy; Humours, Spirits and Parts, are reckoned amongst the Caules of Health, which consist of a good Temperature, and a due Confor - motion; Faculties and Actions are comprehended under the Effects of Health, Blanchard,,

resnon.c: RES Non - naturales: Things that are not Natural, are Six: Air, Meat and Drink, Motion and - Reft, - Sleeping and Waking, the Affe & ions of the Mind, Things that are let out of, and things retained in the Body. They are so called, because that if they exceed their due bounds, they often occasion Dis - eafes. Blanchard.

resolvend.c: RESOLVEND, a term in the Extraction of the Square and Cube Roots, &c. signifying that Num - - ber which arises from augmenting the Remainder after Subtraction, by drawing down the next Square Cube, &c, and writing it after the said Re - mainder.

resolution.c: RESOLUTION ( in Mathematicks ) is a Me - tho of Invention, whereby the Truth or Faifhood of a Proposition, or its Possibility or Impossibility if discover ’ d, in an Order contrary to that of Synthesis, or Composition: For in this Analytical Method, the Proposition is proposed as already known, gran - ted, or done; and then the Confeqnences thence deducible are Examined, till at last you come to D loose W known Truth or Falftiood, or Impossibility, whereof that which was proposed is a necessary Consequence, and from thence j'uftly conclude the Truth or Impossibility of the Proposition: Which if true, may then be demonstrated in a Synthetical Method. This Method of Revolution consists more in the Judgment, Penetration and Readiness of the Enquirer or Artist, than in any Particular Rules: Tho ’ those of Algebra are of necessary Use, and a good Treasure of Geometry in his Head will be of great Advantage to him in all manner of Invefti - nations

resortorreftort.c: RESORT, or Reftort, is a Law Word, proper - ly used in a Writ of Tail of Coufenage, as Descent is in the Writ of Right.

respectu.c: RESPECTU computi viee - comitis hahendo, is Writ for the respiting of a Sheriff ’ s Account, upon just occasion directed to the Treasurer and Barons of the Exchequer.

respiration.c: RESPIRATION, ' kvamvwi, includes both In and Expiration, and is an alternate Dilatation and Con - traction of the Chest, whereby the Air is taken in by the Wind - pipe for the accension of the Blood, and by and by is driven out again with other Va - porous Effluviums. The cause of Respiration does not seem to consist in the Dilatation and Contra - ction of the Thorax, as is commonly thought, but in the Contraction of the Tunic, which covers the upper Part of the Oesophagus and the Wind - pipe, as far as its closest Recedes. Blanchard. There are many Opinions about the Uses of Re - spiration: Some think the chief, if not the some Design of it, is to cool and temper the Heat of the Blood, and the Heart. Others will have the Substance of the Air to get by Respiration into the Vessels of the Lungs to the left Ventricle of the Heart; not only thereby to cool the Blood, but also help generate aerial Spirits, This was the Opinion of Hippocrates, Arijlotle, and Galen. Others take, with more Probability, Respiration to serve for the Ventilation of the Blood in the Lungs, in its passage through them, whereby ’ tis disburthened of many Excrementitious Steams and Superfluous Serofities, which are carried off by the Breath in Expiration; so that the Blood may be advantageously depurated, by what is carried off by the EmunCtory of the Lungs. In the Phi Ins. Trans. Nts, there is a very pretty Account of the Cause and Manner of Relpirarion, by the Famous Laur. Bellini.

RESPIRATION. How such Globules of the Blood as by uniting together in the Veins, from others too large for any Secretion, and are there - fore necessarily afterwards broken on the Lungs by the Force of Respiration, Dr. Jfeil shews in his Animal Secretion, p., And to dlifcnate the Force by which the Air is thrust out of the Lungs, in Exfpiration he took a thin Hog ’ s Bladder which he could easily blow up with the Breath of one Exfpiration; and having moistened it, that it might neither resell the Air in blowing up, nor the Weights which were laid upon it: He fix ’ d a small Tube, whose Diameter was part of an Inch, to the Neck of the Bladder; and then filling the ! Bladder with Air, he put a Weight of lb. on the Top of it: And repeating the Experiment several Times, he found that this ’ Weight squeezed all the A ir out of the Bladder, through the small Tube in the Space of Vibrations of a Pendulum, swinging Seconds, and by a Calculation which he there gives, he found the Force by which the Aft is forced out of the Lungs at every Exfpiration to be equal to lb. Weight: And therefore. Aft ion and Bastion being Equal, The Pressure of the Air upon the Lungs every Exfpiration must be equal to the Pressure of lb. Weight. That is, up - posing the Gravity of the Air to be always the ' fame, and the Diameter of the Trachea the fame; also in every Exfpiration. But finoe we find by the Barometer, that there is Inches difference be - tween the greatest and the left Gravity of the Air, which is the Tenth - part of its greatest Gravity; there must be likewise the Difference of lb. Weight in ics Pressure upon the Lungs at one Time more than at another. He thinks no one Can doubt but that this Pressure of the Air on the Lungs in breathing, is sufficient to break the Globules of the Blood, and to dissolve all the Cohefions they might T con. - R E T contract: in their Circulation through the Veins and Arteries. And when the Blood is thus dillbived and thrown out by the Heart into the Aorta tis evident that the Re - union of the Particles requires more or lets Time, according to their several At - tractile Powers, even though they all moved with the fame Velocity, and in the fame Direction. But neither doth this happen, for a Fluid moves through a Cylinder or Conical VelTel ( such as the Arteries are ) with a greater Velocity at the Axis, than at the Sides. And again the Blood is thrust into the Aorta, by the whole Force of the Heart: And Fluids when they are pressed, press undequa - que; by which means the Arteries are dilated, and the Blood moves not only forwards, but likewise ppelTes perpendicular on the Sides of the Arteries: And as the Sides of the Arteries ( being Elastick ) return, they prels the Blood from them every way, which must produce an Intestine Motion, and so hinder the Attraction of the Particles; and by this frequent and strong Cohesion of the Particles of the Blood against the Sides of the great Arte - ries, the Cohefions of the Particles, if any of them happen to unite, will be immediately dissolved. Again, this Intestine Motion must greatly increase on the Account that many of the Particles of the Blood are Elastick: For by this Resistance of the Sides of the Vessels, they must necessarily hit one ga. inst another, and being Elastick, reflect from one another, and so increase the Intestine Motion of the Blood. On this Intestine Motion of the Blood its Heat depends; which therefore is every where proportional to the Impetus of the Particles against the Sides of the Vessels; supposing the Elasticity of the Particles every - where the fame. But the Itn - tetus of the Particles against the Sides of the Ves - lels decreases, as the Summ of the Cavities of the Vessels increases: And consequently where the Summ of the Cavities of the Vessels is greatest, there the Intestine Motion of the Blood is least, and the Attractive Powder of the Particles ( ceteris pa - rpbus ) is greatest.

respitedaword.c: RESPITED, a Word used in Law, for delay, for - abearance, or continuance of time.

respitedofhomage.c: RESPITED of Homage, is the forbearing of Ho - mage, which ought first of all to be perforrhed by the Tenant that holdeth by Homage and it had the most frequent use in such as held by Knights - Service in Cap ' to, who did pay into the Exchequer every fifth Term, some small Sum of Money, to be respited the doing of their Elomage. See the Stat. car. a. cap.. whereby this is taken away as a Charge incident or arising from Jfnights - Ser - vice.

responsalisinlaw.c: RESPONSALIS, in Law, he who gives an An - fwer, is he that appears for another in Court at a Day assigned: As if Effoigniator came only to de - clare, the Cause of the Parties Absence, whether Demandant or Tenant; and Responsalis came for the Tenant, not only to excuse his Absence, but also signifie, what Trial he meant to undergo.

restitution.c: RESTITUTION, the returning of Elastical Bodies forcibly bent to their natural State, is cal - led the Motion of Rejlitutioni RESTITUTION, in Law, signifies the yield - ing up again, or restoring of any thing unlawfully taken from another: As alio, the setting him in Possession of Lands or Tenements that hath been unlawfully disseised of them.

restitutions.c: RESTITUTIONS ex tragi ah Ecdefia, is a Writ to restore a Man to the Church, which he had recovered for his Sanctuary, being suspended of Felony.

restitutiontemporalium.c: RESTITUTION Temporalium, is a Writ that lies where a Man being Elected and Confirmed Bishop of any Diocese, and hath the King ’ s Royal Assent thereto for the recovery of the Temporalities or Barony of the said Bifhoprick and it is directed from the King to the Escheator of the County.

restraint.c: RESTRAINT, is when any Action is hundred or stopped contrary to Volition or preference of the Mind.

resummonsinlaw.c: RESUMMONS, in Law, signifies a Second Summons, and Calling of a Man to Answer an Atftion, where the First Summons is defeated upon any occasion, as the Death of the Party, or the like.

resumption.c: RESUMPTION, in a large Sense, signifies the taking again into the King ’ s Hands such Lands or Tenements, as before, upon false suggestion, or other Error, he had delivered to the Heir, or gran - ted by Letters - Patent to any Man.

retaining.c: RETAINING - Fee, is the first Fee given to any Serjeant or Counsellor at Law, whereby to make him lure that he shall not be on the contrary Part.

retemirabilc.c: RETE Mirabilc. In those Creatures that have the Glandula Pituitaria large, ( as in Calves for Instance ) the two Carotid Arteries meeting about the Sell a of the Wedge - like Bone, presently divide themselves into small Twigs, which being inter - woven with ( tho ’ not so numerous ) Twigs from the internal Jugular Veins, and also with nervous Fibres from the larger Trunk of the fifth Pair of Nerves, make on each side a notable Plexus, called Rete Mirabile. There enters into this Rete some Twigs also from the Cervical Arteries; and there pass out of it leveral Twigs into the Glandula Pi - tuitaria. So that in these Creatures that Gland seems to be of the fame use to the Rete Mirabile, as the Glandula Pinealis is to the Plexus Choroides, viz. To separate a serous Matter from the arterial Blood, But in Man ( according to most Anato -, mills ) this Rete is wholly wanting; so that there palling only sometimes a Twig or two, and feme - times none, from the Trunk it self of the Carotid Artery, into the Glandula Pituitaria, that Gland is of less use in him than in other Creatures that have the Rete. Yet Dr. Ridley affirms, That he never found this Rete wanting, or with any Diff - culty discoverable in Men, springing from, and ly - ing on the inside of each Carotid Artery: But con - senses that it is far smaller in them than in Brutes; for which difference he thus accounts. Brutes by reason of their prone Position, would, but for this Rete, be in danger of having their Brains deluged as it were with an over - great Quantity of the in - fluent Blood, and of a Rupture of the Vessels by its violent Ingress; and is this Danger so much the more threatened, by how much the fame Cause which brings it into the Brain with that force, is equally as great and effectual to hinder its proper - tionable A. R E T tionable return. For the. Relief of which Xnconve - nitency, Nature hath contrived a Means for its more easie and safe descent into the Brain, by turning that one largest Stream of Blood ( which through its being pent in one Channel, becomes so rapid j into many more, ( by which means the Carotid Trunk above the Dura Mater in those Creatures is very small to what it is beneath - whereas that Ar - tery in Men, hath the fame bigness on both ides the Membrane ) and they not only reticular - ted and contorted for the more flow and labori - ous descent of the Blood; ( which Contrivance the Ancients thought was only for a more ead Pre - pacation of the Blood for Animal Spirits, ) but also many of ’ em by their Insertion into the Glandula Pituitaria, attended with small Veins issuing thence, to take off some part of the Burthen too. And that to the aforesaid Position of leveral Creatures ou ght chiefly to be ascribed the variety of Magnitude of this Rete in several of them, its size in Dogs seems highly to evince; in whom, by reason of their Horizontal Position, being neither so prone as leveral Brutes who feed on Grass, nor so ered as Man, this Rete is found smaller than in the first, and larger than in the last.

retention.c: RETENTION, is a Faculty of the Mind, whereby it makes a farther Progress towards Knowledge.

RETENTION, is a Faculty of the Human Mind, whereby in Order to a farther Progress in Knowledge, it keeps or retains those Simple Ideas, which it before received by S sensation or Rcflellicn; arid this is done two Ways. Firftby keeping the Idea, which is brought into the Mind, for some Time actually in view, which is called Contem - lation: And Secondly, by Reviving again in our Minds those Ideas, which after imprinting have difappeared, or have been as it were laid out of fight: And this we do, when we conceive Heat or Light, Yellow, or Sweet, the ObjeCt in which those Qualities are, being removed: And this is called ’ Memory; which is as it were the common Store - house of all our Ideas. And our Ideas being nothing but Aftual Perceptions in the Mind, which cease to be any thing, when there is no Perception of them; This Laying up of our Ideas in the Re - pofitory of the Memory, signifies no more than this: That the Mind hath a Power in many Cafes, to revive Perceptions which it once had, with this Additional Perception annexed to them, That it hath had than before. And in this sense it is, that our Ideas are said to be in our Memory; when in - deed they are actually no where: But only there is an Ability in the Mind, when it will, to revive them again; and as it were paint them a - new on it self.

reticularis.c: RETICULARIS plexus, the fame with Cho - r oid. es.

retiformis.c: RETIFORMIS tunica, is the principal Organ of Sight, being a Certain Expansion Of the inner Substance of the Optic Nerve in the Eye, which is to the Eye like a whited Wall in a dark Cham - ber, and receives and represents the visible Spe - cies that are let in by a Hole as it were into a darkened Room.

retiradeinfortification.c: RETIRADE, in Fortification, is a kind of Re - trenchment made in the Body of bastion or other Works, which is to be disputed Inch by Inch, af - ter the first Defences are Dismantled. It usually consists of two Faces, which make a Re - entring Angle.

retort.c: RETORT, is an Instru - ment or Vessel in Chymistry, commonly of this Figure, used for Distillations of Oils and Volatile Salts, and also of Acid Spirits. ’ Tis sometimes made of Glass, sometimes of Earth, and sometimes of Iron, according to the Nature of the Matter to be Distilled, and the degree of Fire necessary to per - form the Operation. Earthen Retorts are bell for the drawing of Acid Spirits, because they will bear the utmost Heat and not Melt, as Glass ones will sometimes do. There - fore when you are forced to use a Glass Retort in so strong a Fire, it must be coated or covered over with Lute. See that Word. There is also another kind of Earthen Retorts, which are flat at the Bottom, and whose Nose or Beak turns upwards, which in great Furnaces are used for the Distillation of Acid Spirits; and they have Earthen Receivers Luted to them.

retractoresalarumnasi.c: RETRACTORES Alarum Nasi & Elevatores Lab ii Superioris: These Muscles arise broad and fleshy from the fourth Bone of t; he Upper Jaw, / RET whence defending obliquely, they are soon Infer - red to the Upper Lip, and Ala Nasi. The r Name shew their Use is to lift up the Nose and Upper Lip -

retrahensauriculum.c: RETRAHENS Auriculum, is a Mufde by some called Triceps Auris, because it has sometimes Be - ginnings. M. du Verney says it is Composed of five or fix fleshy Fibres, which have their Origination from the Superior and Forepart of the Apophysis Mafloides, and descend obliquely to their Infertioxi in the middle of the Concha Auricula.

retrenchmentinfortification.c: RETRENCHMENT, in Fortification; is a Ditch bordered with its Parapet, and secure ’ d with Gabions or Bavins laden with Earth. It is some - times taken for a Ample Retirade in part of the Rampart, when the Enemy is so far advanced, that he is no longer to be Refilled, or beaten from the first Post.

retrocession.c: RETROCESSION of the Equinoxes, is rhe Annual going backward of the Equinoctial Points about Seconds. See Equinoxes.

retrogradeinastronomy.c: RETROGRADE, in Astronomy, is ufiialiy ap - propriated to the Planets, when by their proper Motion in the Zodiack, they move backward of contrary to the Succession of the Signs: As from the second Degree of Aries to the first, Of. But this Retrogradation is only apparent, and occasioned by the Observers Eye being placed on the Earth: For to an Eye at the Sun, the Planet will appear always Dired, and never either Stationary or Retro grade.

returninlaw.c: RETURN, in Law, hath two several Applica - tions. ‘ The one is the Return of Writs by Sheri ffs and Bayliffs, which is only a Certificate made to the Court of that which he hath done touching the execution of their Writ directed to him. And this among the Civilians is termed Certificatorium: Of Returns in this Signification speaks the Statute of Wefimln. a Cap.. So is rhe Return of a Com - million, a Certificate or Answer to the Court of that which is done by the Commissioners, Sheriffs, or other, to whom such Writs Commiiiions, Pre - cepts or Mandates are directed. Also, certain Days in every Term are Called return Days, or Days in Bank; and so Hilary Term hath four Re - turns, viz. Ottabis Elilarii, Quin den a Hilarii, Cra - Jlino Purifications & Ottabis Purifications Eaftef Term hath Five, vi Quindena Pafche, Ties Pafche, Sense Pafche, Quinq. Pafche, and Crafiino afcen - fionis Domini. Trinity Term hath Four, Crafiino Trinitatis, Ottabis Trinitatis, Quindena Trinitatis Tres Trinitatis and Michaelmas Term Six, vi. T res Michaelis, Sense Michaelis, Crafiino Anima - rum, Crafiino Martini, Ottabis Martini, Quindena Martini. The other Application of this Word is in Case of Replevin for if a Man Distrain Cattle for Rent, &c. and afterwards justifie or a vow his Ad, so as it is found Lawful, the Cattle before - delivered unto him that was distrained, upon Se - curvity given to follow the Adion, hail now be returned to him that distrained them.

returno.c: RETURNO habendo, is a Writ that lies upon him that has avowed a Distress made of Cattle and proved his Distress to be lawfully taken for re - turning to him the Cattle distrained, which before were replevied by the Party distrained, upon Sure - ty given to Prosecute the Adion; or when the Plaint or Adion is removed by Recordari, or Acce - das ad Curiam, into the Court of Common - Pleas, and he whose Cattle were distrained makes De - fault, and doth not Prosecute his Suit. D z RETUR -

returnum.c: RETURNUM avetiorum, is a Writ Judicial, granted to one Impleaded for the taking the Cattle of another, and unjust detaining them contra vadium & Plegios, and appearing upon Summons, and is dismissed without Day, because the Plaintiff makes Default and it lies lor the return of the Cattle to the Defendant, whereby he was Summoned, or which were taken for Se curvity of his Appearance upon the Summons.

RETURNUM ineplegiabile, is a Writ Judicial, sent out of the Common - Pleas to the Sheriff for the final restitution or return of Cattle to the Owner, tinjuftly taken by another, as Damage pleas ant, and so found by the Jury before Justices of Aflizein the Country, or otherwise by Default of Profecu - tion.

revenue.c: REVENUE, lignifies properly the Rent that accrues to every Man from his Lands and Poles - lions.

reverberate.c: REVERBERATE: The Word lignifies pro - perly to strike, rested:, or beat back again. The Chymifts fay, Make the Flame Reverberate on the Cop pel. That is, Let either the Flame of the Wood be so blown with the Bellows, as that it may be beaten back down on the Metal or else, make the sides of the Furnace so close all about, that the Flame striking against its sides, may be beat back again down on the Matter to be Melted. For Which latter Purpose they have a Particular Fur - name called the

reverberatoryfurnace.c: REVERBERATORY Furnace which is a strong fixt Furnace of two Bricks thickness, and inst be large enough to hold a Retort, or more than one, for the Distillation of Acid Spirits, and other things. The Mortar or Lute for luch a Fur - name is usually one Part Potters Earth, as much Horse - dung, and two Parts of common Sand knead - ed in Water. The All - hole mull be about a Foot high, and the Door contrived, if possible, so as that the Air may come freely to it, to light the Fire the more easily, or to encrease the Flame. The Fire - place need not be quite so high: At the top of it are two Iron Bars placed cross - wile, to fet the Retort on and then the Furnace is rais ’ d about a Foot higher, to cover or close the Retort: Then is there fitted to this a Dome or Cover with its Him - new, which is fet on the top of the Dome on a little Hole, which when the Chimney is not used, hath a Stopple to it. This Dome may be made of the lame Past that Portable Furnaces are usually made of which fee under Furnaces. And one may make according to his Fancy, Room, or Convenience, a Furnace of this kind; and there is no need of keeping exactly to this Form, especially as to the Dome, which in a large Re - verberatory may be made with Tiles or Bricks placed over the Retorts, and Plaiftered over with a Lute made of Allies, melted with common Water. Here follows the Figure of Mr. Lemerys Rever - beratory, which will serve to give an Idea of the former Description. a The All - hole. e The Fire - place. I d The Dome or Cover. h The Chimney,; c The Receiver / The Retort. Such a Furnace as this, will also serve for many Uses, as well as Distilling per Reverb erdum as to Distil with the Refrigeratory, in Balneo, &c. for the Copper Body may be placed on the Bars, and the Vessel holding the Water, Sand, Allies, &c. as a little Practice will soon teach the young Chymist.

reversioninlaw.c: REVERSION, in Law, hath a double accept - tation, one is Jus revertendi cum flatus pojfejflonis defecerit, and this is but an Interest in the Land, when the Possession shall fall. Secondly, When the Possession and Estate which was parted with for a time, ceafeth, and is deter - mined in the Persons of the Alienees, Affignees, Grantees, or their Heirs, or effectually returns to the Donor, his Heirs or Afllgns whence it was de - rived. The Difference between a Reversion, and a Re - mainder's that a Remainder is general, and may re - main to any Man, but to him that granteth or con - veyeth the Land, &c, for Term of Life only, or o - otherwise. A Reversion is to himself, from whom the Conveyance of the Land, proceeded, and is Commonly perpetual, as to his Heirs also. And yet sometimes Rever [ ton is confounded with Re - mainder.

reviewabillofreviewinchancery.h: REVIEW a Bill of Review in Chancery
reviewabillofreviewinchancery.c: REVIEW, A Bill of Review in Chancery, is where a Cause hath been heard, and the Decree signed and enrolled and some Error in Law ap - pears upon the Decree made, which Bill cannot be exhibited, but by Licence of the Court.

revive.c: REVIVE, when any mix ’ d Body is restored a - gain to its Natural Form and Condition, from out of the Difguiles it was in, by being mixed with some other Body, they fay it is Revived. Thus when Mercury is distilled from Cinnabar, they call it Mercury revived from Cinnabar be - cause the Mercury was made into Cinnabar only for safety and convenience of its being carried from Place to Place. See Mercury, Bill RHO R I E Bill of REVIVER, is where a Bill Hath been exhibited in Chancery, against one who answers, and before the Cause is heard, or if heard, before the Decree enrolled, either Party dies: In this case a Bill of Reviver must be brought, that the former Proceedings may stand revived, and the Cause be finally determined.

revivinginlaw.c: REVIVING, in Law, signifies a renewing of Rents and Actions after they be extinguished.

revolutioninallronomy.c: REVOLUTION, in Allronomy, is the Circu - lation of any Celestial Body, till it return to the fame Point in which it was when it first began to move. But,

revolution.c: REVOLUTION, or as some call it, The Refli - tuition of the Anomaly, is the Return of a Planet to any one Point of its ccentricks, after it hath parted from it. , REVULSORIA, V. S. is whereby the Blood that guflies upon one part, is diverted a contrary way, by opening of a Vein in a remote and conve - tient place. This our Surgeons call frequently Bleeding for a Revuljion.

Thus a Right - angled Triangle revol - ving round one of its Legs, as an Axis, generates by that Revolution a Cone. rhabdology.c: RHABDOLOGY, is the Art of computing or numbering by those Rods, commonly called Ne - pers Bones; which fee.

rhachitis.c: RHACHITIS, is according to some, the Spinal Marrow; ( which see in its proper place: ) Also a Disease common amongst the English, which is an unequal Nourishment of the Body, accompanied with Looseness of Parts, Softness, Weakness, Faint - ness, Drowsiness, a great swelling Head, with Leanness below the Head; with Protuberances a - bout the Joints, crookedness of Bones, straitness of the Breast, swelling of the Abdomen, stretching of the Hypochondres, a Cough, &c. The English call it the Rickets: But because the occasion of it often lies in the Spinal Marrow, the Famous Glyjfon calls it appositely enough Rhachitis. Blanchard.

rhagadesthelatins.c: RHAGADES, the Latins fay Scijfura, Fijfurce, Rima, Chinks, Clefts, which as they happen in o - ther parts of the Body, Hands, Feet, Lips, the en - trance oL the Womb; so they may happen in the Fundament, in the Extremity of the Gut ReFlum, and in the Sphincter, or Muscle which closes the Fundament. Rhagades in the Fundament are cer - tain oblong little Ulcers, without swelling, like those which are sometimes occasioned in the Hands by great Cold. Some arefuperficial, others deep: Some are not hard nor callous, others are: Some are moist, and fend forth Matter, others dry and cancrous. Blanchard.

rhegma.c: RHEGMA, is a breaking forth or bursting of a - ny part, as of a Bone, the inner Rind of the Belly, the Eye, ff c,

rheumatism.c: RHEUMATISM, is a wandring Pain in the Body, often accompanied with a small Fever, Swelling, Inflammation, &c. Blanchard.

rhinenchytes.c: RHINENCHYTES, is a little Syringe to ' in - fed ! Medicines into the Nostrils.

rhombesolid.c: RHOMBE Solid, is two equal and right Cones joined together at their B fes.

rhgmbgides.c: RHGMBGIDES, so called from its Figure, is a pair of Muscles of the Scapula, proceeding from the two lowermost Vertebres of the Neck, and from the four upper Spinal Processes of the Verte - bres of the Back: By and by they descend oblique - ly, and being fieihy at the beginning and end, go as far as the Bails of the Shoulder - blade, which they move backward and obliquely upward: It adheres strongly to its Subjacent Muscle the Ser - ratus Superior Pqfticus.

rhombus.c: RHOMBUS See Quadrilateral Figures i RHUMBS. See Rumbs..

rhyqsadisease.c: RHYQS, a Disease of the Eyes, caused by a confumingor diminishing of the Caruncle, or small piece of Flefti in the great corner of the Eye, fb that it can no longer contain its Liquor. Blanchard, RHYPTICA are Scouring Medicines which cleanse away Filth. Blanchard,

rhythmus.c: RHYTHMUS, is a certain Proportion of Pulses, Time, Life; Age, z c, x Blanchard.

ribbonaterminheral.c: RIBBON, a Term in Heral - dry, signifying the eighth part of a Bend; it is born a little cut off from the out - lines of the Efcut - pheon, thus. He beareth Or, a Ribbon Gules. RXBBS of a Ship, are the Timbers of the P ut tocks when the Planks are off; so called, because they are bending like the Ribs of a Carcafe. Those little long wooden Pieces also which be - long to the Parrells of the Yards; and have holes in them like the Comb under the Beak - head, are called the Ribs of the Parrells.

rideaship.c: RIDE, a Ship is said to Ride, when her An - chors hold her fast, so that she drives not away by the force of the Wind or Tide; and a Ship is said to Ride well, when she is built so that she doth not over - beat her self into a Head Sea, as that the Waves over - rake her, ( that is over - wash her ) from Stem to Stern. They fay also a Ship,

rides.c: RIDES a - cross, when fire Rides with her Main - yards and Fore - yards hoisted up to the Hounds; and both Yards and Arms topped alike. She is said to

rideapeek.c: RIDE a Peek., when one end of the Yard is peeked up and the other hangs down: And this is also said of a Ship, when in Weighing she is brought directly over her Anchor, She is laid to

rideathwart.c: RIDE Athwart, when her Side is to the Tide. ' And to

ride.c: RIDE betwixt Wind and Side, when the Wind hath equal force over her one way, and the Tide another; but if the Wind hath more Power over her than the Tide, she is said to Ride Wind Rode. She is said to

ridehawsesul.c: RIDE Hawsesul, when in a Stress of Weather fire falls so deep into the Sea, with her Head, that Water runs in at her Hawses. She is said to RIDE Fortife, when her Yards are struck up - on the Deck, or when they are down Aportlajl.

rideauinfortification.c: RIDEAU, in Fortification, is a Ditch, the Earth whereof is raised on its side, or a small ele - vation of Earth, extending it self in length on a Plain, which serves to cover a Post, being also ve - ry Convenient for those that would besiege a Place at a near distance; and to secure the Workmen irs their Approaches to the Fort of a Forrrefs.

riders.c: RIDERS in a Ship, are great Timbers both in the Hold and also Aloft, which are bolted on to o - ther Timbers to strengthen them, When sis disc - vered a Ship is too weakly built.

riensarreare.c: RIENS Arreare, is a kind of Plea uled to an Action ofDebt upon Arrearages of Account, where - by the Defendant does alledge, There is nothing in Arrear.

riens.c: RIENS pause par le fairs is the Form of aft Ex caption taken in some Cafes to an Action c R I G RlENS er descent, is a Form of Pleading when I an Heir is sued for a Debt of his Ancestor, and he hath no Assets in his Hand, nor any Lands liable to be extended.

rigging.c: RIGGING of a Ship, is all her Ropes whatfoe - ver belonging to her Mads or Yards or any Part about her. A Ship is well Rigged, when all her Ropes are. of their fit size in proportion to her Burden. She is said to be over - rigged when her ropes are too big for her; which wrongs her much in her Sail - ing, and is apt to make her Heel.

rightinlaw.c: RIGHT, in Law, signifies not only a Right for which a Writ of Right lies, but also any Title or Claim, either by vertue of a Condition, Mort - gage, or the like, for which no Addon is given by Law,. but only an Entry. Thus is Jus Proprietatis, a Right of Propriety: Jus Pojfejfionis, a Right of Fofleffion: And Jus Proprietatis & Pojfejfionis, a Right both of Property and Pofleifion, and this was formerly called. Jus duplicatum: As if a Man be disseised of an Acre of Land, the Disseisee hath Jus Proprietatis thesis - seizor hath Jus Pojfejfionis, and if the Disseisee re - lease to the Difteifor, he hath Jus Proprietatis & Pojfejfionis. Right t - angled, a Figure is said to be Right - an - gled, when its Sides are at Right - angles, or stand Perpendicularly one upon another: And this is sometimes inallAngles of the Figures, as in Squares and Redl - angles: Sometimes only in part as in Right - angled Tri - angles. h si l - angled Tri - angle. See Tri - angle. Right t - Angles. See Angles.

right.c: RIGHT - afeenfon, of the Sun or Star, is that Degree of the Equinoctial, accounted from the be - ginning of Aries, which rifeth with it in a Right Sphere. Or, it's that Degree and Minute of the Equinocti - al ( counted as before ) which cometh to the Me - ridian, with the Sun or Stars, or with any Point of the Heavens - The reason of which referring it to the Meridian, is because that is always at Right Angles to the Equi nomial; which the Horizon only is in a Right or Dired Sphere. To find the Suns or Stars Right Afeenfon, by the Globe. Bring the Sun ’ s or Star ’ s Place to the Meridian, and the Number of Degrees intercepted between the beginning of Aries, and that Degree of the F. quint & ial which comes to the Meridian is the Right Afeenfon, if required in Time: Account every Degrees come an Hour, and every Degree to be Minutes. To find the Sun S Right Ascension Trigonometrically having his greatest Declination and Distance from the next EquinoCtial Point given; fay, As Radius is to the Co - fine of the Sun ’ s great efi Declination:: So is the Tangent of his Distance from the next EquinoCtial Point to the Tangent cf the Right Afeenfon. ry Example. Let the Suns Distance from the next Equinocti - al Point be Degrees co Minutes; his greatest Declination be Degrees Minutes. R I G Then to the Co - fine of C -. Add the Tangent of oo ‘ Sum Less Radius is the Tan. of s '. Which is the Right Afeenfon required. The fame may be also found, by having the pre - sent Declination, suppose Degrees Minutes ) and the greatest Declination Degrees, Mi - nutes given. For, As the Tangent of the Suns great efi Declinati - on, is to the Tangent ofhisprefent Declination:: So is the Radius to the Sine of his Right Afcen - fon. The Operation Hands thus: To the Ar. co. of the Tan. of /. Add the Tangent of n ‘ '. Summ adding the Radius S. '..
RIGHT Sine, the sarse with Sine - Which fee.

rightordirestsphere.c: RIGHT or Direst Sphere, is that which has the Poles of the World in its Horizon, and the Equator in the Zenith: The Consequences of living under such a Position, ( as those who live directly under the Line are in ) is that they have no Latitude, nor Elevation of the Pole. They can fee nearly both, Poles of the World j all the Stars do Rife, CuimU name, and fet with them. And the Sun always rises and descends at Right Angles to their Hori - zon, and makes their Days and Nights even; be - cause the Horizon bifleds the Circle of his Diur - nal Revolution. To find the Right Ascension of a Planet, or Star that hath Latitude, use this Proportion. As Co - fine of the Stars Declination is to the Co - fine of its Distance from the next Equinoctial Point:: So is the Co - fine of its Latitude, to the Co - fine of its Right Ascension.

rightthehelm.c: RIGHT the Helm, a Sea Phrase, used by him that Conds to the Man at Helm, ordering him to keep the Helm even with the Middle of the Ship.

rightline.c: RIGHT Line, is the nearest Distance between any two Points. See Line.

rightmuscles.c: RIGHT Muscles of the Head. See Reftus In - ternus Major Minor.

rightsailing.c: RIGHT Sailing, is when a Voyage is perform ’ d on some one of the four Cardinal Points.; If a Ship fail under the Meridian; that is, on the North or South Points, fire variety not in Lon - gitude at all; but only changeth the Latitude, and that just so much as the Number of Degrees ihe hath run. If a Ship fail under the Equinoctial, upon the very East or Weft Points, Ihe altereth not her La - titude at all, but only changeth the Longitude, and that just so much as the Number of Degrees Ihe hath run. If the Ship fail directly East or Weft under any Parallel, she there also altereth not her Latitude, but only the Longitude; yet not ac - cording to the Number of Degrees of a great Circle Ihe hath sailed, as under the Equinoctial; but more more than fb many, according as the Parallel is re - mater from the Equinoctial towards the Pole: For the less any Parallel is, the greater is the Difference of Longitude.. ' ' ‘.

rigor.c: RIGOR, is a Vibration and Concuffiori of the Skin, and Muscles of the whole Body, accompt - nied with Chilnefs.

rigorous.c: RIGOROUS way of explicating Rarefaction is, as it is called by the Moderns, th Lt which is made use of in the Peripatetick School; which fee under EarefaBion.

rim.c: RIM, in a Watch or Clock, is the Circular part of the Balance thereof;

ringofsaturn.c: RING of Saturn is an Opacous Solid, Circu - lar Arch and Plane, like the Horizon of a Globe, of Matter entire encompassing round the Planet and no where touching it; its Plane is at this Time nearly parallel to the Plane of our Earth ’ s E - quator: The Diameter of this Ring is f Sa - turn's Diameters, and the Distance of the Ring from the Planet, is about the breadth of the Ring it self. Galileus first discovered the Figure of Saturn not to be round; but that the Inequality was thus iii the Form of a Ring, Mr Hugens first found out and published in his Syjlema Saturniana,, ’ Tis this Ring, and its various Positions in relpecft of the Sun, f whose Light it refletftslike the Body of Saturn vc self ) and of the Eye of the Spectator which occasions all the various Appearances of Sa - turn with his Aufa ( as they call them ) or with none, with broad, or narrow ones, &c. The following Figures which I borrowed frOrri Dr. Gregorys Astronomy, will very well ilk - ftrate this Matter, The first is a single Figure of the Planet, when his Ring is most visible: And the second explains the several Phenomena of the Ring in all its Po - sition, in refpetft of the Sun at S. during the Pla - nets entire Revolution round the Sun. When the Planet is at A or I, the Ring is scarce visible, be - I cause the Sun ’ s Rays running almost parallel to ir, j can illuminate it but very sparingly. " But when Saturn is at E. or N. then the Sun ’ s Rays falling, almost dire & ly upon the Ring, do render it most J of all confpieuous.

riotinlaw.c: RIOT, in Law, signifies the forcible doing of an unlawful thing by three or more Persons affem - bled together for that purpose.

rising.c: RISING of the Sun or Star, is their appearing above the Horizon. The Rifmg of the Sun may be found by the Globe thus. First rectifie the Globe ( which Word fee; ) then bring the Sun ’ s Place to the East part of the Hori - zon; and the Hour Index will hew the Time ei - ther before or after Six. The Time of the Sun ’ s Rising doubled, gives the Length of the Day. The Rjjing of any Star, may be thus found by he Globe; Re & isle your Globe and Hour Index; bring the Star to the East, and the Index Will hew the Time of the Star ’ s Rising;

risingtimbers.c: RISING Timbers in a Ship, are the Hooks pia -: ced on her Keel; and are so called, because as these rife in Proportion, so her Rake and her Run rife & n her flat Floor by ROM R O P The RISINGS in a Ship are those thick Planks which go fore and aft, on both Sides under the End of the Beams and Timbers of the second Deck unto the third Deck, half Deck, and quar - ter Deck; and on them the Beams and Timbers of the Deck do bear at both ends by the Ships side.

risussardonius.c: RISUS Sardonius, is a Contra & ion of each Jaw, or a Convulfivekind of Grinning caufedby a Con - traction of the Muscles on both sides of the Mouth. ' Blanchard.

riversandsprings.c: RIVERS and Springs; whence they arise, fee under the Word Vapour. A ROAD, is any place near the Land where the Ships may Ride at Anchor, and a Ship riding there is called a Roader.

robbins.c: ROBBINS in a Ship, are those small Lines which make tlie Sail fast to the Yards, being ree - ved into Eylet - holes in the Sail under th Head - rope, for that purpose. The Word is, Make fast the Bobbins: For at Sea they don ’ t fay tie, but make fast.

rollinlaw.c: ROLL, in Law, signifies a Schedule of Paper or Parchment, which pay be turned or wound up with the Hand to the Fafliion of a Pipe; of which there are in the Exchequer several kinds: As, The great Wardrobe Bplf the Cofferer s Bpll, the Subsidy Boll, &c.

ropes.c: ROPES, of a ship are in General all her Cor - age; But Particularly they call by this Name only, . The Entriug - rope which hangs at the Ladder to help People up the Side. . A Top - rope, so called, because belonging to the Top. . A Bolt - rope, into which the Sail is sowed. . A Buoy - rope, which is that to which the Buoy of the Anchor hangs. . The Guest - rope, which tows the Long Boat. . The Keel - rope. . The Bucket - rope, which serves to heave the Bucket in drawing Water. . The studier - rope, which reaved into a Hole of the Rudder near the Head, and also through the Stern - post, both the Ends thereof are spliced together, serving to save the Rudder, if by any Accident it should be beaten off. Also the Preventer - rope, which is a small Rope, seized. cross over the Ties, close at the Ram - head; so that if any one part of the Tie ffiould be broke yet the Remainder ffiould not run Through the Ram - head, to endanger the Yard. There is also a Rope called a Brest - rope, which Lafhes the Parrels to the Mails. And another called the Guy - rope, which is ree - ved through a Block, fastned by a Strop, to the Head of the Fore - matt, and having its end fatten - ed to the Strop of the Winding Tackle to bowse it forwards that it may plumb directly over the Hatch Way, tal than either. / Ar And I il n'Vi iVimir - -: i r And there is also a Boat - rope, by which the Boat hangs, Or is fattened a Stern of the Ship.

rope.c: ROPE - yarn, is the Yarn of any Rope untwist - ed: Tis commonly made of Cables Ends which are Worn out, which are called Junks of the Ca - bles: The Use of it is to serve small Ropes, to make Sinner Matts, &c. also to make Knettles which are of these Rope Yarns, untwisted, toge - ther: Also it helps to make Caburns, i. e. Lines to bind Cables withal and to fatten the Sails to the Yard Arms, &c.

roriferusduflus.c: RORIFERUS Duflus, the fame that Ductus Chyliferus.

ros.c: ROS, in the Account of the Ancients, was the First Moisture that falls from the Extremities of the Vessels, and is dispersed upon the Substance of the Members. Bps, says Galen, is a Third fort of Moisture whereby the Parts of our Body are nou - wished, and is contained in all the Parts of an A - animal, like a certain Dew sprinkled upon them. Blanchard.

rosvitrioli.c: ROS Vitrioli, according to Ang. Sala, is the first Phlegm or Water that is distilled from Vitriol in Balneo Maries.

rosinesofvegetables.c: ROSINES, of Vegetables how made. See Be fine.

rostruminchymistry.c: ROSTRUM in Chymistry, is the Nose of an Alembick.

rotaariftctelica.c: ROTA Ariftctelica, is the Consideration of a Wheel moving along a Plain, till it hath made one entire revolution: For then will its Centre have de - scribed a Line equal to that of the Circumference of the Wheel, and so will all letter Concentrical Circles. See an Explication of this in Boyle against Linus.

rotatormajor.c: ROTATOR Major & Minor, are two. Apophy - fes in the upper Part of the Thigh - Bone, called T richanteres, in which the Tendons of many Muscles are terminated.

rotula.c: ROTULA, the fame that Mol a genu. ROTUL E, See Tabellre.

rotundus.c: ROTUNDUS, ( Sc. Muf cuius ) is a Muscle of the Radius, serving to turn the Palm of the Hand downwards.

round.c: ROUND, is a Military Term, signifying a Walk or Turn, which an Officer attended with a Few Soldiers, takes in a Garrison or Fortifi ’ d Place during the Night, to observe whether the Gentries do their Duty, or not.
ROUND - W / ?, is the uppermost Room or Cab - bin on the Stern of the Ship where the Matter lies.

ROUND - ? ?, or Bound - aft, a Term at Sea be - longing to the Main and Fore - fail: When the Wind largeth, they fay, Let rife the Main - tacks, or the Fore - tack ! Hale aft the Fore - Jbeet to the Cat - head; and the Main - fioeet to the Cubbridge - head And when these Sheets are thus haled down, they keep them from flying up with the Paffar ado - rope. This Work is called, rounding in, or round - ing aft the Sail. R WE in a Ship, is a round piece of Wood or Iron, wherein the Whip goes, being made to turn about, that it may carry over the Whip the easier from side to side.

rowse.c: ROWSE in the Cable, or Bpxvfe in the Hawfr, is a Word of Command at Sea, when a Cable or .: ' Hawser lies too slack in the Water, and they would have it be made more taught; left on the turning of the Tide, the Cable should happen to be foul of the Anchor.

And also to a Bill parted in both Houses of Par - ligament which Assent, in Parliament, being once given, the Bill is endorsed with these Words, Le Boy le vault, i. e. It pleases the Kjng: But if he re - uses to agree to it, then thus j Le By S ' avifera, i. e; The King will Advise.

royalparapet.c: ROYAL Parapet, or, Parapet of the Bampire, in Fortification, is a Bank about three Fathoms broad, and fix Foot high, placed upon the Brink of the Bampire, towards the Country, to cover those who defend the Bampire.

rubigoormildew.c: RUBIGO, or Mildew, is a Disease happening to Plants, caused by a Dewy Moisture which falling upon them, and continuing there for want of fuf - scient Heat of the Sun to draw it up, doth by it ’ s Sharpness, or Acrimony, scorch and Corrupt the In - most Substance of the Plant.

ructationorbelching.c: RUCTATION, or Belching, is a deprived Motion of the Stomach, occasioned by an Efter - vefcence there, whereby Vapours and Flatulent Matter are sent out at the Mouth. Blanchard.

rugitus.c: RUGITUS, is an Effervescence of Chyle and Excrements in the Blood, whereby Wind and fe - veral other Motions are excited in the Guts, and rowl up and down the Excrements, when there ’ s no easie Vent upwards or downwards. Blan - chard.

ruleofthree.c: RULE of Three, or the Bple of Proportion or as it is called, from its excellent Use, The Golden Rule, is that which teaches to find a Fourth Num - ber, which ( hall have the fame Proportion so one of the three Numbers given, as the others have to one another. This Rule of Three is,. Direct.. Indirect. Double - Bule Dir eft.. Double - F ( ule Indirect. Rule of Three Dir eft finds a fourth Number in such Proportion to the Third, as the second is to the first; or, as the first is to the second, so is the third to the fourth i Thus. E R U L R U L i i. z::: This Rule requires ( and is to be known thus: ) That if the second Term be greater or less than the first, the fourth Term shall be likewise greater or lesser than the third. Or in the Question, if more require more, or less require less, then use this Rule DireB and Multiply the second and third Terms together, and divide the Product by the first Term, the Quotient gives the fourth Term required. Note That the first and third Terms, and the second and fourth, are of the fame Denomination: As if the first be of Money, Weights, or Measures, &c. so ( hall the third and so as the second, the fourth. In this Rule, if you Multiply the second and third Terms together, the Product shall be equal to the Prod ud: of the first Term multiplied by the fourth Which may very well serve for a Proof, if required.

RULE of Three hi air eel, or the Backward Rule, is known by being contrary to the DireB; for whereas the former required., that more shall have more, and less less; as if Yards cost s. Yards will cost more than s. because it is double to Yards, and so must the Answer be double to s. that is s. But in this Rule, more will require less, and less more; as, if Horses in Days eat Bulhels of Oats,. Horses will eat Bufhels in a sewer quantity of Days, vi. in. Here Bufhels be - ing common is omitted, and the Question stands thus: :::; ' Here the third Term contains the first, as often as the second doth the fourth: Therefore the Pro - duct of the first and second divided by the third, gives the fourth, As, that the fourth Term required. The Double Rule of Three, both DireB and Indi - reB, may be comprised in one Rule, with two Operations only. I. Observing, That the given Terms are always five, whereof three are Conditional and Antece - dent, or Suppofitious, the other two demand the Question, and are Consequents answering some of the former Antecedents; insomuch, that with the Answer there will be as many Consequents as An - tecedents, which must match one another in the fame Denomination exactly. . For the right placing of the Question and Terms, the three Terms of the Conditional part are duly to be regarded: Let that which is the Principal Cause of Loss or Gain, Increase or De crease, Addon or Passion be put in the first place - and that which betokeneth the space of Time, Di stance of Place, &c. be put in a second Place - and the remaining part in the third. The Conditional part thus stated, the other two Terms where - in the Demand lies, must be placed so under the former Terms, that they may correspond one with another. RULE. I. Then, If the Blank., or Place fought, fall under the third Term, Multiply the three last Terms for a Dividend, and the two first for a Divisor, and the Quotient gives the sixth Term required. RULE II. But, If the Blank, fall under the first or second Terms, Multiply the first, second, and fifth Terms for a Dividend, and the third and fourth for a Di - visor, the Quotient gives the Answer. rumbinnavigation.c: RUMB, in Navigation, is one Point of the Corri - pass, or: Degrees, viz. the k part of the Cir - cumference of the Horizon or Compass Card, which is the Representative of the Horizon.

rumb.c: RUMB - Liwe, is a Line described by the Ship ’ s Motion on the Surface of the. Sea, Steered by the Compass, making the lame or equal Angles with every Meridian. There thumbs are Helifpherical or Spiral Lines, proceeding from the Point where we stand, wind - ing about the Globe of the Earth till they come to the Pole, where at last they lose themselves. But in the Plain and Mercators Charts, they are represented by strait Lines. Their Use is to shew the bearing of any two Places one from ano - ther ' that is, upon what Point of the Compass any Shore or Land lies from another.

ruminantanimals.c: RUMINANT Animals, are such as chew the Cud.

RUMINANT Animals, are such as chew the Cud; and these are Quadrupeds, Hairy and Vi - viparous, and in general, Mr. Pay observes of them, that some have hollow and perpetual Horns j others Deciduous ones, or such as are shed every Year and all the Horned Ruminant Animals have four Stomachs. I. The Ko / a la, Ms ' ah of Arifiotle the Venter Magnus, or what we call the Paunch or Inward. This receives the Meat lightly chewed, retains it a while, and then delivers it back again into, the Mouth, which is what we call the Cud, to be re - chewed and rendred more fit to make Chyle,. The KiKf thpaK ', or Reticulum, which we call the Honey - Comb from its Internal Coat, being divided R U divided To into Cells like Honey - Combs.. The which Mr. R ) ' thinks hath been wrong ! Translated, Omafus; and therefore he would have it called the Echinus: This is so difficult to clear, that our People throw it away, and call it the Manifold.. The ’ ’ Hvvc'eyv of Ariftotls, by Qa a called the Ahomafus. The Stomach in Calves is that which contains the Acid Ferment, which we call the runnet, and is used to coagulate Milk into Cheese Also all Horned Ruminant Animals want the Dentes Primores, or broad Teeth in the Upper jaw. These Kind of Animals have also that Kind of Fat which we call Suet Sebum, Sts ?, which is much harder and simmer, and less liquifi - able in them, than the Adept of other Animals.

rumination.c: RUMINATION, is the Action of chewing the Cud in some Animals -, J. Con Peyerus hath Writ - ten a Tract. De Ruminant ibtis & de RuminaAonc, Printed at Base, in to. In which he takes No - tice, That some Animals do really and truly chevv the Uud j such as Oxen,. Sheep, Deer, Goats of all Kinds, Camels, Hares, and Squirrels; which therefore generally have Stomachs, the Paunch, the Feck, and the Read. But those which seem only to imitate that Motion, he calls Ruminant ia Spuria; luch as the Mole, Cricket, Bee, Beetle, Crab, Lobster, Mullet, and several Birds. And these he affirms to have all of them their Stomachs composed of Mulcular Fibres, by means of which, they do as it were grind and work their Meat up and down something like Ruminating Creatures. He defines Rumination to be a Natural Motion of the Sto - mach, Mouth, and other Parts, which relieve one a - nother in this Action - by which means, the Meat ' eaten hastily at fir ft, is conveyed back to the Mouth again, there Chewed, and then Swallowed down are - cond time, to the great Advantage of the Animal.

rungs.c: RUNGS, the fame with the Floor or Ground - Timbers, being the Timbers in a Ship which end - statute her Floor, and are bolted to the Keel, whose ends are Rung - heads.

runner.c: RUNNER, is a Rope belonging to the Garnet, and to the two Bolt - tackles, vi. That before which comes in the aftermost Shrouds of the Fore - Mast, and that abaft which comes in the foremost Shrouds of the Main - Mast, This Runner is reeved in a Angle Block which is seized to the end of a Pendant, and has at the one end a Hook to hitch into any thing, and at the o - ther end. a double Block, into which is reeved the fall of the Tackle or the Garnet, by which means it doth Purchase more than the Tackle or Garnet can do alone. The Word is Overhale the Runner; that is, bring down that end which has the Hook to it, that it may be hitched into the Sling, &c.
