razing.c: RAZING is a Kind of Soldering of Iromf when the Work is so thin that it will not bear Welding; they lay small pieces of Brass on the Place that is to be brazed, and strew a little Pow - der of Glass upon it to make the Brass run, and give it an Heat in the Forge till they find that the Brass is run, and then they take it out and let it cool.

ruleofaugufi.c: RULE of Augufi, is the Day of St Peter ad Vincules, celebrated formerly and now on the first of Augufi. See Hofpinian de Origine Fejk - rum, Sol..

radechenistorsindooms.c: RADECHENISTORS in Dooms - day - book, is tied for Liberi - Homines; and Spelman thinks it to be what Bracha calls Radc - knights.

radical.c: RADICAL - Curves are Curves of the Spiral - kind, whose Ordinates, if they may be so called, do all terminate in the Centre of the including Circle, and appear like so many Radii or Semi - diameters of that including Circle. See Spiral.

ragman.c: RAGMAN is a word often used in Dooms - day, and seems to be the fame with Made - knight or Rad - kjiight. Others think it comes from Read, Counsel, and then Read man, is a Counsellor.

RAGMAN, is a Statute so called, of Justices assigned by K - Ed.. and his Counsel, to go a Circuit through all England, and to hear and de - terming all Complaints of Injuries done within Years next before Michaelmas, in the fourth Year of his Reign. Coweh

rafters.c: RAFTERS, in any Building, arethofe Pieces of Timber, which stand by pairs upon the Reason, meet in an Angle at the Top, and help to compose the Roof of a Building: They should not stand farther than Inches from one another. Q U O in our Old Synods and Episcopal Constitutions. Rennet Par. Antiquities. rain.c: RAIN - BOW, In Order yet further to explain the Phenomena of the Rain - bow Sir Isaac Newton in his Excellent Treatise of Opticks, p.. Ad - hances this Proposition. By the Properties of Light ( discovered by his New Experiments ) to explain the Colours of the Rain - bow. This Bow never appears but where it rains in the Sun - shine; and it may be artificially made by spouting out Water, which by breaking aloft shall scatter into Drops, and fall like Rain; for the Sun on these Drops certainly causes the Bow to appear to an Eye duly posited to the artificial Rain, and the Sunt And hence it is now agreed, that this Bow is made by the Refraction of the Sun ’ s Light in Drops of falling Rain. This was understood by some of the Ancients, and of late more fully dil - covered, and explained, by Antonins de Dominis, A. Bp. of Spalato in Libra de I adiis vtfus & lucis: Printed at Venice, A. D.. and written above Years before. He ( hews there, how the Inte - rior Bow is made in round Drops of Rain by a Refraction of the Sun ’ s Light, and one Reflexion between them; and the Exterior by two RefraCti - onS and two Sorts of Reflexions between them in each Drop of Water: And he proves his Explica - tions by Experiments made with a Phial full of Water; and with Globes of Glass filled with Wa - ter, and placed in the Sun, to make the Colours of the two Bows appear in them. The fame Expli - cation Des Cartes hath pursued in his Meteors, and mended that of the Exterior Bow. rains.c: RAINS: Our Seamen call thatTratft of the Sea to the Northwards of the Equator bet. and o Degrees of Latitude, and lying between the Me - ridian of Cape Verde, and that of the Eaftermoft Islands of the fame Name, of of the Cape Verde Islands, they call this Traci the Rains Because there are almost continual Calms, conflant Rains, and Thunder and Lightning to a strange Degree there and the Winds, when they do ever blow are only small uncertain Guts, and fliift about all round the Compass so that Ships are sometimes here detained a long While, and can make but very little way.

randezvous.c: RANDEZVOUS, in a Military Sense, is a Place appointed by the General of an Army, for all the Forces to meet on a Day appointed; let what Weather, c. happen that will.

rank.c: RANK, in a Military Sense is the Order or strait Line made by the Soldiers of a Battallion, or Squadron drawn up side by side. Doubling of Ranks is putting two into one.

rapaciousanimals.c: RAPACIOUS Animals, are in general such as live upon Prey: And ’ cis a general Division of Birds, into such as are Rapacious and Carnivorous, and such as are Frugivorous. The Charadteriftidk notes of Birds of Prey are that they have a great Head and a short Neck, hooked, strong and fliarp poin - ted Beak and Talons, fitted for ravine and tearing of Flesh strong and brawny Thighs for striking down their Prey: A broad thick fleshy Tongue like that of a humane Creature j Feathers in their Train and Z flag Feathers in each Wing. The two Appendices, or blind Guts, are always very short They have a Membranous Stomach, and not a Mufeulous one or a Girard, such as Birds have that live on Grain: They are very sharp - sighted, and are not Gregarious, but Solitary generally speaking, though Vultures will fly or in a Company.

rapheinanatomy.c: RAPHE, in Anatomy, is a Ridge or Line which runs along the Under - side of the Penis, and reach - ing from the Frcenum to the Anus, divides the Scrotum and Perineum in two. This line is not usually cut in the Grand Operation of cutting for the Stone, because ’ tis both harder than the Reft of the Skin there - abouts, and also because you must then cut upon the Interstices of the Muscles, which will make the Re - union the more difficult.

ration.c: RATION, is now, in the Army, a Word in use for a certain Proportion of Ammunition - Bread of Sorrage distributed to every Man in the Army, as his Portion for such a Time.

ravishmentdegarde.c: RAVISHMENT de Garde was a Writ that formerly lay for the Guardian by Knights Service, or in Soccage, against him that took away from him the Body of his Ward.

raysoflightwithregardtoopticks.h: RAYS of Light with Regard to Opticks
raysoflightwithregardtoopticks.c: RAYS of Light with Regard to Opticks, are by Sis If. Newton considered, as the lash Parts of that wonderful Fluid and that as well such as are fuccejjive in the fame Lines as contemporary in fe - veral Lines: For ’ tis manifest that Light consists of Parts both fuccefllve and contemporary be - cause in the fame place you may stop that which comes one moment, and let pass that which comes presently after, and in the fame Time you may stop it in any one place, and let it pass in an - other. Wherefore the least Light, or part of Light, which may be stopt alone without the reft of the Light or propagated alone, or do or suffer any thing alone, which the reft of the Light doth not, or suffers not, he calls a Ray of Light. The Mathematicians indeed usually confider the Rays of Light to be Littes reaching from the lum - nous Body to that Illuminated; which were just if Light were propagated in an Instant, as some have supposed: But the Observations of the Eclipses of Jupiter s Satellites made first by Mr. Ropier, do hew that ’ tis propagated in Time, and in particular that it takes up about Minutes in - moving from the Sun to the Earth. The The incomparable Sir If. Nevoton in his Opt. Book Part. p.. After having premiied p.. that thole Surfaces of transparent Bodies re fled the greatest Quantity of Light, which have the great - test Refracting Power; and also that in the Con - fines of equally refrading Mediums there is no Reflexion; and at fag.. That the Transparent parts of Bodies according to their several Sizes mull rested R ays of one Colour, and transmit those of another on the fame Grounds, that thin Plates or Bubbles do transmit or rested those Rays; which he takes to be the ground of all their Co - lours: proceeds, in his Eighth Proposition to enquire into the Cause of the Rays of Lights being rested - ed, and he ( hews that the Cause of Reflexion is nos the impinging of Light on the solid or simper - vious Parts of Bodies as hath commonly been be - lieved as appears from the following Confiderati - ons. ( ) That in the Passage of Light out of Glass into Air, there is a Reflexion as strong as in its Passage out of Air into Glass, and rather some - thing stronger, and much stronger than in its Pas - sage out of Glass into Water: And it seems not probable that Air should have more refleding Parts than Water r Glass. But if that could be supposed it would not do, because the Reflexion is as strong or stronger when the Air is drawn away from the Glass ( as suppose in the exhausted Receiver of Mr. Boy / e ’ s Air - pump ) as when it is adj - cent to it. ( ) If Light in its Passage from Glass to Air be Incident more obliquely than at an Angle of or gr. it is wholly reflected but if less obliquely, it is in a great Measure transmitted. Now it is not to be imagined that Light at one Degree of Obliquity should meet with Pores enough in the Air to trans - mit the greatest Part of it, and at another Degree of Obliquity should meet with nothing but Parts to refletl it wholly; especially considering that in its Passage out of Air into Glass, how obliquely bever it falls, it finds Pores enough in the Glass to transmit the greatest Part of it If it be said, that it is not reflected by the Air but by the ut most Superficial Farts of the Glass there is still the fame Difficulty: Besides, that such a Suppo - sition is un - intelligible, and will also appear to be false by applying Water behind some part of the Glass instead of Air. For so in a convenient Ob - liquity of the Rays, as suppose of or gr. at which they are all reflected where the Air is ad - jacent to the Glass, they shall be in a great Mea - sure transmitted where the Water is adjacent to it: Which argues, that their Reflexion or Trans - mission depends on the Constitution of the Air and Water behind the Glass, and not on the ( liking of the Rays upon the Parts of the Glass. ( J If the Colours made by a Prism placed at the Entrance of a Beam of Light into a darkened Room, be fuccefllvely cast on a second Prism pla - ced at a greater Distance from the former, in such manner that they are all alike incident upon it; the second Prism may, be so enclined to the Incident Rays, that those which are of a blue Co - lour shall all be reflected by it, and yet those of a red Colour pretty copiously transmitted. Now if the Reflexion be caused by the Parts of Air and Glass, how comes th blue, at the fame Obliquity of Incidence, wholly to impinge on those Parts so as to be all reflected, and yet the Red find Pores enough to be in a great Measure transmitted ? ( ) Where Glasses touch one another, as he shews in the. first Observation, there is no sensible Reflexion, yet why should not the Rays of Light impinge on the Parts of Glass, as much when con - tiguous to other Glass, as when so to Air ? ( ) When the Top of a Bubble of Water in Obs.. at last began to grow very thin, there was so very little Light reflected from it, that it appeared intensely black. ', and yet round about where the Water was thicker, the Reflexion was so strong as to make the Water to appear very white. Nor is it only at the lead: Thickness of Bubbles and thin Plates that there is no manifest Reflexion, but at many others continually greater and greater: For he found ( in Obfer.. ) that Rays of the fame Colour Were by turns transmitted at one Thick - ness, and reflected at another, for an indeterminate Number of Succeflions; and yet in the Surface of the thinner Body, where it is of any one Thick - ness, there are as many Parts for the Rays to im - pine on, as where it is of any other Thickness. ( ) If Reflexion were caused by the Parts of refleding Bodies, it would be impdflible for thin Plates or Bubbles at the fame place to rested the Rays of one Colour and transmit those of another, as by the and Observations ’ tis plain they do: For it is not to be imagined that at one Place the Rays which ( for Instance ) exhibit a Blue, should have the Fortune to dash upon the Parts; and those which exhibit a Red should fall upon the Pores of the Body: And then at another Place, where the Body is either a little thicker or thin - ner; that on the contrary, the Blue should fall on its Pores, and the Red upon its Parts polished. ( ) Were the Rays of Light reflected by im - ringing on the solid Parts of Bodies, their Refle - xions from these Bodies could not be so regular as they are. For in polishing with Sand, Glass, Putty, or Tripoly; it is not to be imagined that those Substances can by grating and fretting the Glass bring all its least Particles to an accurate Polish, so that all their Surfaces ( hall be truly plane or truly spherical, and look all the fame way, so as toge - ther to compose one even Surface. The smaller indeed the Particles of these Substances are, the smaller will the Scratches be, by which they continually fret and wear away the Glass until it be polished: But be they never so small they can wear away the Glass no otherwise than by grating and scratching it, and breaking off the Protube - rances; and they polish it no otherwise than by bringing its roughness to a very fine Grain, so that the Scratchings upon it become too small to be vi - sable. And then if Light were reflected by im - ringing upon the solid Parts of the Glass, it would be Scattered as much by the most polished Glass as by the rougheft: Wherefore it remains a Pro - blem, how Glass polished by fretting Substances can rested Light so regularly as it doth; and this can ’ t well be solved, unless the Reflexion of the Ray be effeded, not by a Angle Point of the re - sliding Body, but by some Power of the Body which is evenly diffused all over its Surface, and by which it ads upon the Ray without immediate contact, for that the Parts of Bodies do adders Light at a distance, he shews in another Place. ( See Light. ) And if Light be reflected not by im - ringing on the solid Parts of Bodies but by some other Principle, ’ tis probable that these Rays which do impinge on the solid Parts of Bodies, are not / efleCied but Jiified and loft in the Bodies; for other - ? ' wife two Sorts of Reflexions must be allowed. Should all the Rays be reflected which impinge bn the Internal Parts of Water or Chrystal, these Substances would rather have a cloudy, than a transparent Colour. To make Bodies look black t many of the Rays must be stopt, retained and loft in theirs and it seems not probable that any Rays can be stopt and stilled in them, which do not f impinge on their Parts. After this he hews in jj Prop.. ' That Bodies reflect and refract Light by one jj and the fame Power variously exercised in various ) Circumstances as appears from several Confidera - j tions.. Because when Light goes out of Glass j into Air, as obliquely as it can possibly do, if its Incidence be made still more oblique, it becomes ' totally reflected -, for the Power of the Glass after it hath refracted the Light as obliquely as is pos - sable, if the Incidence become still more oblique, becomes too strong to - let any of its Rays go thro ’, and consequently cause a Total Inflexion.. Be - cause Light is alternately reflected and transmitted by thin Plates of Glass for many Succeffions, ac - cording as the Thickness of the Glass increases in Arithmetical Progression j for here the Thickness of the Glass determines whether the Power by which Glass alts upon Light, shall cause it to be reflected, br permit it to be transmitted. And,. Because those Surfaces of Transparent Bodies, which have the g re ate ft refra & ing Power, reflect the greatest Quantity of Light, as was shewn in the first Pro - pofitioii. And in the Latin Edition of hisOpticks towards the End, under the ft Query, he hews that the Cause of Reflexion and Refraction both, is only the Attraction of the Part of the Body acting upon the Rays of Light at a little distance, as they pass out of, or thro ’ the Surface of the Glass. ( See Light. ) For as the Rays pass out of Glass into a Vacuum, they are always inflected towards the Glass; and if they fall on the Vacuum too obliquely, they will return again to the Glass, and be totally reglet ed. Now this Phenomenon can ’ t be attributed to the Resistance of the Vacuum, ( which is nothing ) but mull be attributed to some force in the Glass, which reduces or draws back the Rays after they are gotten out of the Glass into the Vacuum. For if the hinder Surface of the Glass be covered with dear Water, Gil, pellucid and liquid Honey, a Solution of sublimate, &c. Then the Rays which other wife would have reflected, will pass into that Liquor. And this shews plainly that the Rays are not resale & ed, till after they have pass ’ d the hinder Surface of the Glass, or are beginning to go out of it. For if as they are going out, they fall into any of the Liquors above - mentioned, they then go on in the Course they were in before; because the ! Attraction of the Glass is balanced, by the Attra - ction of the Parts of the Liquor. And this appears yet planer, by the Cotnpfefij - on of two Ptifms, or Object Glasses of a long Te - lefcope, together, when one is plain, and the other a little Convex, for then they will neither exactly touch, nor yet be at any considerable distance one from another, as it may be not above the T - s - dr - v ? part of an Inch. For then the Rays which at passing out of the hinder Surface of the first Glass would have been reflected and turn again to it; if the Distance of the Glass had been considerable, will now all readily in that part, pass through the Second Prism or object Glass, just as if there were a hole thro ’ it. See Sir If. Newt. Observ. x.. and th, of Part x. Book. of his Opticks. It hath been discovered by that Excellent Da - nifh Astronomer, Mr. Rpmer j that tho ’ the Moti - on of the Rays of Light coming from us to the Sun be amazingly swiss, yet it is by no means in -. ftantaneous. And the Velocity of that Motion may be thus determined, in the Figure annexed; let the Circle HLfCEFG represent the Earths Annual Orbit, described by its Revolution round the Sun, which suppose placed in A. Let the Point B represent the Planet Jupiter, calling a Shadow backwards towards those Parts which lie behind him in re - sped to the Sun. Let the little Circle D R C de - note the Orbit of any one of the Satellites of Ju - peter, revolving round that Planet placed in Bi And let the Chord G F be in length equal to the Semi - diameter of the Earth ’ s Annual Orbit AE of AH: As let also L be, on the other hand. i All this supposed, ftis plain that these Immerjiohi of Jupiter ’ s Satellites into his Shadow, and those only which happen from their Conjunction to their Opposition with that Planet, can be visible to the Inhabitants of the Earth, vhich live within the Semi - circjp HG F E: And those Emerfions out of his Shadow, and thole only which happen from the Satellites Opposition to their Conjunction with Jupiter again, can be visible to such as live under the Semi - circle HL Spe; Because the Interpolati - on of the Body of Jupiter, hinders both from be - ing visible. ’ Tis apparent also, that an Observer placed in F, if the Motion of Light were instant - neous, would see the Immgrfion of a Satellite into the Shadow at the fame Moment of absolute Time, as another would do if placed in G - and it would be the fame thing on the other side with regard to the Points K, and L: Bur But if the Propagation of Light take up any fen - sable Time, ’ tis plain that the Observers polked in G and L, being nearer to Jupiter by an entire Semi - diameter of the Magnus Orbis, than those in F, and IQ; must needs see the Immerfions and Emer - signs a little sooner than those can do; and from the Space of Time which is proportionable to that Semi - diameter of the Earth ’ s Annual Orbit, may Eftimatiou be inde of the Velocity of the Rays of Light; and so the thing is in Fa k: For when ever the Earth is in that Part of its Orbit which is nearest to Jupiter, the Immerfions of the Satellites into his Shadow do anticipate the mean Time which they should happen in, according to Cal - cubation; as when the Earth is in the opposite Parts of the Orbit, they do really appear later than by Calculation they Ihould do. And so they will appear later to an Observer placed in F, than to one placed in G; and the Emerfions later to one in IQ, than to one in L: As Mr. Romer first found, and is now agreed on by all Aftronoiriers. There was indeed some doubt about this matter started by Cajfini; but our Accurate Mr. Halley Savilian Pro - seizor of Geometry at Oxford, hath cleared up all the Difficulty; and demonstrated that this Pro - greflive Motion of the Rays of Light, to such a Distance, and in such a given Time, is absolutely necessary to account for the Phenomena of the Eclipses of the Satellites of Jupiter. And as to the Time, or with what determinate Velocity the Rays move, Mr. Romer judged that it required about Eleven Minutes of an Hour, for the Light reflected from Jupiter, to move the Length of the Chord F G in the Figure above; or the Distance of the Semi - diameter of the Earths Annual Or - bit: But this, by CaJJims more accurate Observe - tions seems to be much lessened, for according to him it can ’ t be above Min. and Seconds - Sup - pose then it be reckoned at Minutes, which is the Medium between Romer ’ s Eleven, and Caffini s Seven. Then will the Motion of Light be so pro - digious swift, as to move about Eighty Millions of Miles in Minutes: That is Miles in a Minute; and Miles in a Second; and Miles in a half Second, or while you can pronounce One, Two, distinctly. A Motion, tho ’ not instantaneous, as no one can be; yet so wonderfully swift, that the Motion of a Bullet from the Mouth of a Cannon, or ( any such like Velocity of a Body projected, ) is like the creeping of a Snail, the Motion of the Leggs of the Ignavus, or the Imperceptible Pace of the Hand of a Clock, when compared with it; Nay, the Mo - tion of the Earth it self in the Annual Orbit, which yet is pretty swift, ( vi. at the Rate of Englijh Miles in a Second ) is not the Ten Thou - fandth part of the Velocity of the Rays f Light. From which very surprising Proposition, the In - genious Mr. VPhifton deduces these Corollaries. . That the Eclipses of the Sun, Moon, or Sa - tellites of Jupiter, do not happen at the fame Mo - ment of Time, that they appear to us to do. . That the more remote any Planets are from us, the longer will be the Distance between the true and apparent Time of their Eclipses: Thus, tho ’ the Moon ’ s Eclipses will appear to us to be nearly at the fame Time, at which they really happen; yet those of the Sun must appear later, those of the Satellites of Jupiter, later yet and those of Saturn s Satellites, latest of all. . The apparent Places of the Sun, and the Planets in the Heavens, are not their true and real ones at any Time of Observation. . Supposing the Distance of the fixed Stars from us to t e so immensely great, as we have all the Reason ip the World to conclude it to be; and to which the Distance of the Sun from us hardly bears any sensible Proportion; ' tis plain that the Light of the fixed Stars cannot come to us in many Hours, nor in many Days nor Weeks; perhaps, not in some Months Time. So that, as that Ex - cellent Mathematician the Honourable Mr. Franck Roberts, was once in Discourse fuggefting to me if the Author of Nature should please to annihi - late Syrius, or any other fixed Star; it might be Months Time before we should miss him, and find his Place vacant in the Heavens.

reaction.c: REACTION; The Naturalists fay, that Re action is directly contrary and equal to Action, in Bodies. Or the mutual Actions of two Bodies striking one against another are exactly equal, but made with contrary Direckions. Or yet in other words by the Action and Reackion of Bo - dies one on another, there are produced equal Changes in each; and those Changes are impressed towards ( directly ) contrary Parts, er ways. This will be best understood by Instances: For, what - ever Body presses or draws another, is equally, pressed or drawn by it again. If any one press a Stone with his Finger, his Finger is as much pressed by the Stone: If a Horse by a Rope, &c. draw a Stone, the Horse shall equally be drawn by the Stone; for the Rope being stretched both ways endeavours to relax it self again, and by than means will draw the Horse towards the Stone j and will as much hinder the Progression of the Horse, as it forwards the Proceftion of the Stone. If any Body lightning against another doth by its force any way change its Motion; it self will un - ergo the fame Change in its own proper Motion, but towards contrary Parts, from the Readtion of that Body, and the Equality of its mutual Predi - on. By thele Actions are produced equal Chan - ges, not indeed of the Velocities, but of the Moti - ons of Bodies; ( i. e. in such Bodies as have no Impediment any other way ) for the Changes of their Velocities, being made towards: contrary Parts, ( because the Motions are equally changed ) are reciprocally proportional to the Bodies them - gives.

receptacle.c: RECEPTACLE of the Chyle, was known and described by Bartholomeus Euftachius many Years before the Discovery of the Ladeal Veins, vid. Ifcil's Anatomy, p.,. In living Bodies this Receptacle is easily found, but with greater dis - simulty in Inch as are dead - It lies about the de - sending Trunk of the great Artery, between the Celiack ' and Epiulgent Arteries, surrounded by fe - veral Lyrtiphatick Glands, which are called Glan - dule Lumbares, which discharge their Lympha into it. It appears to be only a large Bag formed by the Union of the second Order of Ladeals, and many Lymphaeduds which open into it; it will contain about an Ounce of Water. Sometimes in Brutes as well as in Men, it is divided into two or three Parts, which at last unite into one Dud a - bout the Bigness of a Goose - quill.

refining.c: REFINING is the Art of separating all other Bodies, from Gold and Silver, and this is perform - ed four Ways. The End of Refining is the Separation of all other Bodies from Gold and Silver, which is performed ways, viz, by Parting; by the Test - by the Almond Furnace or the Sweep - and ' by Mercury,. Parting is done with the Aqua - fortis. Some Refiners, to make the Aquafortis, take Saif Peter pound, and Dantftcly ( not En - gl i / h ) Vitriol pound ( for the Engl i / h Vitriol makes a weaker Water, and Dirty Colour ’ d Ver - diter, and wholly spoils it. ) After they are well Bruised and Mixed in a Mortar, they Distill pound of the Materials, put into a Cast - Iron Pot after this manner. ; Build a Furnace Yards high or more j and at the top place in your Iron Pot: To which fit a Head of Earth, like the Head of a large D ilia - tion for Chymical Oyls, which must have a large Belly, branching it self out Inches from the Iron Pot, into Branches; one whereof in the midffe comes directly straight forward, two other Late - ral ones come Obliquely: All which Branches are or Inches hollow in Diameter, and or long. To these Branches are fitted Glass Bodies, Narrow and Hollow at both Ends, Large and Globous in the'Midft. These must be exceeding - ly well Luted on with Colcothar, Rags, Flour and Whites of Eggs. To this first Glass Body is Luted ' on another Glass, of the fame Figure and Size, and in order. alike in all, till they come to the Receiver, which is an Ordinary Gallon Glass. All These Rows of. Glass lie on Boards, ( heaving from the Head to the Receiver, The two Upper Receivers or Glass Bodies need Exceeding good Luting, for the reft Ordinary Lute will serve. The Lute is made of good Lome, feme Horse - dung, and a little Colcothar although the two for - mer do well. A little Fire and that of Newcastle - Coals does the Work. And you need never Break or Vnlute any of the Receivers, but the Lowermost. The Aquafortis being Di filled off, is put into a Ijirge Earthen Pot, and there is added of Fine Sil - ver, one or two Penny weight ( which is called Fi - xes ) to every Pound of Aquafortis, which with - in hours, will purge it from all Dirt and Impu - city, and make it fit for Parting, which is thus done. If their Silver Gilt be Fine enough for Wire, they only Melt it in a Wind Furnace, and Cast ir. Melted, into a large Tub of Water, that they may have it in small Pieces but if it be but Standard, they first Fine it on the left. These small Pieces ' taken from the Water, being well Dryed, are put into a Glass Taper - fafiiion ’ d, a Foot High, and Inches at the Bottom and then the Gla / fes are Charged with Aquafortis about thirds of it,, and, fet in a Range of Iron covered Inches deep with Sand, and a Gentle Charcoal - Fire is made under it. Small Bubbles - will feon arise, and the Water also run over. If so they take off the Gldjfes, and hold them till it doth: Defervefceire, or else pour our feme of ir into a Vessel which is at Hand. If Lead be Mixed With it, they cannot keep it from Running over. Q. Whm i F When the Water hath been one Quieted, from this Ebullition, it will Rife no more. The Greenness of the Water, manifefteth the Quantity of Copper contained in it. If the Water Boil over, twill Penetrate the Bricks and Wood. They commonly let it stand a Night on the Iron - Range, with a gentle Heat under it, and in the Morning softly pour off the Water impregn - ted with all the Silver all the Gold lying like black Dirt at the bottom; which being walhcd out is put into small Parting - glajfies, and fet over i ' tJSand with their Conduit Water for an hour, and then the Water poured off. This is repeated or times, to Separate the Salt from the Gold, which is now fit to be melted, and call into Ingots. To regain the Silver, they have large Round Wajhing Bovols, lined within with melted Rosin and Pitch ( for otherwise the Water would eat the W ood, and penetrate the sides of the Bowl ) co - vered with Copper Plates Inches long, wide, and Half or more thick. Into which Bovols they pour good store of Water ( the more, the better the Verditer ) and then the Silver Water, which working on the softer Metal of Copper, leaves all. the Silver in most fine Sand at the Bottom, and Sides of the Bewl, and Plates of Copper which being taken out, is Walked, Dryed and Melted for any Use. If any Brass or Shroffe Metal be in the Plates, they gather very little of the Silver the Latter mixing with the Silver. With the Copper - water, poured off from the Sil - ver, and Whiting, Verditer, is made thus. They put into a Tub a Hundred Pound weight of Whi - ting, and thereon pour the Copper - water, and stir them together every Day, for some Hours toge - ther. And when the Water grows pale, they take it out, and fet by for farther Ule, and pour on more of the Green Water and so continue till the Verditer be made; which being taken out, is laid on large Pieces of Chalk in the Sun, ’ till it be dry for the Market. The Water mention ’ d to be taken from the Ver - diter, is put into a Copper, and boiled till it comes to the Thickness of Water - Gruel, now principal - ly consisting of Salt - Peter reduced, ( most of the Spirit of Vitriol being gone with the Copper into the Verditer, ) a Dilh full whereof being put into the other Materials, for Aquafortis, is Re - distil - led, and makes a Double - water, almost Twice as good as that without it. . By the Tejl, all Metals are separated from Silver, except Gold, because they swim over it, when they are all melted together. The Tejl is thus made,, They have an Iron Mould, Oval, and two Inches Deep. At the Bot - tom hereof are Arches of Iron, fet at Equal Distances, Fingers wide, if the great Diameter of it be Inches long; and so proportionable in Greater or Lesser Tells. This Cavity they fill with fine Powder of Bone - Ajhes, moistened with Lixivium, made with Soap - Ajhes. Some use Cakes of Pot - Afhcs, or other Ashes well cleansed, and so pressed well together with a Muller, that it be - comes very close and smooth at the Top. There is left above, a Cavity in the Midst of it, to con - tain the melted Silver. This Cavity is made great - test in the Middle; for the Bone - Ashes come up parallel to the Circumference of the Mould; only a small Channel in that End, which is most re - mote from - the Blajl, for the Running off of the Baser Metals, and so is made Dedive to the Cen - ter of the T ' eft, where ’ tis not above half an Inch deep. The Tejl thus made, is fet Annealing Hours v and then ’ tis fet in a Chimney a Yard High, parallel almost to the Nose of a great Pair of ’ Bel - lows; and then therein is put the Silver. Which being covered all over with Billets of Barked Oak., the Blajl begins, and continues all the while strongly. The Lead, purify ’ d from, all Silver, ( which they call the Soap of Metals ) first put in, melts down with the Silver, and then the Lead and Copper swim at the Top, and run over the Tejl. Whose Motion the Refiner helps with a long Rod of Iron drawn along the Surface of the Sil - ver towards the fore - mention ’ d Slit; and often stirring all the Metal, that the Impurer may the better rife; and by continuing this Course, Sea - ration is made in or Hours. The greatest part of the Lead flies away in Smoak, If the Lead be gone before all the Copper, ’ twill rife in small Red - fiery Bubbles; and then they fay the Metal Drives, and must add mor. e Lead. The force of the Blajl drives the Higher Metals to the lower side of the Tejl, and helps its running over. When the Silver is fully Fined, it looks like most pure Quickjiher and then they take off their Sogs and let it Cool. In the Cooling, the Sil - ver will frequently from the Middle, spring up in small Rays, and fall down again. If tnoijl Silver be put into that which is melted, ’ twill spring into the Fire. A good Tejl will serve two or three Firings. So soon as the Silver will hold together, they take it out of the Tejl, and beat it on an Anvil into a round Figure, for the Melting - Pot which being fet in a Wind - Furnace, surrounded with Coal, and covered with an Irmi - Cap that no Char - coal fall into it, is then melted. If any Dross or Filth be in the Melting - Pot, they throw in some Tineal, which gathers the Dross to - gether, that it may be separated from it. These Melting - Pots are never Burned, but only Dryed, and last a whole Day, if they be not dis - fered to Cool; but if they once Cool, they infalli - bly Crack.. . In the Almond - Furnace or sweep, all Ibrts of Metals are separated from Cinders, parts of melting Pots, Tells, Brick, and all other harder Bodies; which must be first beaten into small Pieces with a Hammer on an Iron - Plate. Those which stick but superficially to the Sil - ver, they Wash off thus; they have a Wooden round Instrument Foot wide, somewhat hollow in the Middle, with a Handle on each side. On this ’ they put the Materials, and hold them in a Tub of Water below the Surface, and so waving it to and fro, all the lighter and looser matter is separated from the Metal. The Furnace is feet High, feet Wide, and feet Thick, made of Brick; having a Hole in the Midst, at the Top Inches over, growing Nar - rower towards the Bottom of it, where on the Fore - part, it ends in ' a small Hole, environed with a Semi - circle of Iron, to keep the Molten Metal. About, the Middle of the Back, there is another Hole to receive the Nose of a great Pair of Bel - lows, When When the furnace is Annealed with Charcoal and Hot, they throw two or three Shovels of Coal, to one of the fore - men tion ’ d Stuff, and so pro - ceed during the whole Work, which continues three Days and Nights, without Intermiiiion. Af - ter Eight or Ten Hours the Metal begins to run; and when the Receiver below is pretty full, they lade it out with an Iron - Ladle, and call it into Sows in Cavities, or Forms, made with Ajhes. They frequently Hop the Passage - hole with In - ders to keep in the Heat; and when they think a Quantity of Metal is melted, they Unstop the Hole to pass it off. If the Stuff be hard to Flux, they throw in feme Slag ( which is the decrement of Iron ) to give it Fujion. A thinking blue Smoal proceeds from the Fur - name, and all By - stander put on the Colour of Dead Men. To get the Silver from thole Metals, and to Re - fine their Copper from the Litharge, they now use no other Art than that of the Tejl. . By Quicft - silver the Filings of Gold and Silver are separated from Du ft, &c. This Dujl is put into a Hand - Mill with Quicft - sever, and being conti - nually Turned upon that and the Metals, an Amal - gam a is made of them, and Fair Water poured in, carries off the Dust as it runs out again by a final ! Quill. This Amalgama is put into an Iron, with a Bolt - head fet into the - Fire, having a long Iron Neck, Feet long, to which is fitted a Receiver. The Fire Diftills off the Mercury into the Receiver, and the Gold and Silver remains in the Bolt - head.

reflecteddialling.c: REFLECTED Dialling is the Art of describing Hour - lines, Azimuths, Parallels of Declination, or of Altitude, &c. and all the Furniture of Dials; on such Places as the Suns dired: Rays can never come to directly, but only by the help of some reflecting Surface; as suppose on the Ceiling of a Room, c. w ere the Beams may be reflected by a piece of Looking - glass placed on the Board, Stool or Tranfome of a Window; or other conve - tient place: And this may be done either by a Glass placed Horizontally, or at oblique Angles to the Horizon. . If the Glass be placed Horizontally, you may, by the following Method, upon any Wall or Cei - ling of a Room, where that Glass can reflect a Spot of Light, draw true Flour Lines, Furniture, See. tho ’ the Surface be never so irregular, as convex, - concave, or of any form whatsoever. First, draw on P aft - board or other Material, or get made in Brass an Horizontal Dial for the La - titude proposed. Then by the help of the Azimuth, or at the time when the Sun is in the Meridian; or by knowing the true Hour of Day, whereby may be drawn several Lines on the Ceiling, Floor, and Walls of the Room: so as in respect of the Cen - tre of the Glass they may be in the true Meridian - circle of the World: For if right Lines were ex - tended from the Centre of the laid Glass by any Point, though elevated in any of those Lines so drawn, it would be diredfly in the Meridian - circle of the World. Now all refiedlive Dialling is performed from that Principle in Optixkj, which is, That the Angle of Incidence is equal to the Angle of Reflection. And as any dired Dial may be made by help of a Point found in the direst Axis, so may any reflected Dial be also made by help of any Point found in the reflected Axis. And in regard the reflected Axis for the must part will - fall above the Horizon of the Glass with - out the Window, so that no Point there can be fix - ed, therefore a Point must be found in the said re - fleded Axis continued below the Horizontal of the said Glass, until it touch the Ground or Floor of the Room in l'ome part of the Meridian formerly drawn, which Point will be the Point in the re - versed Axis desired, and may be found, as fob loweth. One End of the Thred, being fixed at or in the; Centre of the said Glass, move the other End thereof in the Meridian formerly drawn below the said Glass, until the said reversed Axis be de - i pressed below the Horizon, as the dired Axis was elevated above the Horizon, which may be done by applying the Side or Edge of a Quadrant to the Thred, and moving the End thereof to and fro in the said Meridian, until the Thred with a Plum - met cut the fame Degree as the Pole is above the Horizontal Glass, and then that Point where the End of the Thred toucheth the Meridian either on the Floor or Wall of the Room; is the Point in the reflected reversed Axis fought for. Now if the reversed Axis cannot be drawn from the Glass by reason of the jetting of the Window or other impediment, that Point in the reverse Axis may be found by a Line parallel thereto, by fixing one End of it on the Glass, and the other End in the Meridian, so as that it may be parallel to the Floor or Wall in which the reversed Axis - point will fall, and find the Axis - point from that other End of the Lath: so if the lame Distance be fet from that Point backward in the Meridian on the Floor, as is the Lath, the Point will be found in the reversed Axis desired. Thus having found a Point in the reflected re - versed Axis; it is not hard, by help whereof and the Horizontal Dial, to draw the reflected Hour - lines on any Ceiling or Wall, be it never so con - cave or convex. To do which: First note, that all straight Lines in any projedion on any Plane, do always reply - sent great Circles in the Sphere, such are all the Hour - lines. Place the Centre of this Horizontal Dial in the Centre of the Glass, the Hour - lines of the said Dial being horizontal, and t & e Meridian of the World, which may be done by Plumb - lines let fall from the Meridian on the Ceiling: Then fix the End of a Thread or Silk in the said Centre of the Dial or Glass, and draw it directly over any Hour - line on the Dial which you intend to draw at the further side of the Room, and there let one hold or fasten that Thread with a small Nail. Then in the Point formerly found on the rever - fed Axis on the Floor, fix another Thread there ( as formerly was done in the Centre of the Dial ) then take that Thread, and make it just touch the Thread ( on the Hour - line of the Horizontal Dial extended ) in any Point thereof, it matters not where - abouts, and mark where the End of that Thread toucheth the Wall or Ceiling, and there make some Mark or Point. Then again move the lame Thread higher or lower at pleasure, ’ till it, as formerly, touch the said fame Hour - thread, and mark again where - abouts on the - Wall or Ceiling, the End of the said Thread also also toucheth. In like manner may be found more Points at pleasure, but any two will be sufficient for the projecting or drawing any Hour - line on any Plane, how irregular soever. For if you move a Thread, and also your Eye to and fro, until you bring the said Thread directly between your Eye and the Points formerly found, you may project thereby as many Points as you please at every An - gle of the Wall or Ceiling, whereby the reflected Hour - line may be exactly drawn. Again, in like manner remove the said Thread fastned in the Centre of the Horizontal Dial, ( which alio is the Centre of the Glass ) on any other Hour - line desired to be drawn, and as be - fore fatten the other End of the Thread, by a smalt Nail, or otherwise at the further Side of the Room, but so that the said Thread may lie just on the Hour - line proposed to be drawn on the Hori - ontal Dial. Then ( as before ) take the Thread fattened in the Point on the reflected Axis, and bring it to touch the Thread of the Hour - line in any part thereof, and mark where the End of that Thread toucheth the said ' Wall or Ceiling: Then again ' as before ) move the said Thread so, as that it only touch the said Thread of the Hour - line in any other part thereof, and also mark where rhe End of that Thread toucheth the said Wall or Ceiling: So is there found two Points on the Wall or Ceiling, being in the reflected Hour - line defi - red, by help of which two Points the whole Hour - line may be drawn; for if ( as before ) a Thread ! be so situated, that it may interpose between the Eye and the said two Points found, you major make ! many Points at pleasure, whereunto the said Thread may also interpose, which for more Con - veniency may be made at every Angle or bending of the Wall or Ceiling, be they never so many: So that if Lines be drawn from Point to point, that said reflected Hour - line will be also exaCtly drawn. In like manner may the Hour - lines be drawn so, that the Reflex or Spot of the Sun from the said Horizontal Glass situated in the said Win - dow ( as before ) shining amongst the said re - selected Hour - lines drawn on the Wall or Cei - ling, will exaCtly Ihew the Hour of the Day de - fired. Now if Lines be drawn round about the said Room, equal to the Horizon of the said Glass, it will slew when the Sun is in or near the Hori - zon. To draw the / Equator and Tropicus on any Wall or Ceiling to any Horizontal reflecting Glass. I. To draw the reflected / Equator orfEquinoBial - line on the Wall or Ceiling, which repreftcnts a great Circle. Take the Thread fixed in the Centre of the Glass, and move the End thereof to and fro in the Meridian - Sine drawn on the Ceiling, until by help of a Quadrant the said Thread be elevated equal to the Complement of the Latitude, ( which will be always perpendicular to the reversed Axis ) making in the Meridian where the end of that Thread falls, then on that Point and the said Me - ridian, line on the Ceiling ered a perpendicular Line, which Line may be continued on any Plane whatsoever, and is the reflected Equinoctial - line desired. R E F Note that all great Circles are right Lines, an & are always drawn or projected from a right Line. l. To draw the Tropicks. Note, that all Parallels of Declination are lesser Circles, and are Comely Se - ctions. First, make or take out of some Book a Table of the Sun ’ s Altitude for each Hour of the Day, calculated for the Place of the Latitude proposed when the Sun is in either of the Tropicks. Then take the Thread fixed in the Centre of the Glass, and by applying one Side of a Quadrant to the said Thread, and moving one End of it to and fro in the Hour - line proposed, elevate the said Thread answerable to the Suns height in that Hour, when he is in that Tropick you desire to draw, and mark where the End of that Thread lo elevated toucheth in that Hour - line proposed. So may you in like manner find a several Point in each Hour - line for the Suns height in that Tropick, whereby a Line may be drawn on the Wail or Ceiling from Point to point formerly made in the said Hour - lines, which the Tropick desired. In like manner may any Parallel of Declination be drawn: If there be first calculated a Table of the Sun ’ s Altitude at all Hours of the Day, when the Sun hath any Declination proposed, whereby may be cirawn either the Parallels of the Sun s place, or the Parallels of the Length of the Day. To draw the Parallels of Declination to any re fie Bed Glass most easily, by help of a Trigon first made on P aft - board or other Material. Fix the Trigon to the reflected reversed Axis ? so that the Centre of the Trigon may be in the. Centre of the Glass, then will the Equinoctial on the Trigon be perpendicular to the said Axis Then take the Thread fixed in the Centre of the Glass, and lay it along either of the Tropicks, or other Parallels of Declination required, which is drawn on the said Trigon, which Thread must be continued so, that the End thereof may touch any Hour - line, and on that Hour - line mark the Point of Touch, the Thread being still laid on the fame Parallel of Declination on the Trigon: In the fame manner find a Point in each Hour - line. Lastly, draw a Line by those Points so found, which will be the Tropick - line or other Parallel of Declina - tion, as the Thread was laid on, on the Trigon. To draw the Azimuth - lines on any Wall or Cei - ling to any Horizontal refleBing Glass. Notes that all Azimuths are great Circles. In which Point fatten one End of a Thread, which Thread will be of great use in drawing the re - sledded Hour - lines on any Wall or Ceiling whatfo - ever. Now if this Thread, whose End is fatten - ed, in a Point on the reflected reversed Axis, be talcen and brought to touch any part of any one of the Threads of the Hour - lines ( produced to and fattened in the reflected Horizon ) the said Thread being Continued so, as the End thereof may touch the Wall or Ceiling, and also any parr of the said Thread touch the Hour - line or Thread proposed; that Point on the Wall of Ceiling is in the reflected Hour - line desired to be drawn: Also the other Point in the fame reflected Hour - line may be found; if the said Thread, whose End is fa - ttened in, the reflected Axis, be brought to touch fofoe other part of the lame Hour - thread prop - fed; so that when ( as before ) the End of the said Thread toucheth the Waft or Ceiling, some part of that Thread may also touch the Hour - line desired, which Point or Touch oh the Wall or Ceiling, is also another Point in the said reflected Hour - line desired. Water hath a refractive Power in a middle De - gree between those two Sorts of Substances, and probably is of a middle Nature; for out of it ! grow all vegetable and animal Sublfances, which consist as well of sulphureous, fat and inflammable Parts, as of earthy, lean, and alkalizate Ones. Salts and Vitriols have refractive Powers in a middle Degree between those of earthy Subftan - ces and Water; and accordingly ar t compofedof those two Sorts of Substances; for by Diftillatiori and Rectification of their Spirits, Spirits of Wine have a refractive Power in a middle Degree between those of Water and oily Substances; and accordingly seems to be compo - fed of both, united by Fermentation: The Water by means of some Saline Spirits with which it is impregnated, dissolving the Oil, and volatilizing it by the Ablion; for Spirit of Wine is inflammable by means of its oily Parts; and being distilled of - ten from Salt of Tartar, grows by every Diftilla - tion more and more aqueous and flegmatick. So that it seems rational to attribute the Refra - active Power of all Bodies chiefly, if not wholly, to the sulphureous Parts with which they abound: For it ’ s probable that all Bodies abound more or less with Sulphurs. And as Light congregated by a Burning - glass, rests most upon sulphurous Bodies, to turn them into Fire and Flame; so, since all A & ion is mutual, Sulpnurs ought to aeft most upon Light: And that the Action between Light and Bodies is mutual, appears from hence, that the denfeft Bodies which refraeft and refledf Light most strongly, grow hot - ted in the Summer Sun, by the A & ion of the refracted or reflected Light. That having demonstrated in his Princi - pia; that if Refraction were caused by the At - traction of the Rays of Light; the Sine of the Angle of Incidence must be to That of the res railed Angle always in a given Ratio and this being by repeated Experience found to be true in Fact: ’ tis then plain that Attraction is the Cause of the Rays of Light.

refrangibility.c: REFRANGIBILITY of the Rays of Light, Sir jf Newton defines to be their Disposition to be re - fracted, or turned cut of their way, in passing out of one Transparent Body or Medium into ano - ther; and a greater or less Refrangibility of Rays ' Is their Disposition to be turned more or less out of their way ( in Obfervat. of his Opticks ) in like Incidences on the fame Medium. He ( hews also that there is constant Relation between Colours and Refrangibility: The most refrangible Rays being of a violet Colour; the lead refrangible Red; and those of intermediate Co - lours, having proportionably intermediate Degrees of Refrangibility.

H.. cap.. was one, of those Exactions mentioned in that Statute to be claimed heretofore by the Pope in England; and seems to signifie a Bull or Breve, for re - enabling a spiritual Person to exercise his Fundion, that was formerly disabled. RE - INFORMED Ring of a Cannon, is that which is next after the Trunnions, between them and the Vent, and the Re - informed part of a Gun, is from the Base Ring to the Re - informed Ring, This part is made thicker in Metal than any other part of the Piece.

relation.c: RELATION in the Law - sense is the fame as Fi & io Juris, to make a Nullity of a thing from the beginning ( for a certain Intent ) which had Essence, Vide Co. Lib.. sol.. Butler and Bakers Case; but more plainly thus: Relation is where, in con - sideration of Law, two Times, or other things are considered so, as if they were all one; and by this the thing subsequent is laid to take its Effed by Relation, at the Time f rence ding. As if A de - liver a Writing to B, to be delivered to C, as the Deed of A, when C has paid a Summ of Money. Here when the Money is paid, and the Writing delivered; this ( hall be taken as the Deed of A, at the Time when it was first delivered. And so Bills of Parliament, to which the Queen a ( Tents on on the laji Day of Parliament ( hall Relate, and be of Force from the firji Day of the Session.

reliefrelevamen.c: RELIEF, Relevamen, ( in Doomsday Relevant ), Re lev ium ) was a certain Summ of Money, which the Tenant holding by Knights - Service, Grand - Sergeanty, or other Tenure, for which Homage or Regal Service is due; or by Soccage, for which no Homage is duely paid to his Lord at his Entrance, Mag. Cart. c.. and, E.. Scat. i. Skene de Verbor. faith Relief was given by the e - nant or Vassal that was of perfect Age, after the expiring of his Wardship, to the Superior Lord, of whom he held his Lands in Knight - Service: That is by Ward and Relief - for by payment thereof he Relieves, and as it were relevant, rai - set up again his Lands after they were funk into his Superiors Hand, by Reason of Wardship, &c. reliefrelevium.c: RELIEF, Relevium, was a Fine formerly paid to the King by every one that came to the Inhe - ritance of Land held in Capite, or Military Ser - vice, to Relieve, or as it were to redeem their E - state, and to hold Pofleflion of it. At first it con - sided in Horses and Arms, till by the Assise of Arms in Henry. every Man ’ s Armour was preserved for his Heir, and the Relief payable in Money, of which the fixt Rates were determin - ned by Magna Charta.

reliefs.c: RELIEFS were payable also not only to the King as Supreme Lord, but to all Barons and Knights by those Tenants who held under them by Military Service. Relevare was the word for paying such Relief, and for obtaining by that means PolTeilion of such Estate, Some Cuftoinary and Servile Tenants paid a Relief for renewing of a Tenure, on the Death of the last Possessor. Rennets Paroch. Antiquit.

repulseorreaction.c: REPULSE or Reaction, it is one of the Laws of Nature, ( Sir If. Newtons third ) that Pppulfe or Reaction is always equal to Impulse or Adiorn That is, the Adion of two Bodies one upon an - other, is always equal, but with a contrary Dire - dion in other words; the fame Force with which one Body strikes upon another, is returned back by that other on it, and the Forces are impfefled with Diredions directly contrary. Thus if one Body press or draw another, ’ tis just as much prest or drawn by it: If a Man press a Stone with his Hand, the Stone equally presses his Hand - if a Horse draw forward any Weight by a Rope, the Weight equally draws back the Horse. For the Rope being equally stretch ’ d both ways, ad upon both equally: So ’ tis in all Blows and Strokes, the thing ft ruck ( suppose with a Hammer ) strikes the Hammer with equal Force. The Iron draws the Load - stone as much as the Load - stone draws it; as will appear, by Experiment if you make them both flote in Water. Thus also in the Descent of heavy Bodies the Stone attrads the Earth, as much as the Earth the Stone; or the Earth gravitates as much towards the Stone, as it doth towards the Earth. For the Motions produced by both these Gravitations are equal in both: Only the Stone be - ing very inconsiderable in rested of the Bulk of the Earth, the Velocity bf the Earch towards, the Stone must be so too, and confequCnrly insensible, in comparifonof the Motion of the Stone towards it. And so it is llniverfally, in all the Adions of Bodies: For if one Body ad on another and change its Motion any manner of way, that other Body will make the fame Change in the Motion of this Body, but with a Contrary Direction: So that by these. Adions there are made equal Chan - ges, not of the Velocities but of the Motion: For

Prerog,. fee Resumption. RE ISTENCE of a Fluid Medium. The in - comparable - Sir If Newton at the End of the Lat. Edit, of his Opticks, Qu., faith that the Rest - stance of Fluid Mediums arises partly from the At. tuition of the Parts of the Medium; and partly, from the Vis Inertia Materia, or Inactivity ofMat - ter. And supposing a Body to be perfectly she - rical, the Resistence arising from the Former of these two, or from the Attrition of the Parts of the Medium, is as the Rectangle under the Diameter, and the Velocity with which the Body moves. But the Reliftence arising from the Vis Inertia, is, as the Square of that Product. And by this dis - ference may the two Kinds of Reliftence in all Me - diums be distinguished: And line the Kinds are rhus distinct, it will appear that the Reliftence of Bodies which are of a proper Magnitude and Ve - locity, whether ’ they move in Air, Water, Quick - Ever, or in any other Fluid, will almost all arise from the Vis Inertia of the Parts, of the. Fluid. For that Part of the Reliftence of any Medium which arises from Friction, Attrition, or Tenaci - ty of the Particles of the Fluid, may be diminish - ed, by supposing the matter to be divided into smaller Particles, and those also to be rendred more smooth and slippery. But that Part which arises from the Vis Inertia answers in Proportion to the Density of the Matter, and can neither be dimi - nilhed by dividing the Matter into smaller Parti - cles, nor by any other Means, than by the Dimi - nution of the Density it self. Whence it is, that Density of Fluid Mediums becomes very nearly proportionable to the Resistence. For those Liquors. which differ insensibly as to Density, as Water, Spirit of Wine, Oil of Tur - pontine, warm Oil of Olives, and such like, have very little difference also as to the Force of Reli - stance. Water being or Times lighter, and consequently rare than Quick - silver, hath its Re - fiftence less than that of Mercury in the fame Pro - portion as he tried by the Experiment of Pendu - lums swimming in those two Fluids. The common Air such as we usually breath in, is about or hundred Times lighter, and rare than Water, and he found the Reliftence Air to be less in that Ratio, by the fame Kind of Trials. And in a thinner and rare Air, the Reliftence must ft ill be less; till at last in the Thoughts of all, it will grow insensible. A Feather in the exha lifted Receiver Aefce nils with equal Celerity as a Stone or a Piece of Lead, tho ’ in the open Air it find a very great Resilience to its Descent.: And by all the Experiments he could make he found the Resistence of all Fluid Mediums to depend only on their Density, and a little on their Tenacity; But there must needs be another Sort of Resistence, if the Pores of all F uids were filled with another, yet more Subtile Matter or Fluid. Now if the Resistence in the Exhausted Receiver of the Air - Pump, Ihould be only a too Times less than in the common Air, it would be a Million of Times less than that of Quick - silver: But it is certainly much less than that, and much less yet in the Celestial ! Spaces or Regions at or Miles in height above our Earth. For the Honourable Mr. Boyle hath shewn that Air may be rarified in Glass - Vessels to above Times its natural State, and the Celestial Regions must be much more empty of Air, than any Space which we can here evacuate by an Air - Pump: Because since our Air is here compressed by the weight of the Incumbent Atmosphere, and its Density proportionable to that compressing Power; it will follow by Calculation, that the Air at Miles above the Earth ’ s Surface will be Times as rare, as here; at theDiftance of Miles Times as rare and so on in the fame Ratio: So that at the Distance of Miles from the Earth, the Air will be, -. or Millions of Millions of Millions of Times thinner or rare than ’ tis here. We find that Heat conduces much towards the Fluidity of many Bodies, by diminishing their Tenacity; for it renders many Bodies. ( as all Metals and some Minerals ) Fluid, which are - not naturally so; and it increases the Fluidity of Te - nacious Liquors, such as Oil, Balfams, Honey, and by that Means diminifties the Power of their Resistence. And yet it doth not much diminifli the Resistence of Water; which it must certainly do, if any considerable Degree of the Resistence ois that Fluid arose from the Attrition or Tenacity of its Particles. And therefore we may fairly con - crude that the Resistence of Water arises chiefly from the Vis Inertia of its Matter. And conse - quently, if the Celestial Regions or Spaces, were equally dense with Water, they could not have & much less Resistence than it: If they were as dense as Quick - silver, they would have a Rest - stance near as great as that: And if they were perfectly and completely dense, or full of Matter without any Pores or Vacuities at all interspersed, they would have a much greater Resistence than Qiiiek - silver A Globe perfectly solid, in such a ' Medium would lose above half of its Motion, before it could move of its own Diameters in length. And a Globe not perfectly solid, such as are those of the Planets, would be stopt much sooner. Where - fore there is a Necessity of supposing that the Re - gions where the Planets and Comets move should be devoid of all matter: Except perhaps some very thin and fine Vapours and Exhalations, or Effluvia which may arise from the Atmosphere of the Earth of the Planets and Comets. That Fictitious Sub tile Matter therefore with which some have filled the Heavens, is by no means useful for the Solu - tion of the Phanomena of Nature; since the Mo - tions of the Planets and Comets may be much better explained without by the Laws of Gravity j and Gravity it feif hath never yet been well ac - counted for by that Subtile Matter. In Reality, that Subtile Matter, can only serve to obftrud and disturb the Morions of the Heavenly Bodies, and if there were any such thing would destroy and overt to withe Course and Order of Nature. And if you suppose it interspersed also within the hidden Pores an & Meatus of Bodies, it will do no - " ' thing ES thing there but flop and obstruct the Vibrating Mo - tions of the Particles of Matter, in which their Heat and all their Energy and Active Power con - lifts. And as it is of no use but to do mischief, so there are no good Reasons at all to enduce us to believe the Existence of any luch thing, as a Mate - ria Subtilis in their Sente.

resistance.c: RESISTANCE of the Air to the Motion of Projects; In Phil. i rays. N.. There is theme - lure of this given very largely - and accurately by Dr. Wallis; He lays down at first this Lemma. That the resistance of Bodies is proportional to their Celerity; and then branches out into all the parti - cular Varieties that can well be imagined, and at last computing different Mediums one with an - other, he concludes their different Reliftances to be as their Specifick Gravities, obstructed from the Viscidity of the Particles of some Fluids: And also that the Specifically Heavier Project once in motion ( being equally swift with another that is lighter, &c. ) will move through the fame Medium more strongly in proportion to its greater In - tensive or Specifick Gravity, In the Able Eruditormn Lipfice for July, Mr. G. G. Leibnit proposes feme New Dcmonftra - tions about the Refiftances of Solid Bodies; which are very Geometrical and Curious. And in the Leipfick. A ls for January. He reduces his Thoughts on this Subject into a Dis - serration. Entitled, A Discourse concerning the Resistance of Mediums, and theMotionof Projects in refilling Mediums. As to the Geometrical Confederations of the Rest - ance of Bodies of different Figures in one and the fame Medium: Mr. James Bernouli in the Able Lipfice for May. gives these Rules. . If an Ifoceles Triangle be moved in the Fluid according to the Direction of a Line which is Normal to its Base; First with the Vertex fore - most, and then with its Base; the Refiftances will be of the Leggs, and as the Square of the Base, and as the Summ of the Leggs. . The Resistance of a Square moved according to the Direction of its Side, and of its Diagonal, is as the Diagonal to the Side. . The JRefiftance of a Circular Segment ( less than a Semi - circle ) carried in a Direction perpen - dicular to its Basis, when it goes with the Base foremost, and when with its Vertex foremost ( the fame Direction and Celerity continuing, which is all along supposed ) is as the Square of the Dia - meter, to the fame less f of the Square of the Bale of the Segment. Cor. Hence the Refiftances of a Semi - circle, when its Base, and when its Vertex goes foremost, are to One another in a Sefquialte - ral patio. . A Parabola moving in the Direction of its Axis, with its Basis, and then its Vertex foremost, hath its Refiftances, as the Tangent to an Arch of a Circle whose Diameter is equal to the Parame - ter, and the Tangent equal to half the Basis of the Parabola. . The Refiftances of an Hyperbola, oraSemi - Ellipsis; when the Base and when the Vertex goes foremost, may be thus computed: Let it be, as the Summ ( or Difference of the Transverse Vol. II. Axis, and Latus Eptlutn is to the Transverse Axis if So is the Square of the Latus P cclum, to the Square of the Diameter of a certain Circle, in which Circle apply a Tangent equal to half the Basis of the Hyperbola or Ellipsis. Then fay a - gain, as the Summ and Difference of the Axis and Parameter, is to the Parameter; so is the amoret - said Tangent to another Right - line. And further, as the Summ ( or Difference ) of the Axis and Parameter, is to the Axis:: So is the circular Ark corresponding to the aforesaid Tangent, to ano - ther Arch. This done, the Refiftances will be as the Tangent to the Summ ( oi Difference ) of the Right - line thus found, and that Ark last menti - oned. . In General, the Refiftances of any Figure whatsoever going now with its Bale foremost, and then with its Vertex, are as the Figures of the Ba - sis to the Summ of all the Cubes of the Element a of the Basis divided by the Squares of the Elcmen - ta of the Curve - line. All which Rules he thinks may be of Use in the Fabrick or Conftnfolion of Ships, and in perfect - ing the Art of Navigation universally. retraxit.c: RETRAXIT, in the Law, ( lo called from be - ing the Effectual Word in the Entry, ) is where the Plaintiff or Defendant comes into Court, and declares he hath with - drawn his Suit, and will pro - ceed no further; and this is a Bar of all other ACtions of a like or inferior Nature. I he Diffe - rence between a Retraxit and a Non - suit, is that the former supposes the Plaintiff or Defendant to be ' actually present in Court; whereas a Non - suit is upon a Demand made, when he should appear, and he makes default. A Rptraxit also is a Bar, but not a Non - suit; for then he may commence a New Action of the like Nature.

rome.c: ROME - So ? was formerly here an Annual Tri - but of a Penny for every Family, and paid to Rome at the Feast of St. Peter ad Vincula, being the First of August. Cambden tells us it was first granted by Ossa; but others attribute its Original to In a. King of the Weft Saxons; vho being in Pilgrimage at Rome, A. D., gave it as an - Alms. It amounted to three hundred Marks and one Noble yearly. Of this Mark of Slavery to Rome, our Ancestors fre - quently complained as a Burden and Scandal to the English Nation ’ It was first forbidden to be paid by Ed.. Tho before complained of in Parliament as a Grievance in K. Johns Time, A. D.. This Payment was abrogated. H... But servilely restored again and. Phil, and Mary; and at last utterly abolished, I Eli..

rootsofplants.c: ROOTS of Plants are, either . Fibrous, which fend out only small Strings from the Bottom of the Plant, distend from each other. . MorfThick. or Gross, which have a Body thick and gross, either branched out into Subdivi - signs or Arms; or else fending out Fibres from it ail along. These last are either Carnous, which are either ft. Broad and Swelling. v.. Long and Slender, which commonly are more hard and woody. rhe Broad and Swelling are ri. Bulbous, which consist but of one Globe or Head, and fend out Fibres from the Bottom, and are either f Squammofc, oh Scaly, as Lilies or Mar J talon. Coated, which are involved in S kins or Coats, as Cepa, Hyacinthus, Allium, See. . Tuberous, which are of a carnous, solid, and like - continued Consistence j and these ei - ther Simple, with but one Globe or Head, as Rapa, Crocus, &c. .. Many fold, as Afphodelus, Pabnia, &c. JLong Roots are either . Sarmentous ( i. e. ) Twiggy or Branching which ftioot or creep out transverse, or in breadth: Of these some are Geniculate, Kjiotty, or Joynty, as Couch - Grass, Mints, ( &c . Cduliformes ( i. e. ) Stemmy or Stalky, which hoot down deep directly; though often hooting out Fibres and Strings from the great Stem; which also it self is some - times divided or branching.

roundness.c: ROUNDNESS, The round Globular or She - rical Form, which Pebbles, Fruits, Berries, ( c. are adorned with and which Drops of Water or Quick - silver, ( c. Bubbles of Air under Water or some such Liquor, melted Oil, ( c. do generally put on, seems to arise from the Incongruity of their Particles, with those of the ambient Fluid; which prevents them from coalescing together, and by priding upon them, and environing them all round equally, turns them into a round Form. This seems plain, as Dr. Hocl hath long ago well observed from the way of making small round Shot of several Sizes, without carting the Lead into any Molds, from Drops of Rain being for - med in their falling into round Hail - stones; and from a Drop of Water falling upon small Sand, or Dust, which will strait produce an Artificial round Stone: And from the small round red - hot Balls ( easily seen with a Microscope ) which are formed by the Ccllifion and Fusion of the Flint and Steel in striking Fire, and perhaps the Principle of Gra - vitiation, if principally concerned in this Matter.

rounds.c: ROUNDS, in a Garrison, is a Night - Watch commanded by an Officer that goes round the Rampart of the Garrilon, in order to listen if any thing be stirring without the Works, to fee that the Sentries are watchful, and upon Duty, and that all things be in good Order. In strict Gar - grisons, the Rounds go every quarter of an Hour, that the Rampart may be still furniffied. The Centries ought to challenge at a Distance; and to reft their Arms as the Rounds pass, and to let no one come near them. When the Round is near the Corps de garde, the Centre calls aloud, Who comes there ? And when the Answer is The Round, he says. Stand; and then galls for the Corporal of the Guard, who draws his Sword, and calls also, Who comes there ? And when ’ tis answered The Rounds; jie that hath the Word must advance, and deliver the Word to the Corporal who receives it with his Sword pointed at the Givers Breath.
